If grace cannot be resisted, then the human response to God is not truly free, and love — which must be freely given — is impossible.

Perseverance of the Saints vs. Conditional Perseverance

The final point concerns the question of whether a genuinely saved person can lose their salvation. Calvinism teaches the perseverance of the saints: those whom God has elected, called, and justified will persevere in faith until the end. They may stumble, they may sin grievously, they may experience seasons of doubt and spiritual dryness, but they will not finally and permanently fall away. This is not because of the strength of their faith but because of the faithfulness of God, who finishes what he starts.

Classical Arminianism is more cautious on this point than is commonly recognized. Arminius himself was reluctant to make a definitive statement, saying that the question required further study. His followers, the Remonstrants, eventually taught that genuine believers can, through persistent and unrepentant sin, finally and irrevocably fall from grace. This is not the popular caricature of "losing your salvation" over a single sin. It is the teaching that a sustained, willful, unrepentant rejection of Christ constitutes a real apostasy from which there may be no return.

Where Both Sides Agree

The agreements between Calvinism and Arminianism are more substantial than the popular debate suggests. Both affirm that salvation is entirely a work of God's grace. Both deny that human beings can save themselves. Both affirm the necessity of faith in Christ. Both affirm the authority of Scripture. Both affirm the reality of human sin and the need for divine redemption. Both affirm that God is sovereign over creation and history. Both affirm the final judgment and the reality of heaven and hell.

The disagreement is, at bottom, about two attributes of God that are both biblical and that exist in tension: God's sovereignty and God's justice. Calvinism emphasizes sovereignty — God's absolute right to dispose of his creation as he sees fit. Arminianism emphasizes justice — God's commitment to deal fairly with the creatures he has made. Both are biblical emphases. The question is which one has hermeneutical priority — which one serves as the lens through which the other is interpreted.

The Molinism Middle Ground

A third option, increasingly popular in philosophical theology, is Molinism — named after the sixteenth-century Jesuit theologian Luis de Molina. Molinism attempts to affirm both divine sovereignty and genuine human freedom through the concept of middle knowledge (scientia media): God knows not only what will happen and what could happen, but what would happen under every possible set of circumstances. Before creating the world, God knew what every possible creature would freely do in every possible situation, and he used this knowledge to select the actual world — the set of circumstances in which his sovereign purposes would be accomplished through the genuinely free decisions of his creatures.

Molinism appeals to those who find Calvinism's account of human freedom inadequate and Arminianism's account of divine sovereignty insufficient. It allows one to say that God is truly sovereign over the outcome of history — nothing happens that he has not decreed — while also maintaining that human beings make genuinely free choices that are not determined by divine causation. The philosophical price is the concept of middle knowledge itself, which both Calvinists and many Arminians find problematic: Calvinists because it makes God's decree dependent on creaturely decisions (even hypothetical ones), and Arminians because it seems to smuggle determinism back in through the backdoor of divine world-selection.

Why the Debate Still Matters

This is not a debate for professional theologians alone. It shapes how ordinary Christians read Scripture, how they pray, how they evangelize, and how they understand suffering. The Calvinist who believes that God sovereignly controls all things has a framework for enduring suffering that the Arminian may lack: the assurance that nothing — not even this — is outside God's sovereign plan. The Arminian who believes that God genuinely desires the salvation of all people has a motivation for evangelism that the Calvinist may struggle to articulate: the conviction that every person they encounter is a genuine object of God's saving love, not a potential reprobate for whom Christ did not die.

The debate matters for pastoral care. When a church member loses a child, does the pastor say, "God ordained this for his glory" (a Calvinist emphasis), or "God weeps with you and did not will this evil" (an Arminian emphasis)? Both answers have biblical support. Both have pastoral dangers. The Calvinist answer risks making God monstrous. The Arminian answer risks making God impotent. The pastoral task is to hold both truths — God is sovereign, and God is grieved by evil — without resolving the tension prematurely.

The wisest Christians in both traditions have always recognized that the mystery of God's sovereignty and human freedom exceeds the capacity of any theological system to fully capture it. Calvin himself acknowledged the mystery with uncharacteristic humility: "The will of God is the supreme and first cause of all things, because nothing happens except by his command or permission." Arminius, for his part, insisted that he had no desire to diminish the sovereignty of God, only to preserve the justice of God in condemning those who reject the gospel. Both were trying to be faithful to Scripture. Both were aware that they were pressing against the limits of human comprehension. The debate between them is not a problem to be solved but a tension to be inhabited — with humility, with charity, and with the recognition that the God they are arguing about is larger than either system can contain.
excerpt: The oldest and most consequential debate in Protestant theology is also the most misunderstood. What Calvin and Arminius actually taught, and why the argument still matters.

title: Liturgical vs. Contemporary Worship: What We Gained and What We Lost
body:
Every Sunday, across tens of thousands of churches, two fundamentally different visions of Christian worship are enacted, often without their participants understanding the assumptions behind either one. In one church, a congregation stands and sits and kneels in choreographed rhythm, following a printed order of service that includes a call to worship, a confession of sin, a declaration of pardon, the reading of three Scripture lessons, a sermon tied to the lectionary, the recitation of the Nicene Creed, the celebration of the Eucharist, and a benediction. In the church down the road, a worship band opens with twenty minutes of singing, the congregation remains standing with hands raised, the pastor delivers a forty-five-minute topical sermon with video clips and personal stories, an altar call is given, and the service ends with a closing song.

Both of these are Christian worship. Both involve the reading of Scripture, prayer, singing, and preaching. But they are built on different foundations, shaped by different histories, and — most importantly — they form different kinds of Christians. The question of liturgical versus contemporary worship is not, at bottom, a question of preference. It is a question of formation: What is worship for, and what does it do to us over time?

What Liturgy Actually Means

The word "liturgy" comes from the Greek leitourgia, which means "the work of the people." In ancient Athens, a liturgy was a public work performed by a wealthy citizen for the benefit of the community — funding a warship or sponsoring a festival. The early church adopted the term for its public worship, and the etymology is revealing: liturgy is not something performed by clergy for a passive audience. It is the common work of the gathered community, in which every person participates.

In its Christian usage, liturgy refers to a structured, repeating pattern of worship that follows a set order — an ordo — rooted in the practice of the early church. The basic shape of this pattern is remarkably consistent across traditions that practice liturgical worship (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, and many Reformed and Methodist churches): gathering (the community assembles and is called to worship), word (Scripture is read and preached), table (the Eucharist is celebrated), and sending (the community is dismissed to serve in the world).

This fourfold pattern is not arbitrary. It can be traced to the worship of the second-century church, described in Justin Martyr's First Apology (c. 155 AD): "On the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things. Then we all rise together and pray." Justin goes on to describe the celebration of the Eucharist, with bread and wine consecrated by prayer and distributed to all present.

The liturgical tradition holds that this pattern — word and table, together, every week — is not merely one option among many but the normative pattern of Christian worship, established by the apostolic church and maintained across the centuries. Departure from this pattern is not innovation; it is impoverishment.

The Rise of Contemporary Worship

The contemporary worship movement did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a response to genuine problems in the liturgical tradition as practiced in mid-twentieth-century American Protestantism. Mainline churches in the 1950s and 1960s were, in many cases, liturgically correct but spiritually moribund — going through the motions of worship without passion, conviction, or connection to the lives of ordinary people. The language of the liturgy was archaic, the music was inaccessible, the preaching was cerebral and detached, and the overall atmosphere was formal, reserved, and unwelcoming to outsiders.

The contemporary worship movement sought to address these failures by making worship accessible, emotionally engaging, and culturally relevant. Its roots are multiple: the Jesus Movement of the 1970s, which brought folk and rock music into worship; the Vineyard movement of the 1980s, which developed the "worship set" format of extended, emotionally building musical worship; the seeker-sensitive movement of the 1990s, pioneered by Willow Creek Community Church, which redesigned worship to remove barriers for unchurched visitors; and the global influence of Hillsong Church, which produced a stream of worship songs that became the de facto hymnody of evangelical Christianity worldwide.

What the contemporary movement gained was substantial. It made church accessible to millions of people who would never have crossed the threshold of a traditional church. It recovered the emotional dimension of worship — the sense that worship should involve the whole person, not just the intellect. It demonstrated that the gospel could be communicated in the cultural language of the present, not just the cultural language of the sixteenth or seventeenth century. It created a participatory atmosphere in which people felt free to express their devotion physically — through raised hands, through tears, through spontaneous prayer.

What the Contemporary Movement Lost

But the gains came at a cost, and the cost has become increasingly visible as the contemporary movement has matured. Several losses deserve attention.

The first is depth of content. The hymns of the liturgical tradition — "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," "O Sacred Head Now Wounded," "Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing" — are dense with theological content, drawing on centuries of doctrinal reflection. The average contemporary worship song is built on a much narrower theological range: God's love, God's greatness, the worshipper's response of praise. Studies of the most popular contemporary worship songs have found that they overwhelmingly focus on the subjective experience of the worshipper ("I will praise you," "You are good to me") rather than on the objective acts of God in history (creation, incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection, ascension, coming judgment). The effect, over time, is a congregation that knows how it feels about God but is less clear about who God is and what God has done.

The second loss is continuity with the historic church. When a congregation recites the Nicene Creed, it is saying the same words that Christians have said since 381 AD. When it follows the lectionary, it is reading the same passages that Christians around the world are reading on the same day. When it observes the church calendar — Advent, Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Pentecost — it is living inside a narrative structure that shapes the entire year around the story of Christ. The contemporary worship movement, by and large, abandoned these connections. Most non-denominational churches do not follow a lectionary, do not observe the church calendar (beyond Christmas and Easter), do not recite the creeds, and do not celebrate the Eucharist weekly. The result is a form of worship that is cut off from the church's memory — a perpetual present tense with no sense of the centuries of faith that preceded it.

The third loss is silence. Liturgical worship includes structured moments of silence — after the Scripture readings, after the sermon, during the Eucharist — that create space for reflection, confession, and interior prayer. Contemporary worship tends to fill every moment with sound: the worship band plays continuously, the transitions are seamless, and the emotional arc of the service is carefully managed. The absence of silence is not accidental; it reflects a culture that is uncomfortable with stillness and a theology that associates God's presence with emotional intensity rather than with the "still small voice" of 1 Kings 19.

The fourth loss is corporate identity. Liturgical worship is, by design, communal. The congregation speaks together, sings together, confesses together, receives communion together. The individual is absorbed into the body. Contemporary worship, despite its communal setting, can be a surprisingly individualistic experience — a room full of people having private emotional encounters with God, mediated by music and lighting designed to create a particular mood. The shift from hymnals to projected lyrics is emblematic: the hymnal was a shared text that connected the congregation to each other and to a tradition; the projected lyric, appearing and disappearing on a screen, connects the individual to a momentary experience.

The Worship Wars

The so-called "worship wars" of the 1990s and 2000s — the bitter conflicts within congregations over music style, instrumentation, and worship format — were never really about music. They were about two competing visions of what the church is and what worship is for. The liturgical vision holds that worship is the church's participation in the eternal worship of God — an objective reality that exists whether or not the worshippers feel anything. The contemporary vision holds that worship is the church's response to God's presence — an experience that should be felt, expressed, and emotionally authentic.

Both visions have biblical warrant. The Psalms include both liturgical instruction ("Lift up your heads, O gates") and emotional expression ("My soul thirsts for you"). The worship of Revelation is both highly liturgical (structured around hymns, acclamations, and ritual actions) and overwhelmingly experiential (the worshippers fall on their faces, cry out, and are consumed by the glory of God). The early church practiced both form and freedom, structure and spontaneity.

The worship wars were destructive not because the underlying questions were unimportant but because they were conducted without theological sophistication. Churches split over whether to use drums rather than over what worship is meant to accomplish in the lives of believers. The question of formation — what kind of people does this worship produce over a lifetime? — was rarely asked.

Blended Worship: Compromise or Synthesis?

Many churches have attempted to resolve the tension through "blended worship" — services that combine elements of both traditions. A typical blended service might include a call to worship and a responsive reading (liturgical elements), followed by a set of contemporary worship songs, a topical sermon, and a closing hymn. Some churches offer separate services in different styles; others attempt to weave the traditions together in a single service.

The results are mixed. At its best, blended worship draws on the strengths of both traditions — the theological depth and historical continuity of the liturgical tradition, the accessibility and emotional authenticity of the contemporary tradition. At its worst, it satisfies no one — the liturgical elements feel perfunctory, the contemporary elements feel shoehorned in, and the overall experience is incoherent rather than integrated.

The most successful examples of blended worship tend to be those that begin with the liturgical ordo — gathering, word, table, sending — and express it in contemporary musical and cultural language, rather than those that begin with a contemporary framework and insert liturgical elements as decoration.

Why Young People Are Returning to Liturgy

One of the more striking trends in American Christianity over the past decade has been the movement of young adults — particularly those raised in contemporary evangelical churches — toward liturgical traditions: Anglicanism, Catholicism, Orthodoxy, and liturgical expressions of Lutheranism and Presbyterianism. The trend is not statistically enormous, but it is culturally significant, and it has generated a substantial body of personal testimony and sociological analysis.

The reasons are multiple. Young people raised on contemporary worship often report a hunger for depth, substance, and historical rootedness that their experience of Christianity did not provide. They want to be connected to something older than last week's sermon series. They want a worship experience that does not depend on the charisma of the lead pastor or the quality of the worship band. They want structured silence in a world of constant noise. They want the Eucharist — the physical act of receiving the body and blood of Christ — rather than the monthly or quarterly memorial meal that many contemporary churches offer.

There is also a generational factor. Millennials and Gen Z have grown up in a culture saturated with commercial entertainment, and they are often the first to recognize when worship has become indistinguishable from a concert. The aesthetic of the contemporary megachurch — the fog machines, the light shows, the high production values — can feel, to a generation weary of being marketed to, less like worship and more like another consumer experience.

Evaluating Worship by Formation, Not Preference

The most productive way to evaluate any worship practice is to ask not "Do I like it?" but "What is it doing to me?" Worship is not entertainment. It is not self-expression. It is, in the deepest sense, formation — the slow, repetitive, often unconscious process by which a community is shaped into a particular kind of people. The question is not whether the music is good or the sermon is interesting. The question is: Over a lifetime of participation, what kind of Christian will this worship produce?

A worship practice that never exposes the congregation to the full narrative arc of Scripture — creation, fall, redemption, consummation — will produce Christians with a truncated understanding of the faith. A worship practice that never includes corporate confession of sin will produce Christians who are unaware of their own brokenness. A worship practice that never celebrates the Eucharist will produce Christians who are disconnected from the central act of Christian worship for the first nineteen centuries of the church's existence. A worship practice that never makes space for silence will produce Christians who cannot hear the voice of God apart from amplified music.

Conversely, a worship practice that is all form and no feeling will produce Christians who can recite the creed but have never been moved by it. A worship practice that refuses to engage the culture will produce a church that talks only to itself. The goal is not to choose one tradition over the other but to ask, honestly and courageously, whether the worship we practice is forming us into the people God intends us to be — or merely confirming us in the preferences we already have.
excerpt: The worship wars of the 1990s were never really about music. They were about what worship is for — and the answer to that question shapes what kind of Christians we become.

title: Creeds, Confessions, and Statements of Faith: Why the Church Wrote Them Down
body:
There is a common assumption in contemporary Christianity — especially in non-denominational and low-church evangelical circles — that creeds are unnecessary impositions on the simplicity of biblical faith. "No creed but Christ" is the popular slogan, and it carries a certain appeal. Why do we need human documents when we have the Bible? Why add to Scripture? Why bind the conscience with the words of dead theologians?

The answer, which the early church learned at extraordinary cost, is that the Bible does not interpret itself. Every heresy in the history of Christianity has claimed biblical support. Arius quoted Scripture to prove that Christ was a creature. The Gnostics quoted Scripture to prove that the material world was evil. The Docetists quoted Scripture to prove that Christ did not really suffer. The creeds were not additions to Scripture. They were the church's authoritative summary of what Scripture teaches — drawn up because false teachers were using Scripture to teach things that Scripture, rightly understood, does not say.

Why the Early Church Needed Creeds

The earliest Christians had no formal creed. They had confessional formulas embedded in their worship — "Jesus is Lord" (Romans 10:9), "Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4) — but nothing approaching a systematic statement of faith. For the first two centuries, this was sufficient. The church was small, persecuted, and united by shared experience and apostolic memory.

But as the church grew and spread across the Roman world, two problems emerged. The first was Gnosticism — a diverse family of religious movements that claimed secret knowledge (gnosis) as the path to salvation. Gnostic teachers infiltrated Christian communities, using Christian vocabulary while filling it with radically different content. They taught that the God of the Old Testament was a malevolent or ignorant deity (the Demiurge), that the material world was inherently evil, that Christ was a divine spirit who only appeared to have a human body, and that salvation was achieved through knowledge of one's true spiritual identity rather than through faith in Christ's death and resurrection. The Gnostic threat was existential: if left unchecked, it would have transformed Christianity into a Platonic mystery religion with a Christian veneer.

The second problem was the Arian controversy. Arius, a presbyter in Alexandria in the early fourth century, taught that the Son of God was the first and greatest of God's creatures — divine in a derivative sense, but not co-eternal or co-equal with the Father. "There was when he was not," Arius famously argued. The teaching was plausible, biblically literate, and extraordinarily popular. It spread through the Eastern churches like a contagion, generating riots, depositions of bishops, and decades of theological warfare.

It was in response to these threats — Gnosticism in the second century, Arianism in the fourth — that the church produced its foundational creeds. The creeds were not abstract theological exercises. They were emergency measures, drawn up to preserve the identity of the faith against teachings that would have destroyed it.

The Apostles' Creed

The Apostles' Creed is the oldest and simplest of the Western creeds. Despite its name, it was not written by the twelve apostles. The legend that each apostle contributed one article is a medieval invention. The creed developed gradually over the second and third centuries, evolving from the baptismal interrogation used in the Roman church: "Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? Do you believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord? Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?" The candidate answered each question affirmatively and was immersed three times.

The creed reached its present form by the eighth century, but its core content is much older — it represents the doctrinal consensus of the second-century church. Its structure is Trinitarian: it moves from the Father (creator of heaven and earth), through the Son (conceived, born, suffered, crucified, buried, descended, risen, ascended, seated, coming again), to the Holy Spirit (the holy catholic church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, the life everlasting).

Every clause of the Apostles' Creed guards against a specific error. "Maker of heaven and earth" rejects the Gnostic claim that the material world was created by an evil deity. "Conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary" affirms both the divinity and the genuine humanity of Christ, rejecting Docetism (the denial that Christ had a real body) and Adoptionism (the claim that Jesus was an ordinary man adopted by God). "Suffered under Pontius Pilate" anchors the faith in history — this is not a myth but an event that happened under a particular Roman governor, in a particular place, at a particular time. "He descended into hell" (or "to the dead") affirms that Christ's death was real and complete. "The resurrection of the body" rejects the Greek philosophical preference for the immortality of the soul and insists on the Jewish and Christian hope for the redemption of the whole person — body included.

The Nicene Creed

The Nicene Creed is the most important theological document in the history of Christianity. It was produced at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD and expanded at the Council of Constantinople in 381 AD (hence its technical name: the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed). It is affirmed by Catholics, Orthodox, and most Protestants — the only doctrinal statement that can claim truly universal Christian authority.

The creed was forged in the fires of the Arian controversy. Its central concern is the relationship between the Father and the Son, and its key term is homoousios — "of one substance" or "of one being" with the Father. The Son is "God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one Being with the Father." Every phrase is a rejection of Arian theology. "Begotten, not made" denies that the Son is a creature. "Of one Being with the Father" denies that the Son is a lesser deity. "Through him all things were made" ascribes to the Son the divine prerogative of creation.

The creed also expanded the pneumatological section, affirming the full divinity of the Holy Spirit: "the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified." This was directed against the Pneumatomachians ("Spirit-fighters"), who accepted the divinity of the Son but denied the divinity of the Spirit.

The most famous controversy surrounding the Nicene Creed is the filioque — the Latin word meaning "and the Son," which the Western church added to the creed's statement about the Holy Spirit. The original text says the Spirit "proceeds from the Father." The Western addition says the Spirit "proceeds from the Father and the Son." This addition, which was made unilaterally by the Western church without the consent of an ecumenical council, was one of the theological factors in the Great Schism of 1054 between East and West. The Orthodox churches regard the filioque as both theologically erroneous (it subordinates the Spirit to the Son) and ecclesiologically illegitimate (it altered a conciliar text without conciliar authority). The dispute remains unresolved.

The Chalcedonian Definition

The Council of Chalcedon in 451 AD addressed the question that the earlier councils had left partially unanswered: if Christ is fully divine (Nicaea) and fully human (against Apollinarianism, which denied Christ's human mind), how do the two natures relate in one person? The council produced not a creed but a "definition" — a precise, technical statement that established the boundaries within which all subsequent Christological reflection would take place.

The Definition declares that Christ is "acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation." Each of the four negatives targets a specific heresy. "Without confusion" rejects Eutychianism, which taught that Christ's two natures were blended into a single hybrid nature. "Without change" rejects any suggestion that the divine nature was altered by the Incarnation. "Without division" rejects Nestorianism, which was understood to teach that Christ was two persons — one divine and one human — rather than one person with two natures. "Without separation" rejects any attempt to pull the two natures apart as though they were merely associated rather than united.

The Chalcedonian Definition is not a positive explanation of how the Incarnation works. It is a set of boundary markers that defines the space within which orthodox Christology operates. It tells you what you cannot say about Christ (you cannot say the natures are confused, changed, divided, or separated), but it does not tell you exactly how two natures subsist in one person. The mystery remains. The definition protects the mystery from being dissolved by premature explanation.

Reformation Confessions

The Protestant Reformation produced its own body of confessional documents, which functioned differently from the ancient creeds. Where the creeds were produced by ecumenical councils and claimed universal authority, the Reformation confessions were produced by particular churches and claimed authority only within those communities.

The Augsburg Confession (1530), written primarily by Philip Melanchthon and presented to the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, was the foundational confession of Lutheranism. It is irenic in tone, seeking to demonstrate that Lutheran teaching was consistent with the catholic faith and differed from Rome only on specific points of abuse and corruption. The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), produced by the Westminster Assembly during the English Civil War, became the foundational confession of Presbyterianism. It is comprehensive, precise, and rigorously systematic — a complete theological system in thirty-three chapters. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563), produced in the Palatinate region of Germany, is structured around three themes — human misery, divine deliverance, and grateful obedience — and is notable for its pastoral warmth and devotional quality. The Belgic Confession (1561), written by Guido de Bres, a Dutch Reformed pastor who was martyred for his faith, is a personal and passionate defense of Reformed theology.

These confessions share a common structure: they affirm the authority of Scripture, summarize the doctrines of the Trinity and the person of Christ, articulate a Protestant understanding of justification and sanctification, describe the nature of the church and the sacraments, and address the relationship between church and state. They differ in emphasis, in scope, and in the degree of detail with which they treat disputed questions, but they represent a shared tradition of confessional Protestantism that takes doctrine seriously, believes that the church's faith can and should be articulated in precise language, and submits to the authority of confessional documents as subordinate standards under Scripture.

Why Some Churches Refuse Creeds

Not all Christians accept the authority of creeds and confessions. Baptists, for instance, have historically been suspicious of creedalism, insisting that the Bible alone is sufficient as a rule of faith and practice. The Baptist theologian E.Y. Mullins articulated the principle of "soul competency" — the idea that every individual is competent, under the Holy Spirit's guidance, to interpret Scripture for themselves, without the mediation of creeds, confessions, or ecclesiastical authority.

The Restoration Movement (Churches of Christ, Christian Churches) took the anti-creedal position even further, arguing that creeds and confessions are inherently divisive — that they elevate human opinion to the level of divine authority and create tests of fellowship that go beyond Scripture. Thomas Campbell's famous Declaration and Address (1809) argued that "nothing ought to be inculcated upon Christians as articles of faith; nor required of them as terms of communion, but what is expressly taught and enjoined upon them in the word of God."

These traditions do not, however, operate without doctrinal standards. Baptists produce "statements of faith" (the Baptist Faith and Message, for instance) that function in practice very much like confessions — they define the theological boundaries of the community, serve as the basis for hiring decisions in denominational institutions, and articulate the consensus of the denomination on disputed questions. The difference between a "statement of faith" and a "confession" is, in many cases, more rhetorical than substantive. The anti-creedal tradition has creeds; it simply does not call them that.

The Difference Between a Creed, a Confession, and a Statement of Faith

The terms are often used interchangeably, but they carry different levels of authority and serve different functions. A creed (from the Latin credo, "I believe") is a concise summary of essential Christian doctrine, typically produced by an ecumenical council and claiming universal authority over all Christians. The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed are the two primary examples. A confession is a more detailed and comprehensive statement of doctrine, produced by a particular church or tradition and claiming authority within that community. The Westminster Confession, the Augsburg Confession, and the Belgic Confession are examples. A statement of faith is typically the least formal and most flexible of the three — a document produced by a particular church or organization that summarizes its theological commitments but may be revised more easily than a confession.

The relationship between these documents and Scripture is crucial. In all traditions that use them, creeds, confessions, and statements of faith are understood as subordinate to Scripture — they are authoritative insofar as they faithfully summarize what Scripture teaches, but they do not possess the same authority as Scripture itself. They can, in principle, be corrected if they are shown to be inconsistent with the biblical text. The difference between Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant understandings of this relationship is largely a difference about how much weight to give to the church's traditional interpretation of Scripture — but all three families affirm that Scripture is the ultimate norm.

Why Every Christian Should Know the Nicene Creed

Even if your church does not recite the Nicene Creed — and many do not — there are compelling reasons to know it intimately. First, it is the closest thing Christianity has to a universally accepted summary of the faith. It is affirmed by Catholics, Orthodox, and the vast majority of Protestants. To know the Nicene Creed is to know what unites the church across its deepest divisions.

Second, the creed is a remarkably efficient theology lesson. In fewer than three hundred words, it covers the doctrine of God, the doctrine of creation, the person and work of Christ (incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection, ascension, and second coming), the person of the Holy Spirit, the nature of the church, the meaning of baptism, and the Christian hope for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. There is no more compressed summary of Christian doctrine in existence.

Third, the creed connects you to the church across time. When you say, "We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth," you are saying the same words that Athanasius said, that Augustine said, that Thomas Aquinas and Martin Luther and Dietrich Bonhoeffer said. You are joining a conversation that has been going on for seventeen centuries, and you are affirming your continuity with every generation of Christians that preceded you. In an age of rootlessness and historical amnesia, this is no small gift.

Finally, the creed teaches you how to think theologically. Its structure — Father, Son, and Spirit — is the structure of the Christian faith itself. Its careful, precise language — "begotten, not made," "of one Being with the Father," "who proceeds from the Father" — models the kind of theological precision that is necessary when speaking about matters of ultimate importance. Sloppy language about God produces sloppy thinking about God, and sloppy thinking about God produces a faith that cannot withstand pressure. The creed is not a substitute for Scripture. It is a guide to reading Scripture rightly — a map that keeps you on the road that the church has traveled for two millennia, a road that runs straight through the heart of the biblical witness to the God who creates, redeems, and sustains all things.
excerpt: The ancient creeds were not bureaucratic exercises. They were battle lines drawn against heresies that threatened to gut the faith from within. Understanding them is understanding what Christianity will and will not tolerate.

title: The Charismatic Movement Inside Every Denomination
body:
In 1960, Dennis Bennett, the rector of St. Mark's Episcopal Church in Van Nuys, California, stood before his congregation and announced that he had received the baptism of the Holy Spirit and spoken in tongues. The announcement produced an immediate crisis. Some parishioners walked out. The local bishop asked Bennett to resign. The story made national news — not because speaking in tongues was new (Pentecostals had been doing it for half a century) but because Bennett was not a Pentecostal. He was an Episcopalian, a mainline Protestant, a man in a clerical collar with a graduate degree. The Holy Spirit, it seemed, had crossed a social boundary that American Christianity thought was firmly established.

Bennett's experience was not an isolated event. It was the opening act of a movement that would, over the next six decades, penetrate every major Christian tradition on earth — Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist — and reshape the landscape of global Christianity in ways that are still unfolding. The charismatic movement is, by virtually any measure, the most significant development in Christianity since the Reformation. Understanding it requires understanding its three distinct waves, its theological claims, its extraordinary gifts, and its equally extraordinary dangers.

The First Wave: Classical Pentecostalism (1901-1960)

The origins of Pentecostalism are conventionally traced to January 1, 1901, when Agnes Ozman, a student at Charles Parham's Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Kansas, reportedly spoke in tongues after Parham laid hands on her and prayed. Parham, a former Methodist minister, had been studying the book of Acts and had concluded that the "initial evidence" of baptism in the Holy Spirit was speaking in tongues — a doctrine that would become the defining distinctive of classical Pentecostalism.

But it was the Azusa Street Revival of 1906-1909, led by William Seymour, an African American Holiness preacher and former student of Parham, that transformed Pentecostalism from a local curiosity into a global movement. Seymour established a mission in a converted stable at 312 Azusa Street in Los Angeles, and for three years, services ran almost continuously — morning, afternoon, and night — characterized by speaking in tongues, prophetic utterances, healings, and what participants described as overwhelming encounters with the presence of God.

The Azusa Street Revival was remarkable for several reasons beyond its pneumatological claims. It was radically interracial at a time when American society was rigidly segregated. Frank Bartleman, a white journalist who covered the revival, wrote, "The color line was washed away in the blood." Black, white, Hispanic, and Asian worshippers prayed together, laid hands on each other, and shared leadership in ways that were extraordinary for 1906 Los Angeles — or for most of American Christianity a century later. This interracial character was not incidental to the movement's theology; Seymour understood the crossing of racial boundaries as itself a sign of the Spirit's work, a fulfillment of the Pentecost narrative in which the Spirit was poured out "on all flesh."

The interracial unity did not last. Within a decade, the Pentecostal movement had largely segregated along racial lines, producing separate denominational structures for black and white believers. The Assemblies of God, founded in 1914, was predominantly white. The Church of God in Christ, which had actually predated the Assemblies of God as an organized body, became the primary African American Pentecostal denomination. The racial division of the movement was one of its earliest and most consequential failures — a failure that Pentecostal historians have increasingly confronted with candor.

Classical Pentecostalism established several theological distinctives that would shape all subsequent waves: the doctrine of baptism in the Holy Spirit as a distinct, post-conversion experience; the expectation of speaking in tongues as the initial evidence of this baptism; the continued operation of all the gifts of the Spirit described in the New Testament (prophecy, healing, miracles, discernment of spirits); and an eschatological urgency rooted in the conviction that the outpouring of the Spirit was a sign of the last days.

The Second Wave: Charismatic Renewal (1960s-1980s)

Dennis Bennett's 1960 announcement marked the beginning of what historians call the charismatic renewal — the penetration of Pentecostal experience into the mainline Protestant and Catholic churches. The distinction between "Pentecostal" and "charismatic" is significant: Pentecostals left (or were expelled from) their existing denominations and formed new ones. Charismatics, by contrast, remained within their denominations, seeking to renew them from within.

The charismatic renewal spread with remarkable speed across denominational lines. By the mid-1960s, there were charismatic prayer groups and renewal movements among Episcopalians, Lutherans, Presbyterians, and Methodists. The movement attracted both clergy and laity, and it produced a substantial body of theological reflection that attempted to integrate charismatic experience with the doctrinal traditions of the host denominations.

The most significant — and to many observers, the most surprising — development was the emergence of the Catholic charismatic renewal. In February 1967, a group of faculty and students at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh attended a retreat during which several participants reported being baptized in the Holy Spirit and speaking in tongues. The movement spread rapidly to the University of Notre Dame and the University of Michigan, and within a decade, it had become one of the largest movements in the Catholic Church, with millions of participants worldwide.

The Catholic charismatic renewal was theologically distinctive in ways that set it apart from both classical Pentecostalism and Protestant charismatic renewal. Catholic charismatics did not generally teach that tongues were the initial evidence of Spirit baptism — a doctrine that sat uneasily with Catholic sacramental theology, which understood baptism and confirmation as the normative channels of the Spirit's gift. Instead, they spoke of a "release" or "renewal" of the Spirit already received in the sacraments. They maintained their commitment to the Mass, to the Marian doctrines, to papal authority, and to the full range of Catholic devotional practice. The renewal was not a Protestantization of Catholicism; it was an experiential intensification of an existing sacramental framework.

Pope Paul VI cautiously welcomed the movement, and subsequent popes — John Paul II, Benedict XVI, and Francis — have affirmed its place within the life of the church, while also warning against excesses. Today, the Catholic charismatic renewal claims over 120 million participants worldwide, making it one of the largest movements in the history of Catholicism.

The Third Wave (1980s-Present)

The "Third Wave" is a term coined by C. Peter Wagner, a former professor at Fuller Theological Seminary's School of World Mission, to describe a movement of Christians who practice charismatic gifts (healing, prophecy, spiritual warfare) without identifying as either Pentecostal or charismatic. Third Wave theology emphasizes "signs and wonders" as normative for Christian ministry, and it tends to be less interested in the doctrine of Spirit baptism (the defining concern of classical Pentecostalism) and more interested in the practical exercise of spiritual power.

The Vineyard movement, founded by John Wimber in the early 1980s, was the most influential institutional expression of the Third Wave. Wimber, a former musician and church growth consultant, combined Reformed evangelical theology with an openness to the gifts of the Spirit that he called "power evangelism." Vineyard worship — intimate, emotionally intense, focused on personal encounter with God — became the template for contemporary worship in evangelical churches worldwide, whether or not those churches identified as charismatic.

The Third Wave also produced the controversial "Toronto Blessing" (1994) and the Brownsville Revival (1995), both characterized by unusual physical manifestations — "holy laughter," falling, shaking, animal sounds — that deeply divided the evangelical world. Supporters saw these manifestations as evidence of the Spirit's overwhelming presence. Critics saw them as emotional excess, psychological manipulation, or worse. The debates revealed a fault line within evangelical Christianity between those who regarded experiential phenomena as inherently suspicious and those who regarded the absence of experiential phenomena as evidence of spiritual deadness.

Cessationism vs. Continuationism

The theological debate behind the charismatic movement is, at its core, a debate about whether the miraculous gifts described in the New Testament — tongues, prophecy, healing, miracles — continue to operate in the church today or ceased with the death of the apostles and the completion of the New Testament canon.

Cessationism — the view that the miraculous gifts ceased — has been the dominant position in Reformed and confessional Protestant theology since the Reformation. Its most influential modern articulation is Benjamin Warfield's Counterfeit Miracles (1918), which argued that miracles served as the credentials of the apostles and were no longer necessary once the apostolic testimony was inscripturated in the New Testament. John MacArthur's Strange Fire (2013) represented a more combative version of the same argument, accusing the charismatic movement of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

Continuationism — the view that all the gifts continue — argues that there is no biblical warrant for a cessation of any spiritual gift. The New Testament nowhere teaches that the gifts will cease before the return of Christ. Paul's statement that tongues "will cease" and prophecy "will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:8) is set in the context of the coming of "the perfect" (1 Corinthians 13:10), which continuationists identify not with the completion of the canon but with the return of Christ and the full consummation of the kingdom.

A significant middle position has emerged in recent decades, sometimes called "open but cautious" — the view that the gifts have not necessarily ceased but that their contemporary manifestations should be evaluated with rigorous biblical and theological discernment. This position, associated with scholars like D.A. Carson and Sam Storms, accepts the theoretical possibility of continued miraculous gifts while maintaining a high bar for their authentication.

What the Movement Contributed

The charismatic movement's contributions to global Christianity are substantial and should be acknowledged even by those who disagree with its theological claims. First, it recovered the experiential dimension of faith in traditions that had become arid and intellectualized. The mainline Protestant churches of the mid-twentieth century were, in many cases, so focused on theological precision and social respectability that they had lost the capacity to speak of — or expect — a living encounter with God. The charismatic renewal reminded these churches that Christianity is not merely a system of beliefs but a relationship with a living person, and that the Holy Spirit is not merely a doctrine but a presence.

Second, the movement democratized ministry. Classical Pentecostalism's insistence that the Spirit's gifts are available to all believers — regardless of education, ordination, gender, or race — was a genuinely radical claim with practical consequences. It empowered lay people, elevated women in ministry (many early Pentecostal denominations ordained women long before mainline Protestants did), and created space for leadership from the margins of society.

Third, the charismatic movement has been the primary engine of Christian growth in the Global South. The explosive growth of Christianity in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and East Asia over the past century has been overwhelmingly Pentecostal and charismatic in character. Philip Jenkins's observation that the "typical" Christian in the twenty-first century is not a European or American churchgoer but an African or Latin American Pentecostal is one of the most important demographic facts about contemporary Christianity.

What the Movement Risks

The charismatic movement's vulnerabilities are as significant as its strengths, and honesty requires naming them. The first risk is anti-intellectualism. The emphasis on experience over doctrine, on encounter over analysis, on the Spirit's leading over theological education, has in many contexts produced a Christianity that is emotionally vibrant but theologically shallow. When "God told me" becomes a substitute for careful biblical exegesis, the result is a faith that is vulnerable to every wind of doctrine.

The second risk is authoritarianism. The charismatic movement's emphasis on prophetic authority — the claim that specific individuals can receive and communicate direct messages from God — creates a structural vulnerability to spiritual abuse. When a pastor or prophet claims to speak with divine authority, dissent becomes not merely disagreement but rebellion against God. The history of the charismatic movement is littered with leaders who used claims of prophetic authority to control their followers, suppress criticism, and shield themselves from accountability.

The third risk is emotional manipulation. The worship practices of charismatic churches — extended singing, repetitive musical patterns, high emotional intensity, altar calls, prayers for healing — can produce genuine spiritual encounters, but they can also produce manufactured emotional experiences that are mistaken for the work of the Spirit. The line between the two is not always easy to discern, and the charismatic movement has not always been careful about discerning it.

The New Apostolic Reformation

The most controversial development within the charismatic world in recent decades is the New Apostolic Reformation (NAR) — a loosely organized movement that teaches that God is restoring the offices of apostle and prophet to the contemporary church, and that these new apostles and prophets have authority to direct the church and to influence the political and cultural direction of nations. The movement's leading figures — C. Peter Wagner (who coined the term before his death in 2016), Che Ahn, Bill Johnson, Mike Bickle, and others — teach that the church is entering a new era of spiritual power in which believers will exercise dominion over every sphere of society: government, business, education, media, arts, family, and religion.

The NAR has drawn sharp criticism from both cessationists and mainstream charismatics. Its theology of apostolic authority — which effectively places certain individuals above the accountability structures of the local church — creates obvious potential for abuse. Its "dominion theology" — the teaching that Christians are called to take control of societal institutions before Christ's return — represents a significant departure from the eschatological theology of classical Pentecostalism, which was premillennial and generally apolitical, expecting the world to grow worse before Christ's return rather than better.

The intersection of NAR theology with American political movements — particularly its involvement in the events surrounding the 2020 presidential election and its aftermath — has brought the movement unprecedented public scrutiny. Self-identified prophets within the NAR prophesied specific political outcomes that did not occur, generating a crisis of credibility that the movement has not fully reckoned with. The episode revealed the dangers of combining charismatic authority claims with political activism — a combination that can produce a form of Christianity that is impervious to correction, because its leaders claim to speak for God and its followers have been conditioned to regard skepticism as a lack of faith.

The charismatic movement, in all its waves and expressions, represents one of the most consequential developments in the history of Christianity. Its best impulses — the recovery of spiritual experience, the empowerment of the laity, the expectation that God acts in the present tense — are genuine gifts to the church. Its worst impulses — authoritarianism, anti-intellectualism, the confusion of emotional intensity with spiritual depth — are genuine dangers. The movement cannot be dismissed, and it cannot be embraced uncritically. It can only be engaged with the kind of careful, biblically grounded, theologically informed discernment that the best of the charismatic tradition itself calls for — the discernment of spirits, exercised not in fear but in love, and not in hostility but in hope for the church's faithfulness to the God who is, as the charismatics never tire of reminding us, still speaking.
excerpt: The movement that began in a converted stable in Los Angeles in 1906 has now touched every branch of Christianity on earth. Its story is more complicated, more consequential, and more ambiguous than either its champions or its critics admit.

title: Why People Are Leaving the Church
body:
The numbers are no longer debatable. They have not been debatable for at least a decade, though the institutional church has spent much of that decade debating them anyway, as if the appropriate response to a hemorrhaging wound is a prolonged discussion about whether the patient is actually bleeding.

In 2006, Gallup found that 73 percent of Americans identified as Christian. By 2022, that number had fallen to 68 percent. Pew Research Center's 2021 data showed a steeper picture: only 63 percent of American adults identified as Christian, down from 78 percent in 2007. The Public Religion Research Institute placed the figure even lower, at 61 percent, in its 2023 American Values Atlas. These are not marginal fluctuations within the noise of survey methodology. These represent the most rapid secularization of any major Western nation in the modern era, compressed into roughly fifteen years.

But the headline numbers, as dramatic as they are, obscure what is actually happening. Christianity is not declining uniformly. Evangelical Protestantism has held relatively steady in raw numbers, though its share of the population is shrinking. Black Protestantism has remained stable. It is mainline Protestantism and, increasingly, Roman Catholicism that are experiencing catastrophic losses. The Catholic Church in the United States has lost roughly one-third of its cradle Catholics, a departure that would constitute a demographic emergency in any other institution. Former Catholics now represent the second-largest "denomination" in the country, outnumbered only by current Catholics.

The question that matters, of course, is not merely what the numbers say but why the numbers say it. And here the church has largely failed, not because it has not asked the question, but because it has consistently preferred comforting answers to honest ones.

The Reasons Pastors Assume (And Why They Are Mostly Wrong)

Ask a typical pastor why people are leaving the church, and you will hear a predictable set of explanations. People are too busy. The culture has become too secular. Young people are distracted by technology. Sunday sports leagues compete with worship services. People are selfish, individualistic, consumerist. They want comfort, not commitment. They have been led astray by a hostile media.

These explanations share a common feature: they locate the problem entirely outside the church. The institution is fine. The product is excellent. The customers are defective. This is, to borrow a phrase from the business world, a catastrophically bad diagnosis, the kind that precedes bankruptcy.

The data tell a different story. When researchers actually ask people why they left, the answers are remarkably consistent across multiple studies, and they point the finger squarely at the institution itself.

Josh Packard and Ashleigh Hope's research, published in Church Refugees (2015), found that the people leaving churches were not the nominally committed or the spiritually indifferent. They were, disproportionately, the most involved members: Sunday school teachers, worship leaders, committee chairs, small group facilitators. These were not people who drifted away out of apathy. They were people who had given years, sometimes decades, of committed service and finally concluded that the institution was no longer worthy of their investment.

The Barna Group's extensive research, spanning two decades, has identified five primary drivers of church departure: hypocrisy (perceived disconnect between what the church preaches and how it behaves), political entanglement (the sense that the church has become an arm of a political party), intellectual dishonesty (the refusal to engage honestly with science, history, or difficult questions), exclusion (the treatment of women, LGBTQ individuals, racial minorities, or doubters as second-class members), and clergy abuse and cover-ups (the institutional protection of predators at the expense of victims).

Notice what is absent from this list. Nobody is leaving because worship services need better lighting. Nobody is leaving because the church lacks a coffee bar in the lobby. Nobody is leaving because the sermons are not entertaining enough. The fixation on stylistic upgrades that has consumed American church culture for the past three decades, the millions spent on fog machines and branded sermon series and Instagram-worthy lobbies, has been an elaborate exercise in treating a symptom that does not exist while ignoring the disease that does.

Hypocrisy: The Original Sin of Institutional Religion

When leavers cite hypocrisy, they are not merely observing that Christians sometimes fail to live up to their ideals. Everyone understands that human beings are imperfect. What they are identifying is something more specific and more damaging: the systematic gap between the church's public moral pronouncements and its institutional behavior.

A church that preaches radical generosity while its senior pastor lives in a mansion funded by tithes from working-class families. A denomination that thunders against sexual immorality while quietly reassigning priests credibly accused of molesting children. A congregation that proclaims the equality of all people before God while maintaining an all-white, all-male leadership structure in a diverse community. These are not instances of individual moral failure. They are patterns of institutional dishonesty, and the people who leave can see them with a clarity that those inside the institution often cannot.

The sociologist Robert Wuthnow documented this dynamic extensively in his research on American religion. He found that institutional trust, once lost, is almost impossible to recover, and that the perception of hypocrisy is the single most corrosive force in religious disaffiliation. People can forgive failure. They cannot forgive pretense.

The Political Captivity of the Church

The entanglement of American Christianity with partisan politics, particularly the near-total identification of white evangelicalism with the Republican Party, has driven more people from the church than any theological dispute in modern memory. This is not a partisan observation. It is a demographic fact.

Ryan Burge, a political scientist at Eastern Illinois University and a Baptist pastor, has documented this extensively. His data show that political identity now predicts religious affiliation more reliably than religious affiliation predicts political identity. In other words, people are not joining the Republican Party because they are evangelical. They are leaving evangelicalism because they are not Republican. The causal arrow has reversed.

For younger Americans especially, the association between Christianity and conservative politics has become so tight that many cannot imagine one without the other. A 2022 survey by the Survey Center on American Life found that among Americans under thirty who left their childhood religion, 60 percent cited the church's stance on social and political issues as a significant factor. When a twenty-five-year-old says, "I am not a Christian," she may not be making a theological statement about the divinity of Jesus. She may be making a sociological statement: "I do not belong to the political tribe that has claimed Christianity as its brand."

The tragedy of this is difficult to overstate. A faith tradition that began with an itinerant rabbi executed by the state has become, in the public imagination, a chaplaincy for state power. The cross, which was Rome's instrument of political terror, now appears on the podiums of political rallies. Whether or not individual churches endorse specific candidates, the brand contamination is real, and it is driving a generation away.

What "Leaving" Actually Looks Like

The popular assumption, shared by both anxious churchgoers and triumphant secularists, is that people who leave the church become atheists. They do not. The data on this are unambiguous.

According to Pew Research Center's 2021 study, the fastest-growing religious category in America is not atheism or agnosticism but "nothing in particular," a category that now represents 20 percent of the adult population, up from 12 percent in 2007. This group is distinct from atheists and agnostics in important ways. Many of them believe in God or a higher power. Many pray, at least occasionally. Many describe themselves as spiritual. What they have rejected is not the sacred but the institution. They have not abandoned transcendence. They have abandoned organized religion.

The term that has emerged to describe this population is "spiritual but not religious," or SBNR. It is a clumsy phrase, and it frustrates theologians on both sides: traditional believers think it is shallow, and committed atheists think it is incoherent. But it describes something real. There are tens of millions of Americans who believe that the universe has a spiritual dimension, who seek meaning and connection beyond the material, who may even consider themselves followers of Jesus in some sense, but who have concluded that the institutional church is not the place where these needs can be met. They are not rejecting God. They are rejecting the church's claim to be God's authorized representative.

This distinction, between leaving God and leaving the institution, is one that the church has been catastrophically slow to understand. When a pastor says, "Young people are turning away from God," he is usually wrong. What young people are turning away from is the pastor's institution. The conflation of the two is itself part of the problem. An organization that cannot distinguish between itself and the divine has already lost the capacity for self-criticism that might save it.

What the Leavers Say

In qualitative research, the voices of those who have left are remarkably consistent, and remarkably painful to hear.

"I didn't leave because I stopped believing. I left because I couldn't keep pretending that what was happening in that building on Sunday morning had anything to do with Jesus." This sentiment, expressed with minor variations by hundreds of respondents in Packard and Hope's research, represents the dominant narrative of church departure.

David Kinnaman's research for the Barna Group, published in You Lost Me (2011) and UnChristian (2007), found that young adults who left the church described it as "overprotective" (stifling honest inquiry and engagement with the broader culture), "shallow" (failing to offer intellectually serious engagement with faith and doubt), "anti-science" (requiring rejection of established scientific consensus as a condition of belonging), "repressive" (particularly regarding sexuality, in ways perceived as harmful rather than holy), "exclusive" (unwelcoming to those who do not conform to narrow cultural norms), and "doubtless" (demanding certainty and punishing questions).

The theologian Sarah Bessey, who has written extensively about her own experience of church departure and return, describes what many leavers feel: "The church broke my heart long before the world ever could." This is not the language of indifference. It is the language of betrayal. People do not grieve institutions they never loved.

What makes these testimonies so devastating for the church is that they come disproportionately from people who were deeply invested. These are not outsiders lobbing criticism from a comfortable distance. These are people who sang in the choir, served on the building committee, led vacation Bible school, tithed faithfully, and wept during worship. They left not because they did not care enough but because they cared too much to keep participating in something they had come to see as dishonest.

What the Leavers Still Hunger For

Here is the part of the story that should keep every pastor, every denominational leader, every seminary professor awake at night: the people who left the church did not stop being hungry.

Casper ter Kuile's research at Harvard Divinity School, published in The Power of Ritual (2020), documented the ways in which people who have left organized religion are building alternative communities of meaning, purpose, and connection. CrossFit gyms function as covenant communities with shared suffering, mutual accountability, and communal identity. SoulCycle classes use candles, music, and inspirational language that is indistinguishable from a worship service. The Sunday Assembly movement explicitly offers "church for people who don't do God," complete with singing, readings, moments of reflection, and community meals.

These substitutes are revealing. They demonstrate that the needs the church exists to meet, the hunger for community, meaning, transcendence, moral formation, and encounters with something larger than the self, are not going away simply because the church is failing to meet them. Human beings are, as the sociologist Christian Smith has argued, "moral, believing animals." The question is not whether people will seek meaning and belonging. The question is where.

The research consistently identifies four persistent hungers among those who have left the church. The first is community: not the superficial friendliness of a church lobby but genuine, vulnerable, accountable relationships in which people are known and loved in their complexity. The second is meaning: a coherent narrative that makes sense of suffering, injustice, and death, something more robust than "everything happens for a reason" and more honest than "God has a plan." The third is transcendence: encounter with mystery, beauty, and awe, the sense that the universe is not merely material but shot through with significance. The fourth is justice: the conviction that faith should make the world more humane, not less, and that a God worth worshipping is a God who cares about the poor, the marginalized, and the oppressed.

Notice that every one of these hungers is something the church, at its best, is uniquely positioned to address. The church has two millennia of communal practice. It has a story vast enough to encompass every human experience. It has a liturgical tradition designed to cultivate encounters with the sacred. It has a prophetic tradition that has consistently demanded justice for the vulnerable. The raw materials are all there. The failure is not one of resources but of will, honesty, and imagination.

What the Church Must Hear

The people who have left the church are not its enemies. They are, in many cases, its most honest critics, the ones who loved it enough to be wounded by its failures and clear-eyed enough to name what went wrong. If the church cannot hear their voices without becoming defensive, it will continue to decline, not because the world is hostile to faith but because the institution has become hostile to honesty.

The sociologist Robert Bellah, in Habits of the Heart (1985), warned that American individualism was eroding the institutional structures that made community life possible. He was right. But the solution to individualism is not to demand that people return to institutions that have not earned their trust. The solution is to build institutions worthy of trust, communities that tell the truth about their own failures, that welcome questions instead of punishing them, that practice the justice they preach, and that offer not certainty but faithfulness.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison in 1944, anticipated much of what we are witnessing. "We are moving toward a completely religionless time," he wrote. "People as they are now simply cannot be religious anymore." Bonhoeffer did not see this as a catastrophe. He saw it as an invitation, an opportunity for the church to strip away the institutional scaffolding and cultural prestige that had accumulated over centuries and rediscover what was essential: Jesus Christ, present in the midst of human suffering, calling his followers not to power but to service.

Bonhoeffer was executed by the Nazis in April 1945. He never had the chance to develop his vision of a "religionless Christianity." But his intuition was prophetically precise. The institutional trappings that the church clings to most fiercely, the buildings, the budgets, the cultural influence, the political access, are precisely the things that are driving people away. And the thing the church has always claimed to be about, encounter with a God who enters the world's suffering and transforms it from within, is precisely the thing people are still looking for.

The exodus from the church is not a crisis of faith. It is a crisis of integrity. People are not leaving because they have too little hunger for God. They are leaving because the church has too little hunger for honesty. And until the institution can hear that distinction, the bleeding will not stop.

The question before the church is not how to get people back. That framing already reveals the problem, treating human beings as a resource to be acquired rather than a community to be formed. The question is whether the church is willing to become the kind of community that people would not want to leave: truthful, just, humble, intellectually serious, spiritually alive, and genuinely committed to the way of Jesus rather than the preservation of its own institutional life.

That is a harder question. And the answer, so far, is not encouraging.
excerpt: The exodus from organized Christianity is the defining religious story of our era. The reasons people leave are not the reasons most pastors assume, and what the departed still hunger for should unsettle every congregation that thinks the problem is better marketing.

title: Deconstruction Is Not Destruction
body:
The word "deconstruction" has become, in certain Christian circles, a term of opprobrium, a diagnosis that means the patient has been infected by the culture and is now spiritually terminal. Pastors warn against it from pulpits. Podcasters devote entire series to refuting it. Denominational leaders treat it as a contagion to be quarantined. The anxiety is palpable, and it is almost entirely misdirected.

What most of these critics are reacting to is not deconstruction itself but a caricature of it: a social media phenomenon in which photogenic former evangelicals announce their departure from the faith in a series of Instagram posts, accumulate followers, and monetize their disenchantment. This phenomenon is real, and some of it is indeed shallow. But to confuse it with the actual process of deconstruction is like confusing a fast-food advertisement with the agricultural science that produces the food. The surface presentation tells you almost nothing about what is actually happening underneath.

Deconstruction, properly understood, is not a TikTok trend. It is a philosophical and theological process with deep roots in Western intellectual history, and it describes something that the church's own scriptures commend, demand, and model.

What Deconstruction Actually Means

The term "deconstruction" entered the philosophical lexicon through Jacques Derrida, the French-Algerian philosopher who developed it in the late 1960s. Derrida's project was epistemological: he was interested in how meaning is constructed through language, and he argued that all systems of meaning contain internal contradictions, assumptions, and hierarchies that, upon examination, reveal the instability of what had appeared stable. Deconstruction, for Derrida, was not demolition. It was analysis. It was the patient work of examining the foundations of a structure to understand what they were actually made of.

The theologian John Caputo, who has done more than anyone to bring Derrida's thought into conversation with Christian theology, argues that deconstruction is not the enemy of faith but its ally. "Deconstruction is the hermeneutics of the kingdom of God," Caputo writes in What Would Jesus Deconstruct? (2007). By this he means that the prophetic tradition, the tradition of Jesus himself, is a tradition of questioning established structures, exposing pretense, and refusing to allow human institutions to claim divine authority uncritically.

When applied to faith, deconstruction does not mean tearing everything down. It means examining the layers: distinguishing between the bedrock of genuine encounter with God and the cultural, political, and psychological material that has accumulated on top of it. It means asking which of your beliefs are actually rooted in scripture, reason, and experience, and which are inherited assumptions that you have never questioned because questioning was not permitted.

This is, by any honest account, a necessary process. Every thoughtful person of faith does it to some degree. The question is whether the church will accompany people through it or punish them for undertaking it.

Deconstruction vs. Deconversion

One of the most critical distinctions the church consistently fails to make is between deconstruction and deconversion. They are not the same thing. They may overlap in some cases, but they describe fundamentally different processes.

Deconstruction is the critical examination of one's faith framework: the beliefs, practices, assumptions, and authorities that have shaped one's understanding of God, the Bible, the church, and the moral life. It is interrogation, not abandonment. A person who is deconstructing is asking, "Is what I was taught actually true? Is it faithful to the tradition it claims to represent? Does it produce the kind of life it promises?" These are not the questions of an enemy. They are the questions of someone who cares deeply enough to demand honesty.

Deconversion is the departure from faith altogether. It is the conclusion, reached after examination or exhaustion or both, that the entire framework is untenable, that there is no God, no transcendence, no story worth believing. Deconversion is a real phenomenon, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed. But it is not the inevitable outcome of deconstruction. It is one possible outcome among many.

The church's tragic error has been to treat deconstruction as if it were always the first step toward deconversion, and therefore to resist it at all costs. This resistance has the perverse effect of making deconversion more likely. When a person begins to question their inherited faith and is met with fear, hostility, and threats of damnation, the message they receive is clear: this tradition cannot withstand scrutiny. A faith that punishes questions is a faith that has already conceded it does not have answers. And a person who has been told that questioning is the same as leaving will eventually take the church at its word and leave.

What Gets Deconstructed

It is essential to be specific about what people are actually deconstructing, because the objects of deconstruction are rarely the things the church assumes.

Most people who describe themselves as deconstructing are not questioning whether God exists. They are questioning whether the God they were taught about exists, the God who sends billions of people to eternal conscious torment for failing to recite the correct prayer, the God who ordained male headship as a cosmic principle, the God who blesses America specifically, the God who requires young-earth creationism as a condition of salvation, the God who hates the same people the congregation hates. They are not deconstructing the divine. They are deconstructing a particular construction of the divine, and they are discovering, often with great relief, that the construction is not the same as the reality.

Others are deconstructing toxic theology: the prosperity gospel's equation of faithfulness with financial success, purity culture's reduction of human sexuality to a set of prohibitions and shame, the nationalist theology that equates Christianity with Western civilization, the authoritarian ecclesiology that demands unquestioning obedience to pastoral authority. These are not peripheral issues. They are, for millions of people, the only version of Christianity they have ever known.
