Barna's research has found that the most common perception of the church among non-churchgoing young adults is that it is "anti-homosexual" — more common than "judgmental," "hypocritical," or "too political," all of which also rank high. PRRI's 2023 data shows that 79 percent of Americans aged 18-29 support same-sex marriage, including 51 percent of young white evangelicals. The gap between the church's official teaching and the moral convictions of an entire generation is not a gap. It is a chasm.

This is not the place to adjudicate the theological question of same-sex relationships. Faithful Christians hold a range of positions, and the exegetical and hermeneutical arguments are complex. But what must be said — what the church cannot avoid saying if it wants to understand why young adults are leaving — is that the way the church has engaged this issue has been, for millions of young adults, the single most powerful evidence that the church is not a safe or credible institution.

Young adults have watched churches use LGBTQ+ people as rhetorical targets while ignoring divorce, materialism, and gossip. They have watched pastors devote sermon after sermon to sexual ethics while remaining silent on racial injustice. They have watched denominations invest millions of dollars in political campaigns against same-sex marriage while cutting budgets for homeless ministries. They have watched families expel their own children in the name of biblical fidelity. The message received — regardless of the message intended — is that the church's moral passion is selective, and that its selectivity correlates suspiciously with the populations it finds most culturally threatening.

For a generation that counts LGBTQ+ people among their closest friends, family members, and colleagues — and that sees no contradiction between this reality and genuine faith — the church's posture is not merely a disagreement. It is a moral emergency. And increasingly, it is a dealbreaker.

The Hypocrisy Factor

Beneath the specific issues of justice and inclusion lies a deeper problem: the perception — grounded in abundant evidence — that the church does not practice what it preaches.

Young adults watched eighty-one percent of white evangelicals vote for a thrice-married casino owner who bragged about sexual assault, and then heard those same evangelicals lecture them about sexual morality. They watched church leaders who preached "family values" endorse policies that separated migrant children from their parents at the border. They watched pastors who thundered against "the world" accumulate personal wealth that would have scandalized the apostle Paul. They watched denominations that preached the authority of scripture ignore the parts of scripture that addressed their own sins while weaponizing the parts that addressed other people's.

The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his landmark A Secular Age, argued that the modern "malaise of immanence" — the sense of spiritual flatness that characterizes secular societies — is not primarily the result of intellectual arguments against God but of the failure of religious institutions to embody a compelling alternative to consumer capitalism. Young adults are not, by and large, philosophical materialists. Surveys consistently show that the majority describe themselves as "spiritual" even when they reject organized religion. They have not lost interest in transcendence. They have lost confidence that the church has access to it.

This is the hypocrisy factor at its deepest level. It is not merely that individual Christians are imperfect — every young adult understands that, and most would be drawn to a community that honestly acknowledged its imperfection. The problem is that the church as an institution systematically behaves in ways that contradict its own stated values, and then deploys theological language to justify the contradiction. When a pastor preaches humility from a stage designed to center his own celebrity, the medium contradicts the message. When a church preaches generosity while building a $130 million worship center, the budget contradicts the sermon. When a denomination preaches the authority of scripture while ignoring the 2,000 verses about poverty, the selectivity reveals the real authority: not the text, but the culture that determines which parts of the text to emphasize.

Young adults see this with devastating clarity, and they do not have the institutional loyalty to overlook it.

The Digital Factor

The pandemic accelerated a trend that was already well underway: the migration of spiritual life from embodied community to digital consumption. By 2021, the Barna Group found that one in three practicing Christians had stopped attending church entirely, with many replacing in-person participation with online content — podcasts, livestreams, YouTube sermons, and the curated social media presence of celebrity pastors.

For young adults, this shift has a particular valence. They have grown up in an ecosystem of parasocial relationships — one-directional connections with media figures who feel intimate but are not. A young adult who listens to a popular pastor's podcast three times a week, follows that pastor on Instagram, and watches their sermon livestream on Sunday may feel genuinely connected to that pastor and that community. But the connection is illusory. There is no mutual knowledge, no shared obligation, no friction, no cost. It is community without covenant — all the emotional resonance of belonging with none of the demands.

This is, in one sense, the ultimate consumer religion: a spiritual experience optimized for individual preference, available on demand, and requiring no sacrifice. It is also profoundly insufficient. The New Testament knows nothing of disembodied faith. The church, in Paul's theology, is a body — not a metaphor for a body, but an actual community of people who bear one another's burdens, confront one another's sins, share one another's meals, and are physically present to one another in suffering. You cannot weep with those who weep through a screen. You cannot bear a burden you do not know about because your only connection to the community is a weekly livestream. You cannot be formed into the image of Christ by a parasocial relationship with a charismatic communicator.

The digital factor is thus both a symptom and a cause of the exodus. It is a symptom because it reveals what young adults find missing in actual churches — they would not seek digital substitutes if the embodied reality were compelling. And it is a cause because the more spiritual life is consumed digitally, the less capacity people develop for the difficult, friction-filled, deeply transformative experience of actual community. The church's competitor is not other churches. It is the entire architecture of digital life, which offers an endless supply of content that feels like connection without any of the cost.

What Churches That Are Reaching Young Adults Do Differently

Despite the bleak data, there are churches that are reaching young adults — not by chasing cultural trends but by recovering something ancient. These churches share several characteristics that are worth examining closely because they point toward a way forward that does not require the church to abandon its identity.

They practice radical honesty. These churches do not pretend to have all the answers. They create space for questions, doubt, and intellectual struggle. They engage seriously with science, philosophy, and the genuine difficulties of biblical interpretation. They do not treat doubt as a spiritual disease to be cured but as a necessary companion to mature faith. The model here is not the certainty of the lecture hall but the honesty of the seminar room — a community of learners wrestling together with texts and traditions that are genuinely difficult.

They engage justice concretely, not abstractly. These churches do not merely preach about justice; they practice it. They run legal clinics for undocumented immigrants. They organize tenant unions. They show up at school board meetings. They partner with community organizations that address systemic issues. Their justice engagement is not a program staffed by volunteers; it is embedded in the church's identity and budget. Young adults can tell the difference between a church that talks about justice and a church that spends money on it.

They demand something. This may be the most counterintuitive finding: the churches that attract young adults are not the ones that ask the least of them but the ones that ask the most. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's distinction between cheap grace and costly grace is acutely relevant here. A faith that costs nothing is worth nothing, and young adults know it. The churches that are growing among this demographic tend to have rigorous membership processes, high expectations for community participation, and a clear sense of shared mission that requires actual sacrifice. Young adults are not looking for a low-commitment social club. They are looking for something worth giving their lives to.

They practice genuine community. Not community as a buzzword in a mission statement, but community as a daily reality — shared meals, mutual aid, physical proximity, honest conflict and honest reconciliation. These churches tend to be smaller, often meeting in homes or shared spaces rather than purpose-built campuses. They emphasize small groups not as a program but as the primary expression of church life. They create structures in which people actually know one another — not as fellow audience members at a weekly performance, but as members of an actual body with actual obligations to one another.

They separate the faith from partisan politics. Young adults have watched the church become so entangled with one political party that the gospel itself has become a partisan artifact. Churches that reach young adults tend to be politically engaged but not politically captured. They speak prophetically to both parties. They refuse to let the gospel be reduced to a voter guide. They recover the biblical tradition of prophetic critique that stands outside all human power structures rather than baptizing any one of them.

"The church that is married to the spirit of this age will be widowed in the next." — William Ralph Inge

The path forward for the American church is not more fog machines. It is not better branding. It is not a hipper pastor or a sleeker app. The path forward is the painful, exhilarating work of becoming what the church claims to be: a community that tells the truth, practices justice, welcomes the stranger, sits with suffering, demands sacrifice, and points beyond itself to a reality that consumer culture cannot provide. Young adults are not leaving the church because they have outgrown the need for transcendence. They are leaving because the church has failed to provide it.

The good news — and it is genuinely good news — is that the solution is not innovation but recovery. Everything the church needs to reach this generation, it already possesses. The prophetic tradition. The practice of radical hospitality. The theology of a God who enters suffering rather than explaining it away. The vision of a community that crosses every boundary the world erects. The church does not need to become something new. It needs to become what it always claimed to be. And if it does — if it trades performance for honesty, comfort for justice, and cultural power for prophetic faithfulness — it will find that the generation it thought it had lost was waiting for it all along.
excerpt: The exodus of 18-to-35-year-olds from American churches is not a mystery, and it is not about worship style. It is about credibility — and the church is losing on every front that matters to this generation.

title: Is God Real? An Honest Assessment
body:
The question is not going away. It has not gone away in twenty-five centuries of sustained philosophical inquiry, and it will not go away because a New Atheist bestseller declares it settled or because a revival preacher insists it was never really a question at all. "Is God real?" is the question that sits beneath every other question a human being can ask — about meaning, about morality, about whether the universe is the kind of place that notices us or the kind of place that does not. It deserves better than the treatment it typically receives, which is to say it deserves more than slogans, more than bumper stickers, more than the false confidence of people who have never honestly reckoned with the strongest version of the opposing case.

I am a pastor. I have staked my life on the conviction that God is real. But I have also sat across the table from enough honest atheists and enough anguished doubters to know that the question cannot be waved away with a Bible verse or a sunset. The arguments matter. The objections matter. And what we do with the space between the arguments and the objections — that matters most of all.

The Classical Arguments for God's Existence

The case for God's existence is not a single argument but a family of arguments, each approaching the question from a different angle. They do not prove God in the way a mathematical theorem proves a conclusion. But they were never designed to. They are arguments to the best explanation — attempts to account for features of reality that seem to require something beyond the natural order to explain.

The cosmological argument, in its simplest form, asks why there is something rather than nothing. Leibniz formulated it as the principle of sufficient reason: every contingent thing requires an explanation outside itself. The universe is contingent — it did not have to exist, and it has not always existed in its present form. The Big Bang, confirmed by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson's detection of cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965, established that the universe had a beginning approximately 13.8 billion years ago. If the universe began to exist, what caused it? The argument does not claim to identify this cause as the God of Christianity specifically. It claims that the existence of the universe points beyond itself to something uncaused, necessary, and sufficient to account for why anything exists at all.

The Kalam cosmological argument, revived by William Lane Craig from medieval Islamic philosophy, sharpens the point: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore, the universe has a cause. The second premise has been challenged — some physicists, notably Lawrence Krauss, have argued that the universe could have emerged from a quantum vacuum. But as the philosopher David Albert pointed out in his review of Krauss's work, a quantum vacuum is not nothing. It is a highly structured state of affairs governed by physical laws. The question of why those laws exist, why that vacuum exists, remains unanswered.

The teleological argument observes that the universe appears to be fine-tuned for the existence of life. The cosmological constants — the gravitational constant, the strong nuclear force, the cosmological constant governing the expansion of the universe — are calibrated within extraordinarily narrow ranges. The physicist Roger Penrose calculated that the odds of the initial low-entropy state of the universe occurring by chance are on the order of one in ten to the power of ten to the power of 123 — a number so large that it exceeds the number of particles in the observable universe. Martin Rees, the Astronomer Royal, identified six numbers that, if altered even slightly, would render the universe incapable of producing stars, planets, or life. The argument does not claim that this fine-tuning proves a designer. It claims that design is a more plausible explanation than chance, particularly when the alternative — the multiverse hypothesis — is itself an extraordinary metaphysical claim that lacks direct empirical evidence.

The moral argument, advanced by C.S. Lewis in Mere Christianity and given more rigorous philosophical treatment by Robert Adams and William Lane Craig, begins with the observation that human beings experience moral obligations as objective — as binding, as real, as independent of personal preference. If moral values are objective, the argument runs, they require a ground that transcends human opinion. A universe that is nothing but matter in motion cannot generate the category of "ought." Something beyond nature must account for the fact that we experience cruelty as genuinely wrong, not merely as something we happen to dislike. The argument is not that atheists cannot be moral. They manifestly can. The argument is that the moral realism most people instinctively hold — the conviction that torturing children is objectively wrong, not merely culturally disfavored — sits more comfortably within a theistic framework than a purely naturalistic one.

The ontological argument, first formulated by Anselm of Canterbury in the eleventh century and reformulated by Alvin Plantinga using modal logic in the twentieth, argues that the very concept of a maximally great being — a being possessing all perfections in every possible world — entails that such a being exists. This argument has always been the most controversial, and the most brilliant minds have disagreed about it. Kant objected that existence is not a predicate. Plantinga's modal version avoids that objection but introduces a new question: is the premise that a maximally great being is possible itself warranted? The ontological argument is less a proof than an invitation to consider whether the concept of God is coherent — and if it is, what follows.

The Strongest Objections

The case against God's existence is not a matter of intellectual laziness or moral rebellion, whatever some apologists may claim. It is a serious philosophical position with serious arguments behind it, and anyone who dismisses it without engagement has not earned the right to their own belief.

The problem of evil remains the most powerful argument against theism. Epicurus stated it with devastating clarity in the third century before Christ: Is God willing to prevent evil but not able? Then he is not omnipotent. Is he able but not willing? Then he is malevolent. Is he both able and willing? Then why does evil exist? David Hume restated it in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion. J.L. Mackie formalized it as the logical problem of evil: an omnipotent, omniscient, wholly good God is logically incompatible with the existence of evil. The argument hits with particular force not in the philosopher's study but in the children's hospital, at the mass grave, in the aftermath of the earthquake that buried a village. It is one thing to discuss evil as a logical category. It is another to stand in its presence.

The argument from divine hiddenness, developed by J.L. Schellenberg, asks why, if God exists and desires a relationship with human beings, so many people find no evidence of God despite sincere searching. A loving God, Schellenberg argues, would not permit "nonresistant nonbelief" — the situation in which a person is genuinely open to God's existence but cannot find sufficient reason to believe. The hiddenness of God is not merely an intellectual puzzle. It is, for many, a source of genuine anguish. They have prayed. They have searched. They have found silence. And they deserve more than the accusation that they did not search hard enough.

Naturalistic explanations for religion — the cognitive science of religion developed by scholars like Pascal Boyer, Justin Barrett, and Ara Norenzayan — offer an account of why human beings tend to believe in gods without requiring that any gods actually exist. Our cognitive architecture, shaped by evolution, disposes us toward agency detection (we see intentions behind events), toward teleological thinking (we see purposes in nature), and toward belief in minds without bodies. These cognitive tendencies, the argument goes, are sufficient to explain why every human culture has developed religious beliefs. You do not need God to explain belief in God. The explanation is in the wiring.

What We Can Know and What We Cannot

Here is what honesty requires: neither side has a knockdown argument. The classical arguments for God's existence are strong but not conclusive. The objections are serious but not decisive. The cosmological argument points to something beyond the universe, but it does not specify what. The problem of evil is devastating, but Alvin Plantinga's free will defense has shown that the logical problem of evil — the claim that God and evil are logically incompatible — does not hold. The evidential problem of evil — the claim that the amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence unlikely — is harder to answer, but it depends on the assumption that we should expect to understand why God permits what God permits, and that assumption is itself debatable.

The cognitive science of religion explains why we are disposed to believe in gods. It does not explain whether any god is actually there. Evolutionary debunking arguments cut both ways: if our cognitive faculties are unreliable when they produce belief in God, why should we trust them when they produce belief in atheism? Alvin Plantinga's evolutionary argument against naturalism presses exactly this point. If our cognitive faculties were shaped entirely by natural selection for survival rather than truth, we have no reason to trust them in any domain — including the domain of philosophical reasoning about God's existence.

The multiverse hypothesis can explain fine-tuning without God, but at a cost: it posits the existence of an incomprehensibly vast number of unobservable universes, which is itself a metaphysical commitment of staggering proportions. Trading one unobservable reality for another is not obviously a gain in parsimony.

The Difference Between Proof and Evidence

Much of the frustration in the God debate arises from a confusion between proof and evidence. Proof belongs to mathematics and formal logic. It is deductive, airtight, and conclusive. Evidence belongs to virtually every other domain of human inquiry. It is cumulative, probabilistic, and subject to interpretation. We do not prove the guilt of a defendant; we weigh the evidence. We do not prove a scientific hypothesis; we test it against the data and judge whether it is the best available explanation. We do not prove that our spouse loves us; we live inside a web of evidence — words, actions, presence, sacrifice — that makes the conclusion reasonable.

The question of God's existence belongs to the domain of evidence, not proof. And the evidence is not all on one side. There is evidence that the universe is the product of intelligence: its fine-tuning, its mathematical elegance, its capacity to produce minds capable of comprehending it. There is evidence that points in the other direction: the gratuitous suffering of innocents, the silence of God in the face of desperate prayer, the capacity of naturalistic explanations to account for much of what was once attributed to divine action. The honest inquirer must weigh both sets of evidence and make a judgment — a judgment that will inevitably be shaped not only by logic but by experience, by temperament, by the communities in which one is embedded, and by what one is willing to risk.

This is not relativism. It is realism about the kind of question we are asking. The question of God is not a question that can be resolved by a single argument, however elegant. It is a question that must be lived into.

Why Certainty Is Not the Goal

The demand for certainty — a demand made by both aggressive atheists and anxious believers — is itself a distortion. It treats faith as an intellectual achievement rather than a posture of trust. It assumes that the goal of the inquiry is to arrive at a conclusion so ironclad that doubt becomes impossible. But this has never been the biblical model of faith. Abraham left Ur without a map. Moses argued with the burning bush. The psalms are saturated with the language of doubt, complaint, and bewildered protest. Thomas demanded to put his fingers in the wounds — and Jesus did not rebuke him for the demand. He showed up.

The philosopher Paul Ricoeur described the movement of mature faith as a journey from "first naivete" through "critical distance" to "second naivete." The first naivete is the uncritical faith of childhood — accepting what one is told without examination. Critical distance is the period of questioning, deconstruction, and doubt that dismantles the childhood faith. Second naivete is the return to faith on the other side of criticism — a faith that has passed through the fire of honest inquiry and emerged not as certainty but as trust. Trust that is deeper than certainty because it knows what it has survived.

I believe God is real. I believe it because the cosmological and teleological arguments point toward a reality beyond the material. I believe it because the moral argument accounts for the sense of obligation I cannot shake. I believe it because the historical evidence for the resurrection of Jesus — the empty tomb, the post-mortem appearances, the transformation of the disciples, the emergence of the church — is, in my judgment, best explained by the hypothesis that God raised Jesus from the dead. I believe it because I have experienced, in prayer and in the community of faith, a presence that I cannot reduce to psychology or wish fulfillment.

But I hold this belief as trust, not as proof. I hold it with the full awareness that I could be wrong — and that the willingness to be wrong is not the enemy of faith but its condition. A faith that cannot survive doubt was never faith to begin with. It was denial wearing the mask of conviction.

The question "Is God real?" will not be settled by this essay or any other. It will be settled — if it is settled at all — in the life of the person who asks it honestly, follows the evidence where it leads, and is willing to live with the weight of a conclusion that can never be fully certain. That is not a weakness. That is what it means to be human, asking the largest question a human being can ask, in a universe that does not hand us the answer key.

The gap between the evidence and the conclusion is not empty space. It is the space where faith lives — or does not. And what you do with that space will shape everything else.
excerpt: The question of God's existence deserves more than slogans from either side. It deserves the best arguments, the hardest objections, and the honesty to sit with what remains when both have had their say.

title: Why Does God Allow Suffering?
body:
The question arrives not in a seminar room but in a hospital corridor. It arrives at 2:00 a.m. when the phone rings with the news that reshapes everything. It arrives in the oncologist's office, in the aftermath of the hurricane, in the silence that follows the funeral of a child who should have outlived every adult in the room. "Why does God allow suffering?" is the most human question ever asked, and anyone who answers it too quickly has not understood the question.

I have been a pastor for fifteen years. I have sat in rooms where the question was not academic. I have held the hands of parents burying their children, of spouses burying their partners, of people whose suffering was so acute and so undeserved that any theological explanation would have been an obscenity. I will not pretend that I have an answer that makes suffering acceptable. What I have is a set of responses — philosophical, theological, biblical, pastoral — that I believe are honest, even where they are incomplete. Especially where they are incomplete.

The Problem Stated Honestly

The problem of evil is the oldest and most powerful objection to belief in God. Epicurus framed it with a precision that has never been improved upon: if God is willing to prevent evil but unable, God is not omnipotent; if God is able but unwilling, God is not good; if God is both able and willing, evil should not exist; but evil exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, or God is not good, or God does not exist.

David Hume, in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), put the argument in the mouth of Philo, the skeptic: "Is the world, considered in general, and as it appears to us in this life, different from what a man or such a limited being would, beforehand, expect from a very powerful, wise, and benevolent deity?" The answer, Hume suggested, was obvious. No one looking at the world with fresh eyes — at its earthquakes and cancers, its famines and genocides, its random cruelties inflicted on the innocent — would conclude that it was the product of a being that was both all-powerful and all-good.

J.L. Mackie, in his 1955 essay "Evil and Omnipotence," formalized the argument as a logical inconsistency. The following three propositions, Mackie argued, cannot all be true simultaneously: God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, and evil exists. At least one must be false. If God exists, God is either not omnipotent or not good. The only way to hold all three is to introduce some additional premise that resolves the contradiction — which is precisely what theodicy attempts to do.

The argument is not merely philosophical. It is existential. Fyodor Dostoevsky, in the "Rebellion" chapter of The Brothers Karamazov (1880), put it in the mouth of Ivan Karamazov, who catalogs cases of cruelty to children — a girl locked in an outhouse in the cold by her parents, a boy torn apart by a general's hunting dogs — and then delivers his verdict: even if all of this suffering is somehow necessary for the final harmony of the universe, even if it produces some ultimate good that justifies every tear, he refuses to accept it. "It's not God I don't accept," Ivan says. "It's the world he created." He returns his ticket to divine harmony. The suffering of children is too high a price.

Elie Wiesel, in Night (1960), described the hanging of a boy in Auschwitz and the whispered question from the crowd: "Where is God now?" The answer, Wiesel wrote, came from within him: "Here he is — hanging on this gallows." Whatever else one does with that sentence, one must not domesticate it into a tidy theological resolution. It is a scream.

The Free Will Defense

The most influential philosophical response to the logical problem of evil was developed by Alvin Plantinga in God, Freedom, and Evil (1974). Plantinga argued that God's omnipotence does not include the ability to do the logically impossible. Creating beings with genuine free will and simultaneously guaranteeing that those beings will never choose evil is a logical contradiction — like creating a round square. If God values free creatures — creatures capable of love, moral choice, and genuine relationship — then God must permit the possibility that those creatures will use their freedom for evil.

Plantinga's argument is widely regarded, even by atheist philosophers, as having resolved the logical problem of evil. Mackie himself acknowledged that the free will defense showed the three propositions are not logically inconsistent. But the argument has significant limitations. It addresses moral evil — the suffering caused by human choices — but it does not address natural evil: the earthquake that kills thousands, the childhood leukemia, the tsunami that does not discriminate between the guilty and the innocent. No human free will chose the tectonic plates into motion.

Some theologians have extended the free will defense to natural evil by invoking the regularity of natural law. A world in which fire warms but never burns, in which gravity sustains life but never kills, in which bacteria nourish but never infect, would be a world without consistent natural laws — and therefore a world in which rational action, scientific inquiry, and moral development would be impossible. Richard Swinburne has argued along these lines: a world regular enough to permit meaningful human action must also be a world in which natural processes sometimes cause suffering. The argument has force, but it does not comfort the parents of the child swept away in the flood.

The Soul-Making Theodicy

The soul-making theodicy, rooted in the theology of Irenaeus of Lyon (second century) and developed by the philosopher John Hick in Evil and the God of Love (1966), offers a different framework. The Augustinian tradition understood evil as a consequence of the Fall — a corruption of an originally perfect creation. The Irenaean tradition understands creation not as a finished product that was ruined but as an ongoing project in which human beings are created immature and are being shaped, through the challenges and sufferings of life, into the likeness of God.

On this view, the world is not a paradise that was lost. It is a soul-making environment — a place where courage, compassion, perseverance, forgiveness, and love can be forged precisely because they are costly. Courage without danger is not courage. Compassion without suffering is not compassion. Forgiveness without genuine offense is not forgiveness. The qualities that constitute human maturity and moral depth cannot be produced in a world without resistance, without challenge, without pain.

Hick acknowledged that this framework does not account for the worst cases — the suffering that is so extreme, so prolonged, or so pointless that it seems to crush rather than develop the soul. A child dying slowly of a degenerative disease is not being "built up" by the experience. The soul-making theodicy must not be turned into a sanctification of cruelty. It can account for the general structure of a world that includes suffering; it cannot account for every instance of suffering within that world. Hick himself ultimately appealed to eschatology — to the hope that in a life beyond this one, the process of soul-making will be completed and the suffering will be redeemed. This is a hope, not a proof. And it must be held as such.

The Protest Tradition

One of the most neglected resources in the Christian response to suffering is the tradition of protest — the biblical tradition that does not answer the question of suffering but refuses to let it be silenced.

The book of Job is the foundational text. Job is a righteous man who suffers catastrophically — he loses his children, his health, his wealth, his standing. His friends arrive and offer theodicy: you must have sinned; God is disciplining you; there is a hidden purpose. Job rejects all of it. He demands an audience with God. He insists on his innocence. He accuses God of injustice. And the remarkable thing is that when God finally speaks, God does not answer Job's question. God answers out of the whirlwind with a cascade of questions about the foundations of the earth, the habits of the mountain goat, the behavior of the Leviathan — a speech that is, depending on your reading, either a profound assertion of divine mystery or a cosmic change of subject. But the most telling detail comes at the end: God rebukes not Job but his friends. The ones who offered tidy theodicy are the ones God condemns. The one who protested is the one God vindicates.

The lament psalms — Psalm 13, Psalm 22, Psalm 44, Psalm 88 — institutionalize protest as a form of prayer. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a failure of faith. It is a psalm. It is worship. It is the refusal to let go of God even in the experience of God's absence. Psalm 88 is the darkest text in the Psalter — it ends in darkness, with no resolution, no turn to praise, no note of hope. And the tradition preserved it. It included it in the hymnal. It said, in effect: this, too, is a legitimate way to speak to God.

Walter Brueggemann has described this tradition as "the costly loss of lament" — the church's gradual abandonment of the lament tradition in favor of a relentlessly positive worship culture that has no room for darkness, complaint, or protest. The result, Brueggemann argues, is a theology that cannot bear the weight of reality. A God who can only be praised is a God too fragile for the world as it actually is.

What Theodicy Cannot Do

Here is what must be said plainly, with no hedging: theodicy cannot explain a child's death to a parent. It cannot make a genocide intelligible. It cannot redeem the suffering of the Holocaust or the Middle Passage or the cancer ward by fitting it into a system. Any theodicy that claims to have "solved" the problem of evil has betrayed itself. The problem of evil is not a problem like a math problem — something with a solution that, once found, dissolves the difficulty. It is a problem like a wound. It does not want a solution. It wants a presence.

The danger of theodicy is that it can become a way of protecting God from the accusation of the sufferer — and in doing so, it becomes a way of silencing the sufferer. When a parent buries a child and a well-meaning Christian says, "God has a plan," the function of that statement is not to comfort the parent. The function is to comfort the speaker — to preserve their own theological framework from the threat that the parent's grief represents. It is, as Nicholas Wolterstorff wrote in Lament for a Son after the death of his own child, "a way of not looking at the suffering." The sufferer does not need an explanation. The sufferer needs someone willing to sit in the wreckage without explaining it away.

The Cross as God's Answer

The Christian response to suffering is not, finally, a philosophical argument. It is a person nailed to a piece of wood.

The cross is not an explanation of suffering. It is God's entrance into suffering. The incarnation — the claim that God became a human being in Jesus of Nazareth — means that God is not a distant observer of human pain. God has been inside it. God has experienced abandonment, betrayal, torture, and death. The cry of dereliction from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — is not a theological statement. It is a scream from the center of the abyss, uttered by the one who, Christians believe, is the Creator of the universe.

Jurgen Moltmann, in The Crucified God (1974), argued that the cross reveals a God who suffers — not a God who stands above suffering and permits it for mysterious purposes, but a God who enters into the deepest suffering and bears it from within. The cross does not answer the question "Why?" It answers the question "Where is God?" God is not in the observer's gallery. God is on the gallows. God is in the rubble. God is in the oncology ward at three in the morning when the morphine is not enough.

This does not make suffering acceptable. It does not make it purposeful. It does not resolve the philosophical problem. What it does — if it does anything — is reframe the question. The question is no longer "Why does God allow this?" The question becomes "What kind of God enters this?" And the Christian answer is: a God who would rather die than leave us alone in the darkness.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison cell in 1944, put it this way: "Only the suffering God can help." Not the omnipotent God who could prevent suffering but chooses not to. Not the distant God who watches from above. The suffering God. The God who is with us in it, not above it. The God who does not explain the darkness but enters it and refuses to let it have the last word.

What Remains

I do not have an answer to the problem of suffering. I have a response. The response is not a system but a set of convictions held in tension: that God is good, that the world is broken, that free will matters, that suffering can produce depth but is not justified by its products, that protest is a form of faith, that the cross means God is not a spectator, and that the resurrection means suffering is not the final word.

I hold all of these convictions while standing in a world where children die of cancer and earthquakes bury villages and the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer. I hold them not because they resolve the tension but because they are the most honest framework I have found for living inside the tension without either abandoning God or pretending the suffering is not real.

The parent who buries a child does not need my theodicy. They need my presence. They need the community of faith to sit with them in the ashes, to weep with them, to refuse to fill the silence with explanations that serve the explainer more than the bereaved. They need a faith tradition that has room for protest, for rage, for the unanswerable question hurled at heaven. They need a God who can absorb that question without flinching — who has, in fact, already absorbed it, on a cross, in the darkness, with a cry that shook the earth.

That is not an answer. It is the beginning of one. And it is all I have.
excerpt: The problem of suffering is not an intellectual puzzle to be solved. It is a wound that demands not explanation but presence — and the Christian answer begins at the cross, where God enters the wound.

title: Can You Trust the Bible?
body:
The question "Can you trust the Bible?" is asked by two very different groups of people, and they mean two very different things by it. The skeptic means: Is this ancient collection of texts reliable in any meaningful sense, or is it a repository of myths, contradictions, and outdated moral frameworks that no educated person should take seriously? The anxious believer means: Can I still hold on to this book that shaped my faith, given everything I have learned about its composition, its history, its internal tensions, and the uses to which it has been put?

Both questions deserve honest answers. But honest answers require that we first establish what the Bible actually is — not the Bible of popular imagination, whether that imagination is fundamentalist or secularist, but the Bible as it actually exists: a sprawling, multi-voiced, internally diverse collection of texts written across more than a millennium by dozens of authors in multiple languages and genres, compiled and canonized through a centuries-long process of communal discernment, and read in wildly different ways by wildly different communities for two thousand years.

The first step toward trusting the Bible is to stop expecting it to be something it never claimed to be.

A Library, Not a Book

The word "Bible" comes from the Greek ta biblia — "the books." The plural is not incidental. The Bible is a library: sixty-six books (in the Protestant canon; seventy-three in the Catholic; more in the Orthodox), written by more than forty authors over a span of roughly 1,500 years, in at least three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek), across multiple continents and cultural contexts. It includes history, law, poetry, prophecy, wisdom literature, gospel narrative, epistolary correspondence, and apocalyptic vision. To read Genesis and Revelation as if they belong to the same genre is like reading a legal brief and a love poem as if they operate by the same rules.

The diversity of the biblical library is not a weakness to be apologized for. It is a feature to be understood. The Bible contains four Gospels, not one, and they do not always agree on the details of the events they narrate. Matthew and Luke give different genealogies for Jesus. Mark ends without resurrection appearances (in the earliest manuscripts). John includes events and discourses that the Synoptic Gospels do not mention. The early church knew this. It did not harmonize the Gospels into a single narrative. It kept all four, side by side, in a deliberate act of theological polyphony. The message was clear: the truth about Jesus requires more than one perspective to tell.

The Old Testament is similarly diverse. The Deuteronomistic history (Joshua through Kings) interprets Israel's story through the lens of covenant faithfulness: when Israel obeys God, it prospers; when it disobeys, it suffers. The book of Job dismantles that very framework, presenting a righteous man who suffers catastrophically and whose friends' insistence on the prosperity theology is explicitly condemned by God. Ecclesiastes pushes further, questioning whether the patterns of divine justice are discernible at all: "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong." The Bible argues with itself. This is a sign of intellectual honesty, not incoherence.

What Inerrancy Means and Does Not Mean

The doctrine of biblical inerrancy, as articulated in the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), holds that the Bible, in its original manuscripts, is without error in all that it affirms. This is a more careful claim than it is often taken to be. The Chicago Statement itself includes important qualifications: it acknowledges that the Bible uses phenomenological language (the sun "rises"), approximations, and literary conventions; it affirms that genre must be taken into account; it denies that inerrancy requires strict literalism.

The problem is that the popular understanding of inerrancy has little to do with the Chicago Statement. In common usage, "inerrancy" has come to mean something like "every sentence of the Bible is a factual assertion that can be verified by modern standards of accuracy." This is not what the doctrine means, and treating it as such creates problems that the doctrine's careful formulators never intended. When a believer is told that inerrancy means the Bible cannot contain any factual discrepancy, and then discovers that the accounts of Paul's conversion in Acts 9, 22, and 26 differ in their details, the result is not a deeper faith but a crisis of faith — a crisis produced not by the Bible itself but by the expectations placed upon it.

A more robust understanding of biblical authority does not require inerrancy in the popular sense. It requires the conviction that the Bible is the primary and normative witness to God's self-revelation, that it is trustworthy in its central claims about God, humanity, sin, and salvation, and that it functions as the authoritative text of the Christian community for faith and practice. This is the view held by the vast majority of Christian tradition — Catholic, Orthodox, and much of Protestantism — and it does not depend on the absence of every historical or scientific difficulty.

The Transmission Question

A common skeptical argument runs as follows: we do not have the original manuscripts of any biblical text; we have only copies of copies, separated from the originals by decades or centuries; therefore we cannot know what the originals said. This argument has a grain of truth and a mountain of distortion.

The grain of truth: we do not possess the autographs (original manuscripts) of any biblical text. The earliest complete manuscripts of the New Testament date to the fourth century — Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus. The mountain of distortion: the textual evidence for the New Testament is vastly more abundant than for any other ancient text. We have approximately 5,800 Greek manuscripts, 10,000 Latin manuscripts, and thousands of manuscripts in other ancient languages. The earliest fragmentary manuscripts — such as P52, a fragment of John's Gospel — date to within a few decades of the original composition. By comparison, the earliest manuscript of Homer's Iliad dates to roughly 500 years after its composition, and we have fewer than 2,000 manuscripts of it. No classical scholar doubts that we can reconstruct Homer with reasonable accuracy. The textual evidence for the New Testament is orders of magnitude greater.

The field of textual criticism — the scholarly discipline devoted to reconstructing the original text from the available manuscripts — has produced a New Testament text that scholars across the theological spectrum regard as highly reliable. Bruce Metzger, perhaps the greatest textual critic of the twentieth century, estimated that the New Testament text is 99.5 percent certain, and that the remaining variants affect no significant doctrine. Bart Ehrman, Metzger's student and a prominent agnostic scholar, has acknowledged the reliability of the textual tradition even while disagreeing with its theological claims.

The variants that do exist are overwhelmingly minor — spelling differences, word-order changes, the kind of scribal errors one would expect in a hand-copied tradition. The handful of significant variants — the longer ending of Mark, the Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7-8), the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) — are well known, are flagged in every modern translation, and do not affect any central Christian doctrine. The text of the Bible has been transmitted with a fidelity that is remarkable by the standards of the ancient world.

Genre Matters

The single most important skill for reading the Bible honestly is the ability to recognize genre. Poetry is not history. Apocalypse is not prediction. Parable is not journalism. Law code is not systematic theology. When Jesus says, "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out," he is not prescribing self-mutilation. He is using hyperbole — a recognized rhetorical device — to make a point about the seriousness of moral compromise. When the psalmist writes, "The Lord is my shepherd," he is not making a zoological claim about God's profession. He is using metaphor to express trust in God's provision and care.

The creation accounts in Genesis 1-2 are a case study in the importance of genre. Genesis 1 is a highly structured, liturgical text — six days of creation arranged in two parallel triads (forming and filling), culminating in the Sabbath rest. It reads less like a scientific report and more like a hymn. Genesis 2 tells a different creation story with a different order of events (in Genesis 1, animals are created before humans; in Genesis 2, the man is created before the animals). Reading both as journalistic accounts of the same event creates an immediate contradiction. Reading them as two complementary theological narratives — one emphasizing the cosmic scope of God's creative work, the other emphasizing the intimacy of God's relationship with humanity — dissolves the contradiction and reveals the depth of both texts.

The prophetic literature is not primarily about predicting the future. It is about calling the present to account. When Isaiah says, "Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hates" (Isaiah 1:14), he is not making a prediction. He is delivering a divine indictment of a religious establishment that practices ritual without justice. Reading the prophets as a crystal ball for contemporary geopolitics — as much popular prophecy teaching does — is a fundamental misreading of the genre.

The book of Revelation, or the Apocalypse, is the most misread book in the Bible precisely because its genre is so unfamiliar to modern readers. Apocalyptic literature was a well-established genre in the ancient world, with recognizable conventions: symbolic numbers, cosmic imagery, beasts representing empires, a final confrontation between good and evil. First-century readers would have recognized these conventions instantly. Modern readers, unfamiliar with the genre, tend to read Revelation as a literal prediction of future events — an approach that produces endless speculation and very little understanding.

The Bible the Bible Actually Is

The Bible we actually have is stranger, more honest, and more durable than either the fundamentalist or the skeptic imagines. It contains genealogies that do not match, numbers that do not add up, and laws that later biblical texts modify or set aside. It includes the Song of Solomon, which is an erotic love poem, and Ecclesiastes, which flirts with nihilism. It preserves the story of David — the man after God's own heart — committing adultery, arranging a murder, and being confronted by a prophet who tells him a parable to trick him into pronouncing his own judgment. It does not protect its heroes. It does not sanitize its history. It does not resolve its tensions into a neat systematic theology.

And it has endured. It has survived the Roman Empire's attempt to destroy it, the medieval church's attempt to control it, the Enlightenment's attempt to dismiss it, and the modern church's attempt to domesticate it. It has been translated into more than 700 languages. It has shaped the moral imagination of Western civilization — its concepts of human dignity, justice, care for the vulnerable, and the equality of persons before God have become so deeply embedded in Western thought that even secular people who reject the Bible's authority often hold values that are unintelligible apart from it.

How to Read It Honestly

Reading the Bible honestly means reading it on its own terms. It means paying attention to genre, to historical context, to the literary conventions of the ancient world. It means acknowledging the tensions without flattening them and sitting with the difficulties without pretending they do not exist. It means recognizing that the Bible was written in specific historical contexts by authors who shared the cosmological assumptions of their time — a flat earth, a solid dome over the sky, a three-tiered universe — and that these assumptions are part of the cultural medium through which the theological message was communicated, not part of the message itself.

It also means refusing to read the Bible cynically. The skeptic who approaches the Bible looking only for contradictions and moral failures will find them. But this is a way of reading that refuses to hear what the text is actually saying — refuses to sit with the Sermon on the Mount, with the parable of the prodigal son, with the vision of the new heavens and the new earth, with the relentless biblical insistence that the God of the universe cares about the widow, the orphan, and the stranger. A hermeneutic of suspicion, applied without a corresponding hermeneutic of trust, is not honest reading. It is reading with a predetermined conclusion.

Can you trust the Bible? Not if you mean: can you treat it as a science textbook, a history textbook, or a systematic theology that dropped complete from heaven? No. But if you mean: can you trust it as the primary witness to God's self-revelation, as a text that has been tested by centuries of critical scrutiny and has survived, as the book that still has the power to name what is wrong with the world and point toward what would make it right — then yes. You can trust it. Not because it is simple, but because it is honest. And honest things are worth trusting, even when — especially when — they do not give us everything we wish they would.
excerpt: The Bible is not what most people think it is — defenders and critics alike. It is stranger, more varied, more honest, and more resilient than either the fundamentalist or the skeptic imagines.

title: What Christians Actually Believe About Hell
body:
Few doctrines have caused more damage to the Christian witness than the popular version of hell — the one preached from revival stages and painted on highway billboards, the one that reduces the gospel to a fire-insurance policy and God to a deity whose primary attribute is wrath. And few doctrines have been more poorly understood, even by the people who preach them most loudly. The Christian tradition has never spoken with one voice about hell. It has harbored a range of views, some of them held by the most revered thinkers in the history of the church, and the honest conversation about hell requires knowing what the options actually are.

This is not an argument for any single position. It is a map of the terrain. What you do with the map is between you and God. But you owe it to yourself — and to the people damaged by bad theology — to at least know what the tradition actually contains.

Eternal Conscious Torment: The Majority Tradition

The view most commonly associated with Christianity — and the one that has dominated Western theology since the fifth century — is eternal conscious torment (ECT). On this view, those who die without saving faith in Christ are consigned to hell, where they experience conscious suffering for all eternity. There is no exit. There is no reprieve. The punishment is infinite in duration, regardless of the finite nature of the sins committed.

The theological foundations of this view were laid primarily by Augustine of Hippo (354-430), who argued in The City of God that the punishment of the wicked is eternal in the same sense that the blessedness of the righteous is eternal — both are without end. Augustine's influence on Western Christianity was immense, and his interpretation of hell became, for practical purposes, the default position of both Catholic and Protestant theology.

Jonathan Edwards, in his 1741 sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," gave the doctrine its most vivid — and most terrifying — expression in the American context. Edwards described sinners dangling over the pit of hell like a spider held over a flame, preserved from falling only by the arbitrary mercy of a God who is under no obligation to sustain them. The sermon was a masterpiece of rhetorical terror, and it shaped American evangelicalism's relationship to hell for centuries.

The biblical case for ECT rests primarily on a handful of texts: Matthew 25:46, where Jesus speaks of "eternal punishment"; Revelation 20:10, which describes the devil being "tormented day and night forever and ever"; and Mark 9:48, where Jesus, quoting Isaiah, describes a place "where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched." Supporters of ECT argue that these texts, taken at face value, teach a punishment that is both conscious and unending.

The philosophical and moral objections to ECT are formidable. The most common objection is the disproportion between the offense and the punishment. How can a finite life of sin — even a life of extraordinary wickedness — merit infinite suffering? If a human judge sentenced a thief to an eternity of torture, we would call that judge a monster. How can we call God just for doing the same? The traditional response — that sin against an infinite God merits infinite punishment — has struck many theologians, including some firmly within the evangelical tradition, as a rationalization rather than an argument.

Annihilationism: Conditional Immortality

Annihilationism, also known as conditional immortality, holds that the unsaved do not suffer eternally but are ultimately destroyed — that the final punishment is not everlasting torment but the cessation of existence. On this view, immortality is not an inherent property of the human soul but a gift of God, granted to the redeemed and withheld from the lost. The wicked are raised, judged, punished proportionally to their sins, and then annihilated. They cease to exist.

The view gained significant attention in the evangelical world when John Stott, one of the most respected evangelical leaders of the twentieth century, cautiously endorsed it in his 1988 dialogue with David Edwards. "I find the concept intolerable," Stott wrote of eternal conscious torment, "and do not understand how people can live with it without either cauterizing their feelings or cracking under the strain." Stott argued that the biblical language of "destruction" and "perishing" should be taken at face value: the lost are destroyed, not preserved in torment.

Edward Fudge, in his exhaustive study The Fire That Consumes (1982, revised 2011), provided the most thorough biblical case for annihilationism. Fudge argued that the Old Testament consistently presents death as the final punishment for sin, not everlasting torment; that the New Testament language of "eternal punishment" refers to a punishment whose results are eternal (permanent destruction), not a punishment whose process is eternal (unending torment); and that the imagery of fire in the Bible is consistently associated with consumption and destruction, not preservation and ongoing pain.

The annihilationist position has gained significant ground in recent decades, particularly among evangelical scholars. Clark Pinnock, John Wenham, and the contributors to the Rethinking Hell project have all argued for some version of conditional immortality. The Evangelical Alliance in the UK, in its 2000 report The Nature of Hell, acknowledged annihilationism as a legitimate evangelical position, while affirming that ECT remained the majority view.

Christian Universalism: The Hope That All Will Be Saved

Christian universalism holds that God's redemptive purposes will ultimately encompass all of creation — that in the end, every human being will be reconciled to God, and hell, whatever it is, will be emptied. This is not the same as the popular caricature of universalism, which suggests that sin does not matter and everyone goes to heaven regardless. Christian universalists take sin with full seriousness. They simply believe that God's grace is more powerful than human rebellion, and that the story does not end until God's love has won every heart.

The tradition is ancient. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184-253), one of the most brilliant minds in the early church, taught apokatastasis — the final restoration of all things, including the eventual salvation of the devil. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335-395), one of the Cappadocian Fathers and a key architect of Trinitarian theology, held a similar view, arguing that evil is by nature finite and will eventually be consumed by the infinite goodness of God. Both Origen and Gregory stood well within the mainstream of their era; the condemnation of Origen's broader theological system at the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553) was directed at other aspects of his thought, and scholars debate whether apokatastasis itself was formally condemned.

In the twentieth century, Karl Barth's theology left the door open to universalism, though Barth refused to state it as a certainty. Barth insisted that God's election in Christ is an election of all humanity — that in Christ, God has said "Yes" to the whole human race. Whether this "Yes" is ultimately irresistible, Barth would not say. He regarded universalism as a hope that must not be foreclosed, but also as a conclusion that must not be presumed, because to presume it would be to place a limit on God's freedom.

David Bentley Hart, in That All Shall Be Saved (2019), offered the most ambitious recent defense of universalism, arguing that eternal conscious torment is not merely unappealing but logically incoherent — that a God who creates beings he knows will suffer eternally cannot be called good in any meaningful sense of the word. Hart's argument is philosophical, exegetical, and patristic, drawing on the Greek Fathers to claim that universalism is not a modern invention but the deepest current in the earliest Christian tradition.

Purgatory: The Catholic Position

The Catholic doctrine of purgatory offers a fourth framework. On this view, those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified undergo a process of purification after death before entering the fullness of heaven. Purgatory is not a "second chance" for the damned; it is a completion of the sanctification that was begun in this life but left unfinished at death. The doctrine was formally defined at the Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1563), though its roots extend back to the early church's practice of praying for the dead — a practice that implies the dead are in a state where prayers can benefit them.

The logic of purgatory is, in some respects, straightforward. Most people who die in faith are manifestly not saints. They retain habits of sin, disordered loves, and incomplete transformation. If heaven is the full experience of God's presence, and if the unreformed soul is incapable of experiencing that presence fully, then some process of final purification seems necessary. The Catholic tradition locates this process after death. Many Protestant theologians, while rejecting the formal doctrine, have struggled with the same underlying question: how does a partially sanctified person become fit for the full presence of God?

C.S. Lewis, an Anglican, expressed sympathy for something like purgatory in Letters to Malcolm: "Our souls demand Purgatory, don't they? Would it not break the heart if God said to us, 'It is true, my son, that your breath smells and your rags drip with mud and slime, but we are charitable here and no one will upbraid you with these things, nor draw away from you. Enter into the joy'? Should we not reply, 'With submission, sir, and if there is no objection, I'd rather be cleaned first'?"

The Biblical Data

Part of the difficulty in the hell debate is that the biblical data is less uniform than any of the positions typically admits. The key terms themselves are complex. "Sheol" in the Old Testament is the shadowy abode of the dead — all the dead, righteous and wicked alike — and carries no connotation of punishment. It is the grave, the underworld, the place where the dead exist in a diminished state. "Hades" in the New Testament roughly corresponds to Sheol and similarly does not always carry a punitive sense. "Gehenna," the term most often translated as "hell" in Jesus' teaching, refers to the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem — a place associated with child sacrifice in Israel's history and, by the first century, with the burning of refuse. Whether Jesus intended "Gehenna" as a literal description of an afterlife destination or as a vivid metaphor for the consequences of rejecting God's reign is a matter of ongoing scholarly debate.

The "lake of fire" in Revelation 20 is explicitly identified within the text as "the second death" — language that the annihilationist reads as destruction, the traditionalist reads as eternal torment, and the universalist reads as the death of death itself. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) is often cited as evidence for conscious torment after death, but parables are notoriously poor vehicles for extracting doctrinal propositions — no one argues from the parable of the prodigal son that heaven literally involves a feast with fattened calves.

Why It Matters

The hell debate is not an abstract theological exercise. How you understand hell shapes how you understand God, and how you understand God shapes everything else. If hell is eternal conscious torment, then God is a being who sustains the existence of the damned for the sole purpose of punishing them forever — a being whose justice requires infinite suffering for finite offenses. If hell is annihilation, then God is a being who respects the finality of human choices, even the choice to reject God's love, but does not perpetuate suffering beyond what justice requires. If hell is ultimately emptied, then God is a being whose love is relentless enough to pursue every soul until every soul is won.

Each view has consequences for evangelism, for pastoral care, for the way Christians treat those outside the faith. A Christianity built on the terror of eternal torment will produce a certain kind of convert — one motivated by fear rather than love, one whose relationship with God is fundamentally coercive. A Christianity built on the hope of universal redemption will produce a different kind of community — one less anxious, perhaps, but also less urgent. The stakes are not merely theological. They are human.

What I will not do is tell you which view is correct. What I will do is insist that you know what the options are — that you understand the tradition is broader, more diverse, and more internally contested than the version of hell you were probably taught. The God behind the doctrine matters more than the doctrine itself. And whatever hell turns out to be, the God revealed in Jesus Christ is a God who went to the cross to keep people out of it. That much, at least, is not in dispute.
excerpt: The Christian tradition has never spoken with one voice about hell. The honest conversation requires knowing what the options actually are — and what each one reveals about the God who stands behind it.

title: Science and Faith Are Not at War
body:
The narrative is so deeply embedded in Western culture that it feels like a fact: science and religion have always been at war, and science has been winning. The narrative has its canonical stories — Galileo persecuted by the Inquisition, Darwin demolishing Genesis, Copernicus defying the church — and its implicit moral: as scientific knowledge advances, religious belief retreats, because the two are fundamentally incompatible. One deals in evidence; the other in wishful thinking. One progresses; the other regresses. The choice between them is a choice between reason and superstition.

This narrative is largely false. It is not false because the church has always been friendly to science — it has not. It is false because the relationship between science and faith is far more complex, far more collaborative, and far more interesting than the warfare metaphor allows. The conflict thesis, as historians of science call it, was itself an invention — a nineteenth-century polemical construction that serious historians have spent the last several decades dismantling.

The Conflict Thesis and Its Collapse

The idea that science and religion are inherently at war was popularized by two books: John William Draper's History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896). Both were enormously influential. Both were also deeply misleading. Draper and White had agendas — Draper was an anti-Catholic polemicist, and White was the president of Cornell University, which he had founded as a secular institution and needed to defend against religious critics. Their books were not dispassionate histories. They were advocacy documents dressed in historical clothing.

The conflict thesis has been rejected by virtually every serious historian of science working today. David Lindberg and Ronald Numbers, in their landmark edited volume God and Nature: Historical Essays on the Encounter Between Christianity and Science (1986), demonstrated that the relationship between Christianity and the natural sciences has been characterized far more by complexity, collaboration, and mutual influence than by conflict. John Hedley Brooke's Science and Religion: Some Historical Perspectives (1991) came to the same conclusion. The consensus among historians of science is clear: the warfare metaphor is a myth.

This does not mean there have been no conflicts. There have been real and significant episodes of tension between scientific findings and theological claims. But these episodes have been the exception, not the rule, and even the canonical examples — Galileo, Darwin — are far more complicated than the popular versions suggest.

What Actually Happened with Galileo

The Galileo affair is the founding myth of the conflict narrative: a courageous scientist persecuted by an ignorant church for daring to assert that the earth moves around the sun. The actual history is considerably more tangled.

Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) was a devout Catholic who never abandoned his faith. His heliocentric views, published in Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632), drew on the work of Copernicus — who was himself a Catholic canon, and whose De Revolutionibus (1543) had been dedicated to Pope Paul III. The Copernican system had circulated for decades without provoking significant ecclesiastical opposition. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, the most prominent theologian of the era, had stated explicitly that if heliocentrism were scientifically demonstrated, the church would need to reinterpret the relevant biblical passages.

What turned the Galileo case from a scientific debate into a confrontation was a combination of personal politics, ecclesiastical power dynamics, and Galileo's own rhetorical missteps. Galileo's Dialogue placed the geocentric arguments in the mouth of a character named Simplicio — a name that could be read as "simpleton" — and Pope Urban VIII, who had previously been Galileo's patron, believed that Simplicio's arguments were a caricature of his own views. The prosecution of Galileo was driven as much by wounded pride and political calculation as by theological conviction. The Inquisition's condemnation was real, and it was wrong. But it was not a case of science versus religion in any straightforward sense. It was a case of institutional power, personal animosity, and theological overreach — a failure of the church to distinguish between the Bible's theological message and the cosmological assumptions of its authors.

Darwin and the Church: The Actual Record

The popular narrative of Darwin's reception is similarly oversimplified. The story usually told goes like this: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, the church reacted with horror, and the famous debate between Thomas Henry Huxley and Bishop Samuel Wilberforce at Oxford in 1860 settled the matter in science's favor. The actual history is far more diverse.

Many Christians — including prominent theologians and clergy — accepted evolution relatively quickly. Asa Gray, the foremost American botanist and a devout Christian, was Darwin's most important ally in the United States and saw no conflict between evolution and faith. Charles Kingsley, an Anglican clergyman and novelist, wrote to Darwin that it was "just as noble a conception of Deity to believe that He created primal forms capable of self-development" as to believe in special creation. B.B. Warfield, the Princeton theologian most associated with the doctrine of biblical inerrancy, accepted a form of theistic evolution — a fact that would astonish many of his modern admirers.

The Huxley-Wilberforce debate, far from being the decisive confrontation of popular memory, was actually a minor event at the time. The story was embellished and mythologized in subsequent decades, largely by Huxley's allies, to serve the narrative of science's triumph over religion. Contemporary accounts of the debate are inconsistent — witnesses disagreed about what was said, who won, and whether the exchange was as dramatic as later versions claimed.

The opposition to Darwin that did exist came not only from religious quarters. Many scientists — including figures like Lord Kelvin, who objected on thermodynamic grounds, and St. George Jackson Mivart, who offered scientific criticisms of natural selection — resisted Darwin's theory on scientific, not religious, grounds. The debate over evolution in the nineteenth century was genuinely complex. The reduction of that complexity to "science versus religion" is a distortion of the historical record.

Christians and the History of Science

The conflict thesis obscures one of the most remarkable features of the history of science: the central role that Christian institutions and Christian thinkers played in the development of the scientific enterprise. The medieval university system — the institutional framework within which modern science emerged — was a creation of the church. The University of Paris, the University of Oxford, the University of Bologna — all were founded under ecclesiastical authority in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The monks and clerics who populated these institutions were not enemies of learning. They were its custodians.

The list of scientists who were devout Christians is not a list of exceptions. It is a catalog of the founders of modern science. Copernicus was a Catholic canon. Galileo remained a Catholic throughout his life. Johannes Kepler described his astronomical work as "thinking God's thoughts after him." Isaac Newton wrote more pages of theology than of physics. Gregor Mendel, the founder of genetics, was an Augustinian friar. Georges Lemaitre, who proposed the Big Bang theory, was a Catholic priest. The assumption that scientific genius and religious belief are incompatible is contradicted by the very history of science itself.

The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead argued in Science and the Modern World (1925) that modern science was made possible by the medieval conviction, rooted in Christian theology, that the universe is rational and ordered — that it operates according to consistent laws because it is the creation of a rational God. This conviction, Whitehead argued, provided the philosophical foundation for the scientific method: the belief that the universe is intelligible, that its patterns can be discovered, and that the human mind is equipped to discover them. Without this conviction, the enterprise of science would have no warrant.

Scientists Who Believe

The claim that serious scientists cannot be serious believers is refuted by the existence of serious scientists who are serious believers. Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project and served as director of the National Institutes of Health, is an evangelical Christian who has written extensively about the compatibility of faith and science. John Polkinghorne, a Cambridge particle physicist who became an Anglican priest, developed a sophisticated theology of science that integrates quantum mechanics and trinitarian theology. Jennifer Wiseman, a senior astrophysicist at NASA, has spoken publicly about how her study of the cosmos deepens rather than diminishes her Christian faith.

A 2009 Pew Research Center survey found that 51 percent of scientists believe in God or a higher power. The number is lower than the general population, but it is not negligible — and it demolishes the claim that scientific expertise is incompatible with religious belief. The National Academy of Sciences includes members who are devout Christians, Jews, Muslims, and adherents of other traditions. They do not check their faith at the laboratory door.

Models for the Relationship

If science and faith are not at war, what is their relationship? Several models have been proposed, each with strengths and limitations.

Stephen Jay Gould proposed the NOMA model — Non-Overlapping Magisteria — in his 1999 book Rocks of Ages. On this view, science and religion address fundamentally different questions: science asks how the natural world works; religion asks what it means and how we should live. The two domains do not overlap, and conflict arises only when one trespasses on the other's territory. The NOMA model has the virtue of clarity, but many thinkers — both scientific and theological — find it too neat. If God created the universe, then God's creative action must have some relationship to the universe that science studies. And if science discovers features of the universe that bear on questions of meaning — the fine-tuning of cosmological constants, the emergence of consciousness — then the magisteria do overlap, whether we want them to or not.

The dialogue model, associated with Ian Barbour and others, holds that science and religion address different questions but that their answers interact and can inform each other. Scientific discoveries about the age of the universe, the evolution of life, and the nature of consciousness raise questions that theology has resources to address. Theological convictions about the goodness of creation, the value of human life, and the reality of moral obligation raise questions that science alone cannot answer. The two disciplines are in conversation, not competition.

The integration model goes further, arguing that science and theology can be woven into a single, coherent framework. Teilhard de Chardin, the Jesuit paleontologist, attempted a grand synthesis of evolutionary biology and Christian theology.
