The parent cannot imagine how a thoughtful person could abandon the faith. The adult child cannot imagine how a thoughtful person could maintain it. Both are wrong. Thoughtful people, with access to the same evidence, reach different conclusions about the most fundamental questions of existence. This has been true for the entire history of human thought, and it will remain true long after your family argument is over.

The Specific Pain of Shared Holidays

Holidays concentrate the conflict into a single day, a single table, a single prayer that someone at the table no longer believes in and someone else at the table considers the most important moment of the meal. Christmas, Easter, Thanksgiving — these are the dates on which the theological divide becomes physically present, sitting across from you, passing the potatoes.

The believing parent who insists on the traditional prayer before the Christmas meal is not merely saying grace. They are, in the experience of the adult child who has left the faith, asserting a reality the child can no longer affirm. The adult child who refuses to bow their head is not merely declining a ritual. They are, in the experience of the parent, rejecting the family's deepest identity. Both interpretations are real. Neither is complete. And the only way through is the willingness to hold both realities simultaneously — to let the prayer happen without demanding participation, and to let the non-participation happen without interpreting it as an attack.

Some families develop rituals that honor both realities. A moment of silence rather than a spoken prayer. A gratitude practice that does not require theological commitment. A new tradition that belongs to the whole family as it is now, not as it was. These accommodations are not compromises in the pejorative sense. They are creative acts of love — the family's effort to build a container large enough to hold all of its members, even the ones who have changed.

Maintaining Relationship Across the Divide

The first principle of maintaining relationship across a theological divide is the simplest and the hardest: stop trying to fix each other. The parent who is constantly slipping devotional books into care packages is not expressing love. They are expressing the conviction that their child is broken and needs repair. The adult child who is constantly sending secular critiques of religion is not sharing interesting reading. They are expressing the conviction that their parent is deluded and needs correction. Both gestures, however well-intentioned, communicate the same message: "I cannot accept you as you are."

The second principle is to learn the difference between your grief and their problem. If your child has left the faith, your grief is legitimate. But it is your grief, not their crisis. Processing that grief is your responsibility — through prayer, through conversation with a trusted friend or counselor, through the slow work of releasing the outcomes you cannot control. It is not your child's responsibility to manage your grief by pretending to believe what they do not believe. The moment you make your emotional wellbeing contingent on their theological compliance, you have weaponized the relationship.

The third principle is to find the ground that remains. Even in families where the theological divide is total, there is almost always shared ground: shared values (honesty, compassion, justice), shared loves (family, nature, art, good food), shared history (the stories, traditions, and inside jokes that constitute the fabric of family life). A family that cannot worship together can still eat together, laugh together, serve together, and show up for each other in crisis. These shared practices are not a consolation prize for the loss of shared faith. They are the substance of family life, and they have their own integrity and their own capacity to bear the weight of love.

Setting Boundaries Without Severing Ties

Boundaries are not walls. This distinction is crucial, because in families where faith is contested, both sides tend to confuse the two. The parent who cannot stop proselytizing needs a boundary, not a wall: "Mom, I love you. I know my faith journey worries you. But I need you to stop bringing it up every time we talk. If you keep doing it, I will have to limit our conversations, and I do not want to do that." The adult child who cannot stop mocking their parent's faith needs the same: "I am glad you have found a way of seeing the world that works for you. But when you dismiss what I believe, it hurts me. I need you to stop."

These conversations are excruciating. They require the willingness to name the harm without abandoning the relationship — to say, in effect, "What you are doing is hurting me, and I am asking you to stop, but I am not going anywhere." The boundary preserves the relationship by protecting it from the behavior that is destroying it. The wall terminates the relationship altogether. The goal is the boundary, not the wall.

There are situations in which the wall is necessary. When the family member's behavior crosses from disagreement into abuse — when the proselytizing becomes harassment, when the dismissal becomes contempt, when the theological difference is used as a weapon to control, shame, or manipulate — the wall is a legitimate act of self-preservation. But it should be the last resort, not the first response, and it should be accompanied by the honest acknowledgment that you are making a choice with consequences you cannot fully foresee.

The practical mechanics of boundaries in faith-divided families deserve specific attention. A boundary is most effective when it is stated clearly, maintained consistently, and accompanied by a visible demonstration of continued love. The family member who sets a boundary about religious conversations but then shows up faithfully for birthdays, calls regularly about non-theological matters, and demonstrates genuine interest in the other person's life is communicating something essential: "I am not rejecting you. I am protecting our relationship from the one thing that is destroying it." The boundary without the continued presence is experienced as rejection. The continued presence without the boundary is experienced as permission to continue the harmful behavior. Both elements are necessary.

Time is an underestimated factor in these conflicts. The acute crisis of discovery — the initial revelation that a family member's faith has changed — is almost always the worst moment. Emotions are raw, fears are at their peak, and neither side has developed the capacity to hold the new reality. Six months later, the situation is usually different. A year later, more different still. Families that can survive the initial shock often find, over time, that the theological divide does not determine the quality of the relationship nearly as much as they feared. The relationship adjusts. New patterns emerge. The family discovers that it is larger than its theology, that its bonds are deeper than its beliefs, and that love, while not omnipotent, is remarkably durable.

The deepest truth about faith transitions and family conflict is that they expose the quality of the family's love. A family that can only love each other when they agree about God does not actually have the kind of love that God demands. The love described in 1 Corinthians 13 — love that is patient, kind, that does not insist on its own way, that bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things — is precisely the love that is needed when the agreement breaks down. It is easy to love someone who shares your faith. It is the work of a lifetime to love someone who does not. And it may be that this particular work is the one your faith was always preparing you for.
excerpt: Faith transitions do not happen in isolation. They happen in families. And the family that cannot hold theological difference cannot hold each other.

title: Christianity After Christendom
body:
On February 27, 380 AD, Emperor Theodosius I issued the Edict of Thessalonica, declaring Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire. With a single imperial decree, the faith of a persecuted minority became the faith of the state. Churches that had met in catacombs and private homes were suddenly building basilicas with public funds. Bishops who had been imprisoned became advisors to emperors. The cross, which had been the instrument of the movement's founder's execution, was mounted on the standards of the imperial legions. The transformation was so complete and so rapid that within a generation, it was nearly impossible to remember what Christianity had been before it had power.

That transformation — from persecuted sect to established religion, from voluntary community to cultural default — is what historians call "Christendom." And for approximately 1,600 years, it was the dominant mode of Christian existence in the Western world. Whether you were born in medieval France, Reformation Germany, colonial New England, or mid-twentieth-century America, Christianity was the water you swam in — the assumed religious framework of your culture, the default setting of public morality, the invisible architecture of your social world. You did not choose Christianity. It chose you, by virtue of your birth into a civilization shaped by its institutions, assumptions, and calendar.

Christendom is over. The sociological evidence is overwhelming and has been accumulating for decades. Charles Taylor, in his magisterial A Secular Age, traces the shift from a society in which belief in God was the unquestioned default to one in which it is merely one option among many — and not the most culturally prestigious option at that. In 1960, the sociologist Peter Berger predicted that by the twenty-first century, religion would persist only in small, embattled enclaves. He was partially wrong about the global picture — religion has proven far more resilient worldwide than secularization theorists predicted — but he was remarkably prescient about the West. In America, in Europe, in Canada, in Australia, the cultural dominance of Christianity has collapsed within a single lifetime.

The question that confronts every thoughtful Christian is not how to reverse this collapse. That project has been tried, repeatedly and with increasing desperation, and it has failed. The question is what Christianity looks like when it is no longer the cultural default — when being a Christian is not something you inherit but something you choose, at a cost, against the grain of the culture rather than with it.

The End of Cultural Christianity

The most significant consequence of the end of Christendom is the disappearance of the cultural Christian — the person who identified as Christian not out of conviction but out of convention. In 1972, when the General Social Survey first asked Americans about their religious identity, less than 5 percent said "none." These were not all devout believers. Many were nominal — attending church on Easter and Christmas, checking "Protestant" on forms, vaguely assenting to theism without it making any discernible difference in their lives. They were Christian the way they were American: by accident of birth, reinforced by social expectation, never seriously examined.

The rise of the "nones" — from 5 percent in 1972 to 29 percent in 2023 — does not primarily represent a wave of deconversion. It represents the departure of the nominally committed. The people who are leaving are, by and large, the people who were never really there — who attended out of social obligation, who identified out of cultural habit, who held the label without the substance. Their departure is not a loss of faith. It is the shedding of a pretense.

This should not be mourned. It should be recognized for what it is: a clarification. For the first time in 1,600 years, the boundary between the church and the culture is becoming visible again. The people who remain — who continue to identify as Christian, who continue to attend worship, who continue to practice the faith — are increasingly people who have made a deliberate choice. They are there because they believe, not because they are expected to be there. And a church composed of people who have chosen to be there is a fundamentally different institution from a church composed of people who have never considered the alternative.

Before Constantine

The pre-Constantinian church — the church of the first three centuries — is the closest historical analogue to the situation Western Christians now face. And its characteristics are instructive, not as a template to be replicated but as evidence that Christianity can not only survive without cultural power but can thrive without it.

The pre-Constantinian church was small. At the time of Constantine's conversion in 312, Christians comprised approximately 10 percent of the Roman Empire's population — perhaps six million people in an empire of sixty million. They were a minority, and they knew it. Their self-understanding was shaped not by triumphalism but by vulnerability. They were, in the language of 1 Peter, "foreigners and exiles" — people whose primary citizenship was elsewhere, who lived in the empire but did not fully belong to it.

The pre-Constantinian church was communal. The primary unit of Christian life was not the individual believer or the nuclear family but the ekklesia — the gathered community. Early Christian worship took place in homes (the archaeological evidence for purpose-built churches before 250 is almost nonexistent), and the house church functioned not merely as a worship space but as an economic community. Members shared resources. The wealthy subsidized the poor. Widows, orphans, and the destitute were supported from a common fund. The Roman observer Lucian of Samosata, writing in the second century, noted with evident bafflement that Christians "look after their poor" and that "their first lawgiver persuaded them that they are all brothers."

The pre-Constantinian church was costly. To become a Christian in the second century was to accept social exclusion, economic disadvantage, and the real possibility of state-sponsored violence. The catechumenate — the process of preparation for baptism — lasted up to three years and involved not merely doctrinal instruction but a comprehensive reordering of the candidate's social and economic life. Certain professions were incompatible with baptism: soldiers, gladiators, actors, prostitutes, magistrates who administered capital punishment. To be baptized was to accept that certain doors were now closed to you, certain social networks severed, certain career paths abandoned. It was, in every meaningful sense, a death — a voluntary death of the old self and its allegiances, in exchange for a new identity that the empire regarded with suspicion and occasionally with lethal hostility.

The pre-Constantinian church was prophetic. Because it had no political power, it had no political obligations. It could speak truth to the empire without worrying about the electoral consequences. It could critique the emperor without fearing the loss of its tax-exempt status. It could champion the cause of the poor without calculating the impact on its donor base. The prophetic voice of the early church was credible precisely because it came from a position of powerlessness. The church that speaks from the steps of the Capitol does not sound the same as the church that speaks from the catacombs, even if it is saying the same words.

The Four Marks of Post-Christendom Faith

If the pre-Constantinian church is our closest historical precedent, then the faith that is emerging in the post-Christendom West will be marked by four characteristics that mirror the early church's experience — not because we are trying to replicate it, but because the same conditions produce the same adaptations.

The first mark is voluntariness. Post-Christendom faith is chosen faith. Nobody drifts into it. Nobody inherits it without examination. Nobody maintains it out of social convention because there is no longer a social convention to maintain. This means that the Christianity that survives the end of Christendom will be a Christianity of conviction — smaller, yes, but more intentional, more committed, and more capable of articulating why it believes what it believes. The cultural Christian, who never had to give a reason for the faith, is gone. The post-Christendom Christian must know what they believe, why they believe it, and what it costs them — because someone will ask, and "because that's how I was raised" is no longer a sufficient answer.

The second mark is costliness. When Christianity is the cultural default, believing costs nothing. When it is a minority position, believing costs something — social capital, professional advancement, the easy assumption that your worldview is normal. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's distinction between "cheap grace" and "costly grace" was prophetic: "Cheap grace is the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, baptism without church discipline, Communion without confession. Cheap grace is grace without discipleship, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ, living and incarnate." Christendom was, in many ways, a system for the mass production of cheap grace. Its end may be the recovery of the costly kind.

The third mark is communality. The individualistic Christianity of modern America — in which faith is a personal relationship with Jesus that requires no community, no accountability, no institutional commitment — is a product of Christendom. It was possible to be a "lone ranger" Christian only because the culture did the work of formation that the community should have been doing. Without cultural Christianity to provide the ambient support, the individual Christian who is disconnected from community will not survive. The post-Christendom church will be, of necessity, a community of mutual formation — a people who gather not because it is socially expected but because they cannot sustain their faith alone.

The fourth mark is prophetic witness. The church that has divested itself of political power is the church that is free to speak prophetically again. The reason the American church's moral voice has been so thoroughly discredited is not that it has spoken too much but that it has spoken from a position of power, using the language of prophecy to advance the interests of empire. The post-Christendom church, stripped of its political influence, can recover the prophetic voice — speaking truth to power rather than as power, advocating for the marginalized rather than for its own institutional interests, critiquing the culture from a position of costly solidarity rather than comfortable distance.

Why This Might Be the Best Thing

There is a persistent fear among American Christians that the end of Christendom is the end of Christianity. This fear is understandable but historically unfounded. Christianity was born as a minority movement in a hostile empire, and it not only survived but transformed that empire — not through political power but through the quality of its common life. The faith that survived the Roman arena, the barbarian invasions, the Islamic conquests, the Mongol devastation, the French Revolution, and Soviet persecution is not going to be defeated by the American nones.

The end of Christendom is the end of a particular arrangement — the fusion of Christian faith with cultural power — that has been as much a liability as an asset for the church's mission. Christendom gave the church buildings, budgets, social prestige, and political influence. It also gave the church the Crusades, the Inquisition, the justification of slavery, the persecution of Jews, the suppression of scientific inquiry, and the confusion of the gospel with Western civilization. The ledger is, at best, mixed. And there is a strong case to be made that the liabilities have outweighed the assets — that the church's entanglement with power has done more to obscure the gospel than any persecution could have accomplished.

The missionary Lesslie Newbigin, returning to England in 1974 after decades of service in India, was struck by a paradox: the post-Christian West was, in many ways, harder mission territory than pre-Christian India. India had never heard the gospel and was curious. England had heard it, domesticated it, and was bored. The challenge of post-Christendom is not ignorance of Christianity but familiarity with a distorted version of it — a version so entangled with power, privilege, and cultural conformity that the original message has been obscured beyond recognition.

And yet the collapse of Christendom has also produced something unexpected: a generation of people who are genuinely hungry for the things the gospel offers — community, meaning, moral formation, hope in the face of death — but who have never encountered those things in a form untainted by institutional corruption and political manipulation. The post-Christian person is not, typically, hostile to Jesus. They are hostile to what the church has done with Jesus. And that distinction matters enormously, because it means the mission field is not closed. It is waiting for a version of the faith that matches the original. The sociologist of religion Rodney Stark demonstrated that the early church grew not through evangelistic campaigns but through the attractiveness of its common life — through the visible evidence that Christians loved each other and their neighbors in ways the surrounding culture could not replicate. The post-Christendom church has the opportunity to demonstrate the same thing, and the advantage of not having to overcome the baggage of establishment religion to do it.

There are signs that this is already happening. The growth of intentional Christian communities, the renewed interest in ancient liturgical practices among young adults, the emergence of churches that prioritize justice, intellectual honesty, and hospitality over political alignment and cultural conformity — these are not the signs of a faith in retreat. They are the signs of a faith in renovation. The building is being stripped to its foundation, and what is being discovered beneath the layers of Christendom is a foundation that is more solid, more radical, and more compelling than many had dared to hope.

The opportunity, then, is not to rebuild Christendom — to "take back" the culture, to restore the Christian consensus, to make Christianity the default again. That project is not only doomed to fail; it is theologically misguided. Jesus did not come to establish a civilization. He came to inaugurate a kingdom — a kingdom that operates by different rules than any empire, that measures greatness by service rather than dominance, and that advances not through the sword but through the cross.

The post-Christendom church has the opportunity to recover that kingdom vision — to rediscover a faith that is voluntary rather than compulsory, costly rather than comfortable, communal rather than individualistic, and prophetic rather than politically captive. This will be a smaller church. It will be a poorer church. It will be a church without a seat at the table of power. But it may also be a church that more closely resembles the one Jesus described — the mustard seed, the leaven in the dough, the treasure hidden in a field. Small, hidden, transformative. Not the empire's religion. The empire's conscience.

That is a future worth moving toward. Not with nostalgia for what has been lost, but with hope for what might be recovered — a faith stripped of its cultural privilege, reduced to its essence, and discovered, perhaps for the first time in sixteen centuries, to be enough.
excerpt: The era when Christianity was the cultural default is over. What comes next may be harder, smaller, and more costly. It may also be closer to the faith that Jesus actually described.

title: The Spirituality of Doubt
body:
The assumption that faith and doubt are opposites — that to believe is to be certain, and to question is to fail — is one of the most damaging ideas in the history of Christianity. It has driven millions from the church, not because they lacked faith but because they had been taught that the experience of doubt was evidence that their faith was defective. The equation is simple, devastating, and wrong: if you doubt, you do not truly believe; if you do not truly believe, you are not truly saved; therefore doubt is not merely an intellectual experience but a spiritual emergency. Under this framework, the questioning mind is not a gift. It is a threat. And the church's response to threat has historically been suppression.

But this equation has no support in Scripture, no precedent in the deepest streams of Christian tradition, and no correspondence with the actual experience of the saints. The biblical narrative is, from beginning to end, a record of people who believed and doubted simultaneously — who trusted God and argued with God in the same breath, who obeyed and protested, who worshipped and wept. The flattening of faith into certainty is a modern invention, a product of the Enlightenment's demand that all knowledge conform to the standard of mathematical proof. It is not a Christian idea. It is a secular one, baptized by fundamentalism and passed off as orthodoxy.

The Biblical Doubters

Abraham is the paradigmatic figure of faith in the Jewish and Christian traditions — the man who "believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6, cited by Paul in Romans 4:3). And yet this same Abraham, having received God's promise of descendants as numerous as the stars, laughed at the absurdity of the promise (Genesis 17:17) and conspired with Sarah to produce an heir through Hagar because he apparently did not trust God to deliver on the original commitment (Genesis 16). Abraham's faith was not the absence of doubt. It was the decision to act on the promise despite the doubt. The believing and the laughing happened in the same person, at the same time.

Moses, at the burning bush, responded to God's commission with a cascade of objections: Who am I to go to Pharaoh? What if they do not believe me? I am not eloquent enough. Please send someone else. These are not the responses of a man filled with confident faith. They are the responses of a man who is being asked to stake his life on a voice from a bush, and who finds the proposition, at minimum, questionable. God does not rebuke Moses for doubting. God provides the signs, the words, and the companion that Moses's doubt requires. The doubt is not an obstacle to the mission. It is the occasion for God to demonstrate the resources available within it.

The book of Job is the most sustained meditation on doubt in the entire biblical canon. Job, the righteous sufferer, does not respond to catastrophic loss with pious acceptance. He responds with protest, accusation, and demand. "Why did I not perish at birth?" (3:11). "Does it please you to oppress me?" (10:3). "Though he slay me, yet will I hope in him — but I will argue my case before him" (13:15, a verse whose Hebrew is so ambiguous that translators disagree on whether Job is expressing trust or defiance, and the ambiguity may be the point). Job's friends, who insist on theological certainty in the face of inexplicable suffering, are the ones God rebukes at the end of the book: "You have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has" (42:7). The doubter is vindicated. The defenders of orthodoxy are corrected.

The Psalms are saturated with doubt. The lament psalms — which constitute roughly a third of the Psalter — give voice to confusion, anger, abandonment, and the experience of God's apparent absence. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1). "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). "Has God forgotten to be gracious?" (Psalm 77:9). These are not the words of people who lack faith. They are the words of people who have enough faith to bring their doubt to God rather than concealing it — who trust God enough to be honest with God, even when honesty means accusation.

Thomas, the apostle who has been saddled with the epithet "Doubting" for two millennia, deserves better. His refusal to accept the resurrection on the testimony of his fellow disciples — "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe" (John 20:25) — is not a failure of faith. It is the demand of a person who has been burned by too many false hopes, who has watched the man he followed die on a cross, and who is not willing to rebuild his entire world on the basis of secondhand reports. Jesus does not rebuke Thomas for doubting. He provides exactly what Thomas asked for: the evidence his doubt required. And Thomas's response — "My Lord and my God" (20:28) — is the highest christological confession in the entire Gospel of John. The doubter makes the deepest declaration of faith in the book.

The Dark Night of the Soul

The medieval mystics understood something about doubt that modern Christianity has largely forgotten: that the experience of God's absence can be a form of God's presence. The Spanish Carmelite John of the Cross (1542-1591) gave this experience its most enduring name: la noche oscura del alma, the dark night of the soul.

For John of the Cross, the dark night is not a punishment, a failure, or a sign of sin. It is a stage of spiritual development — the stage at which God withdraws the consolations of faith (the felt sense of God's presence, the emotional satisfaction of prayer, the intellectual confidence of belief) in order to deepen the soul's dependence on God alone. The dark night strips away everything that is not God — including your feelings about God, your ideas about God, and your experience of God — so that what remains is the naked reality of God, unmediated by sensation, concept, or emotion.

This is the most counterintuitive claim in the entire Christian mystical tradition: that the absence of the experience of God can be the deepest form of the experience of God. That the prayer that feels empty may be more real than the prayer that feels full. That the faith that persists through darkness is stronger than the faith that has never been tested by it.

Mother Teresa's posthumously published letters, collected in Come Be My Light, revealed that she experienced the dark night of the soul for nearly fifty years — from 1948 until her death in 1997. "Where is my faith?" she wrote to her confessor. "Even deep down, right in, there is nothing but emptiness and darkness. If there be God — please forgive me. When I try to raise my thoughts to Heaven, there is such convicting emptiness that those very thoughts return like sharp knives and hurt my very soul." The woman who was, in the public eye, a living saint was, in her interior life, a person living in nearly total spiritual darkness.

And yet she continued. She prayed without feeling. She served without consolation. She maintained the practices of faith in the complete absence of the experience that is supposed to accompany them. This is not the portrait of a woman who lacked faith. It is the portrait of a woman whose faith was so profound that it did not require the support of experience — who loved God without the reward of feeling loved in return. The dark night did not destroy her faith. It purified it, burning away everything that was not essential until only the essential remained: the bare decision to trust, enacted daily, in the dark.

Doubt as Growth

The developmental psychologist James Fowler, whose stages of faith theory has shaped contemporary understanding of spiritual development, described the transition from Stage 3 (Synthetic-Conventional faith, in which beliefs are held because one's community holds them) to Stage 4 (Individuative-Reflective faith, in which beliefs are critically examined and personally owned) as one of the most difficult transitions in human development. This transition is always experienced as doubt because it necessarily involves the questioning of everything that was previously taken for granted.

The critical insight is that this doubt is not the destruction of faith. It is the necessary precondition for a more mature faith. The person who has never doubted has never examined their beliefs. The person who has never examined their beliefs does not know what they believe — they know only what they have been told. And a faith that has never been tested by doubt is like a muscle that has never been tested by resistance: it may look impressive, but it has no actual strength.

Paul Tillich, the Protestant theologian, made a useful distinction between two kinds of doubt. "Methodological doubt" is the deliberate, disciplined questioning of assumptions for the purpose of arriving at a more secure foundation — the doubt of the scientist, the philosopher, the honest theologian. "Existential doubt" is the involuntary experience of uncertainty about the ultimate questions — the doubt that strikes at three in the morning, uninvited and unwelcome. Both kinds of doubt are spiritually productive. Methodological doubt refines theology. Existential doubt deepens dependence on God. Neither is the enemy of faith. Both are its servants.

Sitting with Uncertainty

The practical challenge, for the person living with doubt, is to resist the two equal and opposite temptations: the temptation to resolve the doubt prematurely (by forcing yourself back into a certainty you no longer honestly hold) and the temptation to resolve it by abandoning faith altogether (concluding that because you cannot be certain, you cannot believe at all). Both temptations are driven by the same underlying anxiety — the intolerance of ambiguity, the need for a settled answer, the fear of living in the space between knowing and not knowing.

The theologian Lesslie Newbigin wrote that the proper posture of faith is neither certainty nor uncertainty but "proper confidence" — the confidence of a person who acts on the best available evidence while remaining open to correction. This is the confidence of the scientist who publishes a theory knowing it may be overturned, the doctor who prescribes a treatment knowing it may not work, the lover who makes a commitment knowing it may be broken. It is not the certainty of proof. It is the confidence of trust — trust that is always, by its nature, at risk.

To sit with uncertainty is to accept that some questions do not have answers — at least not answers available to finite human beings in the middle of history. Why does a good God allow suffering? How can a loving God condemn? How does the cross actually accomplish salvation? These are questions that the greatest minds in Christian history have wrestled with and have not definitively resolved. If Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, and Barth could not produce certainty on these matters, you are in good company in your uncertainty. The demand that you produce certainty where the entire tradition has produced, at best, provisional formulations is not a demand of faith. It is a demand of anxiety. And anxiety, as Jesus repeatedly pointed out, is not a reliable guide to the kingdom.

The practices that sustain faith through doubt are not the practices of the certain. They are the practices of the committed: praying when prayer feels empty, gathering with the community when the community's beliefs feel uncertain, reading Scripture with the willingness to be surprised rather than the expectation of confirmation, sitting in silence and allowing the silence to be silent — not filling it with forced devotion but trusting that the silence itself is a form of God's presence, even when it does not feel like one.

Doubt is not the end of faith. It is faith doing its hardest work — the work of growing beyond the container it came in, the work of making room for a God who is larger than your certainty, the work of learning to trust not because you know but because you choose to. That choice, made daily, in the dark, without guarantee, is the most courageous act of faith there is. And it is enough.
excerpt: Doubt is not the opposite of faith. It is faith doing its hardest work. And the Christian tradition has always known this, even when the church forgot.

title: Reconstructing Faith: What Comes After Deconstruction
body:
The word "deconstruction" has become, in the last decade, the dominant metaphor for a particular kind of spiritual experience: the process of questioning, dismantling, and often abandoning the theological framework in which one was raised. The term itself migrated from literary theory (where Jacques Derrida used it to describe a method of textual analysis) to popular culture (where it describes a lived experience of faith unraveling), and in the process it acquired a weight that Derrida never intended and that the experience itself both justifies and exceeds.

The deconstruction conversation has been dominated by two voices, neither of which is particularly helpful. The first is the voice of celebration — the ex-evangelical memoirist, the deconversion influencer, the podcast host who treats every abandoned doctrine as a liberation and every departure from orthodoxy as a step toward enlightenment. This voice is understandable. Many people have been genuinely harmed by the religious systems they are deconstructing, and the relief of escape is real. But celebration as a permanent posture is unsustainable. You cannot build a life on what you have left. At some point, the question shifts from "What am I leaving?" to "Where am I going?" And that question is harder.

The second voice is the voice of condemnation — the pastor who treats deconstruction as apostasy, the apologist who treats it as intellectual weakness, the church leader who treats it as a trend that will pass if they just preach loud enough. This voice is also understandable. If you have spent your life building a theological system and a community structured around it, the sight of people walking away is genuinely threatening. But condemnation is not a pastoral response. It is a defensive one. And it ensures that the people who most need the church's wisdom will never hear it, because they have been told that their questions make them enemies.

Between celebration and condemnation lies the territory that almost nobody is mapping: reconstruction. What comes after the demolition? What gets rebuilt? And what does a faith look like that has passed through the fire of deconstruction and emerged — not unscathed, not unchanged, but intact?

The Wilderness Is Not the Destination

The biblical metaphor for the deconstructive experience is the wilderness — the liminal space between Egypt and the Promised Land, between the old life and the new one, between what was and what will be. The Israelites spent forty years in the wilderness, and the narrative makes clear that the wilderness was not pointless. It was formative. It was the place where the people who had been shaped by slavery were reshaped for freedom — where the habits, loyalties, and identities of Egypt were stripped away and replaced by something new. But the wilderness was never the destination. It was the passage.

This is the critical distinction that the deconstruction conversation often misses. The wilderness is necessary. The questioning is necessary. The stripping away of beliefs that were held for the wrong reasons, in the wrong way, or without adequate foundation is necessary. But it is a phase, not a resting place. The person who remains in the wilderness permanently — who makes a permanent identity out of their questioning, who defines themselves entirely by what they have left rather than what they are building — has confused the journey with the destination.

The philosopher Paul Ricoeur described a movement from "first naivete" through "critical distance" to "second naivete." First naivete is the uncritical faith of childhood — the faith that takes stories at face value, accepts doctrines without examination, and trusts authority without question. Critical distance is the deconstructive phase — the stage at which everything is questioned, examined, and often found wanting. Second naivete is the reconstruction — the return to the stories, the doctrines, and the practices with new eyes, a deeper understanding, and a willingness to inhabit them again, not with the uncritical acceptance of the child but with the chosen trust of the adult who has seen the alternatives and returned, knowing full well what they are choosing.

Second naivete is not a retreat to the original position. It is a new position altogether — one that holds what was true in the original faith while releasing what was false, that engages the tradition with both love and critical awareness, and that can say "I believe" without meaning "I have never questioned."

What Gets Rebuilt

The faith that emerges from reconstruction is not the faith that went into deconstruction. It cannot be. The demolition has done its work, and the materials that survive are not the same materials that went in. But certain things do survive, and naming them is important because the person in the wilderness needs to know that there is something worth walking toward.

What survives is a God who is large enough to contain your questions. The God of the reconstructed faith is not the small, manageable God of Sunday school — the God who fits neatly into systematic theology, who behaves predictably according to doctrinal formulations, who can be captured in a four-point gospel presentation. The God of the reconstructed faith is the God of Job, who answers the sufferer's questions not with explanations but with the overwhelming reality of divine presence. The God who says, in effect, "You cannot understand me, but you can trust me." This God is harder to live with than the Sunday school version. But this God is also more real, more worthy of worship, and more capable of sustaining a faith that has been tested.

What survives is a theology that can hold questions without being destroyed by them. The reconstructed faith does not claim certainty on every doctrinal point. It holds some things firmly (the character of God as revealed in Christ, the reality of grace, the call to love), some things lightly (the precise mechanics of atonement, the details of eschatology, the boundaries of salvation), and some things as open questions that may never be resolved in this life. This is not intellectual laziness. It is intellectual honesty — the acknowledgment that finite human beings working with limited evidence in the middle of history are not in a position to achieve certainty about the infinite. The demand for certainty on every point is not faith. It is anxiety dressed as theology.

What survives is an ethic rooted in the teaching and example of Jesus rather than in the culture war priorities of contemporary Christianity. The person who has deconstructed the political captivity of American evangelicalism often discovers, with some surprise, that the actual teaching of Jesus is more radical, more demanding, and more beautiful than anything the institutional church had led them to expect. The Sermon on the Mount, read without the filters of denominational tradition and political expedience, is a genuinely revolutionary document — a manifesto for a way of life that challenges every human power structure, including the ones the church has built in Jesus's name.

The Practices of Reconstruction

Reconstruction does not happen through argument. It happens through practice. The faith that was deconstructed was, in many cases, a faith of ideas — a set of propositions to be believed, a system to be defended, a worldview to be maintained. The faith that is reconstructed is a faith of practices — a set of disciplines to be enacted, a way of life to be inhabited, a community to be joined. The shift from proposition to practice is one of the most significant transitions in the reconstructive journey.

Liturgy is one of the most common landing places for the deconstructed Christian, and this is not accidental. Liturgical worship — the ancient patterns of prayer, Scripture reading, confession, communion, and benediction that have shaped Christian worship for nearly two millennia — does not demand that you feel a particular way or believe a particular thing at any given moment. It carries you. The words of the liturgy are there when your own words fail. The rhythm of the church year provides a structure for the spiritual life when your own internal structure has collapsed. The Eucharist is offered not to the worthy or the certain but to the hungry — and the person in reconstruction is, above all else, hungry.

Community is essential and terrifying. The deconstructed Christian has, almost by definition, been wounded by community — by a church that demanded conformity, silenced questions, or punished departure. The prospect of entering another community, of being vulnerable again in a space where vulnerability was previously exploited, is daunting in the extreme. And yet reconstruction cannot happen in isolation. The faith is inherently communal — a reality that the isolated deconstructionist discovers slowly, sometimes reluctantly, but inevitably. You need people who are further along the path to show you that reconstruction is possible. You need people who are at the same stage to share the disorientation. You need people who have not deconstructed to remind you of what was good and true in the tradition you left, the parts you may have thrown away too quickly in your haste to escape.

Silence is a reconstructive practice of enormous power. The deconstructive phase is noisy — full of arguments, podcasts, books, debates, and the constant chatter of the mind processing its losses. Silence interrupts the noise. Contemplative prayer — the practice of sitting in God's presence without words, without agenda, without the need to produce an insight or reach a conclusion — is the spiritual equivalent of letting a field lie fallow. Nothing appears to be happening. Everything is happening. The soil is being restored for the next planting.

Scripture, read differently, is one of the most surprising reconstructive practices. Many deconstructed Christians have abandoned Scripture because their previous relationship with it was toxic — because it was used as a weapon, a rulebook, or a source of proof texts for predetermined conclusions. The reconstructive approach to Scripture is not the fundamentalist approach (every word is literally true and must be obeyed without question) or the liberal approach (the text is merely a historical document with no binding authority). It is something more like the ancient practice of lectio divina — slow, meditative, prayerful reading that approaches the text not as a repository of information but as a living word that speaks differently in different seasons. The person who reads the psalms of lament from the wilderness hears something that the person who reads them from a position of comfort cannot hear. The text has not changed. The reader has.

The People Who Help

Reconstruction is not a solitary project. The people who navigate it successfully almost always do so with help — specific kinds of help that deserve to be named, because the person in the wilderness often does not know what help is available.

Spiritual directors are the most underutilized resource in the contemporary church. A spiritual director is not a therapist, not a pastor, and not a counselor — though the practice shares elements with all three. A spiritual director is a companion on the spiritual journey, trained to listen for the movement of God in another person's life without imposing their own agenda. The director does not tell you what to believe. They help you notice what is already happening in your interior life and discern its meaning. For the person in reconstruction, a spiritual director provides something that is almost impossible to find elsewhere: a non-anxious presence, a person who is not threatened by your questions, not invested in a particular outcome, and not in a hurry to get you somewhere.

Therapists are essential, and this is not a concession to secularism. Many of the wounds that drive deconstruction are not merely theological. They are psychological — the product of toxic leadership, spiritual abuse, shame-based formation, or the religious reinforcement of family dysfunction. These wounds require professional attention, not merely spiritual counsel. The pastor who tells a person recovering from spiritual abuse to "just pray about it" is not offering pastoral care. He is extending the abuse. A therapist who understands the intersection of faith and psychological health can help the deconstructed Christian distinguish between the wounds inflicted by the institution and the wounds inflicted by the theology, between the damage done by bad leaders and the damage done by bad ideas. Not all the damage is the same, and not all of it heals the same way.

Honest friends — people who will neither celebrate your departure nor condemn it, who will listen without agenda, who will tell you when you are being self-indulgent in your deconstruction and when you are being too hard on yourself — are perhaps the most valuable resource of all. The reconstructive journey is full of false starts, overcorrections, and the temptation to construct a new certainty to replace the old one. Honest friends are the guardrails that keep you on the road.

What Reconstructed Faith Looks Like

The faith that emerges from reconstruction is smaller than the faith that went in. It makes fewer claims with certainty. It holds fewer positions with the conviction that everyone who disagrees is wrong. It has released the need to have an answer to every question and a position on every issue. This smallness is not weakness. It is the strength of a faith that has been tested and has released everything that could not survive the test.

The faith that emerges is harder. It does not provide the easy comfort of certainty, the social belonging of tribal identity, or the psychological security of a comprehensive system that explains everything. It lives in the tension between knowing and not knowing, between the already and the not yet, between the God who has been revealed and the God who remains hidden. This tension is uncomfortable. It is also the native habitat of genuine faith, which has never been about certainty and has always been about trust.

The faith that emerges is truer. Not true in the sense of having finally arrived at the correct set of propositions — that ambition is itself one of the things that was deconstructed. True in the sense of being honest: honest about what is known and what is not, honest about the tradition's failures as well as its gifts, honest about the limits of human understanding and the persistence of human hope. The reconstructed faith is a faith that can say "I believe" and mean it, while also being able to say "I do not know" without panic. It is a faith that has learned to live with paradox, to hold contradictions in tension, and to trust a God who is larger than any theology constructed to contain him.

If you are in the wilderness, you are not lost. You are in passage. The wilderness is not the end of your faith. It may be the beginning of a faith that can actually hold the weight of your life — a faith that does not need certainty to survive, does not need cultural reinforcement to persist, and does not need the approval of the people who told you that questioning was sin. That faith exists. People are living it. And the road from where you are to where it is, while long, is not a road you walk alone.
excerpt: Deconstruction is not the destination. It is the demolition phase of a renovation. The harder question — and the one fewer people are asking — is what gets rebuilt.

title: The Sexual Abuse Crisis: A Reckoning the Church Cannot Avoid
body:
In January 2002, the Boston Globe's Spotlight team published the first of a series of investigative reports documenting the systematic sexual abuse of children by Catholic priests in the Archdiocese of Boston. The reporting revealed that Cardinal Bernard Law and his predecessors had known about the abuse for decades. They had not merely failed to stop it. They had actively enabled it — transferring accused priests to new parishes, suppressing complaints, pressuring victims into silence, deploying church lawyers to intimidate families who came forward. The institution had chosen its reputation over its children.

The Boston reporting was not the beginning. Allegations had surfaced for years — in Louisiana in the 1980s, in documents uncovered by attorney Jeff Anderson, in the courageous testimonies of survivors who were dismissed as liars or opportunists. But the Globe's investigation achieved what individual complaints had not: it established a pattern. Not isolated cases. Not a few bad actors. A system. A system designed, at every level, to protect the institution at the expense of the vulnerable.

What followed was a global reckoning. Grand jury reports in Pennsylvania documented over a thousand child victims and three hundred predator priests across six dioceses, spanning seven decades. Investigations in Ireland, Australia, Germany, Chile, and dozens of other countries revealed the same architecture of abuse and concealment. The case of Theodore McCarrick — a cardinal, one of the most powerful figures in American Catholicism — demonstrated that the rot reached the highest levels of church leadership. McCarrick had abused seminarians and minors for decades while ascending to positions of extraordinary influence. People knew. The institution knew. It advanced him anyway.

The Protestant Reckoning

For years, many Protestants watched the Catholic crisis with a mixture of horror and self-congratulation. The problem, they told themselves, was celibacy. The problem was hierarchy. The problem was a closed institutional culture unique to Rome. They were wrong on every count.

In 2022, the Southern Baptist Convention released the findings of an independent investigation conducted by Guidepost Solutions. The report documented a pattern of abuse, cover-up, and institutional self-protection that mirrored the Catholic crisis in its essential features. The SBC's Executive Committee had maintained a secret list of accused abusers while publicly resisting calls to create a database or implement safeguards. Leaders who advocated for survivors were marginalized. Christa Brown, who had spent years pressing the SBC to act, was dismissed and demeaned by the very leaders charged with protecting the vulnerable. The Guidepost report revealed internal communications in which SBC leaders discussed strategies not for addressing abuse but for avoiding legal liability.

The SBC was not alone. Willow Creek Community Church — once the flagship of the American megachurch movement — faced its own crisis when founder Bill Hybels was accused of sexual harassment and misconduct spanning decades. The church's initial response was to defend Hybels, attack his accusers, and circle the institutional wagons. An independent investigation eventually substantiated the allegations, but only after years of institutional resistance and incalculable damage to the women who came forward.

Ravi Zacharias, perhaps the most prominent Christian apologist of his generation, was posthumously revealed to have engaged in a sustained pattern of sexual abuse, including the abuse of massage therapists at spas he owned. His organization, RZIM, had received complaints during his lifetime and failed to investigate them meaningfully. After his death, an independent investigation documented the scope of his predation. The organization that bore his name eventually shut down — but only after decades of institutional complicity.

The pattern extends to independent churches, parachurch organizations, mission agencies, and Christian schools. Sovereign Grace Churches faced allegations of systematic abuse cover-up. The Institute in Basic Life Principles, founded by Bill Gothard, protected its leader despite years of sexual harassment complaints. Bob Jones University hired an independent firm to investigate its handling of sexual abuse — then fired the firm when its findings became uncomfortable. The list is long. It is still growing.

The Structure That Produces the Pattern

Individual predators exist in every institution. What distinguishes the church's abuse crisis is not the existence of abusers but the structural conditions that enable them and the institutional reflexes that protect them. These conditions are identifiable. They are predictable. And they are, in most churches, still firmly in place.

The first condition is unaccountable authority. Churches that concentrate spiritual authority in a single leader — and that teach congregants to equate questioning that leader with questioning God — create the perfect environment for abuse. When a pastor is treated as God's anointed representative, challenging his behavior becomes an act of spiritual rebellion. Victims who come forward are not merely disbelieved. They are recast as enemies of the faith.

The second condition is theological manipulation. Abusers in church settings routinely weaponize the language of faith to silence their victims. Forgiveness becomes a tool of coercion: victims are told that a failure to forgive their abuser is a sin. Submission becomes a mechanism of control: women and children are taught that obedience to authority is obedience to God. Grace becomes a shield for the perpetrator: calls for accountability are reframed as failures of Christian charity.

The third condition is institutional self-preservation. When an organization believes it is doing God's work, any threat to the organization's reputation becomes, in the distorted logic of institutional theology, a threat to God's work. Protecting the institution is reframed as protecting the mission. Silencing a victim is reframed as preventing scandal that would harm the gospel. The institution's survival becomes the highest good, and individual victims are sacrificed on its altar.

The church did not merely fail to protect the vulnerable. It constructed theological justifications for leaving them unprotected. That is not a failure of implementation. It is a failure of theology.

What Mandatory Reporting Means and Why Churches Resist It

In most U.S. states, clergy are mandatory reporters — legally required to report suspected child abuse to civil authorities. In practice, compliance is inconsistent. Many states include clergy exemptions when the information is obtained through confidential communications such as confession or pastoral counseling. Some denominations have actively lobbied to preserve these exemptions.

The resistance to mandatory reporting reveals a deeper theological problem. It rests on the assumption that the church's internal processes — pastoral care, church discipline, denominational oversight — are sufficient to address abuse. They are not. Church discipline is designed for matters of spiritual accountability among consenting adults. It is structurally incapable of addressing criminal behavior, protecting victims from ongoing harm, or ensuring that predators face legal consequences. When a church handles abuse internally, it is not exercising spiritual authority. It is obstructing justice.

Every church, regardless of denomination or polity, should adopt a clear, unambiguous policy: all suspected abuse is reported to civil authorities immediately. Not after an internal investigation. Not after consulting with denominational lawyers. Not after praying about it. Immediately. The safety of a child is not a matter for ecclesiastical deliberation.

Independent Investigations: Why They Matter

Churches cannot investigate themselves. This should be obvious, but it is a lesson the church has been extraordinarily slow to learn. When an institution investigates allegations against its own leaders, using its own personnel, following its own procedures, the outcome is predetermined. The investigation exists not to uncover truth but to manage liability.

Independent investigations — conducted by qualified professionals with no institutional loyalty, full access to documents and personnel, and a mandate to publish their findings — are the minimum standard of accountability. The Guidepost investigation of the SBC demonstrated what independent scrutiny can accomplish: it uncovered what decades of internal processes had concealed. The Pennsylvania grand jury reports accomplished what diocesan review boards had not.

The church's resistance to independent investigation is itself diagnostic. An institution confident in its integrity welcomes scrutiny. An institution that fights investigation is telling you, in the clearest possible terms, what it expects the investigation to find.

Victim-Centered Policy

The phrase "victim-centered" is not a concession to contemporary therapeutic culture. It is a theological imperative. The God revealed in Scripture is consistently, relentlessly oriented toward the vulnerable. The prophets measured the faithfulness of Israel not by the magnificence of its worship but by its treatment of the widow, the orphan, the stranger. Jesus reserved his most severe condemnation not for sinners but for religious leaders who burdened the vulnerable and failed to protect the weak. "If anyone causes one of these little ones to stumble," he said, "it would be better for them to have a large millstone hung around their neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea." That is not a metaphor. It is a verdict.

Victim-centered policy means that when an allegation of abuse is made, the institution's first question is not "How do we protect our reputation?" but "How do we protect this person?" It means believing survivors as a starting posture, not as a conclusion reached only after exhaustive institutional self-defense. It means providing material support — counseling, legal assistance, financial help — to those who have been harmed, without requiring them to sign nondisclosure agreements or waive their right to pursue justice. It means removing accused leaders from positions of authority immediately and permanently, regardless of their institutional value.

It means, in short, treating the vulnerable the way Jesus treated the vulnerable. Which is to say: as the point of the entire enterprise.

What Genuine Repentance Looks Like

The church has become skilled at performing repentance without practicing it. Press conferences are held. Statements are issued. The language of sorrow is deployed with professional precision. And then the institution returns to its prior operations with minimal structural change. This is not repentance. It is public relations.

Genuine repentance in the context of institutional abuse requires, at minimum, the following: a full and honest accounting of what happened, conducted by independent investigators and made public without redaction. Direct, personal accountability for leaders who enabled or concealed abuse, including removal from positions of authority and, where applicable, cooperation with criminal prosecution. Material restitution to survivors — not as a legal settlement designed to minimize liability but as an act of justice. Permanent structural changes to governance, accountability, and oversight that make future abuse more difficult and future concealment impossible.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer distinguished between "cheap grace" and "costly grace." Cheap grace is grace without repentance, forgiveness without restitution, absolution without accountability. The church's response to the abuse crisis has been, overwhelmingly, an exercise in cheap grace — grace extended to the institution and its leaders, paid for by the suffering of victims who were told to forgive and move on.

Costly grace demands more. It demands that the institution bear the full weight of what it has done. It demands that leaders who failed be held accountable, not shuffled to new positions. It demands that survivors be heard, believed, and compensated — not as an act of institutional generosity but as the minimum requirement of justice. It demands that the church become, in its structures and practices, the kind of institution where abuse is not merely condemned in sermons but made structurally impossible.

We are not there. We are not close. The church has named the sin in the abstract while protecting the sinners in the particular. It has called for repentance while resisting the concrete changes repentance demands. It has wept publicly while fighting privately to preserve the structures that made the crisis possible.

The reckoning is not optional. It is not a phase the church can wait out. It is the work of a generation — or it is the end of the church's moral credibility in the culture it claims to serve. Those are the only two options. There is no third way.
excerpt: The abuse crisis is not a Catholic problem or a Protestant problem. It is a power problem. And until the church names the structural conditions that produce predators and protect them, it will keep producing both.

title: Why the Church Lost the Culture War
body:
In 1979, Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority with an explicit political objective: to mobilize conservative Christians as a voting bloc capable of shaping American law and policy according to biblical principles. The strategy was clear, the coalition was large, and the early results were impressive. Ronald Reagan was elected in 1980 with overwhelming evangelical support. The religious right became a permanent fixture of Republican politics. For a generation, white evangelical Christians wielded disproportionate influence over judicial appointments, social policy, and the terms of public moral discourse.

By any conventional political measure, the movement succeeded. It elected presidents. It shaped a Supreme Court. It passed legislation. It built institutions — think tanks, media networks, lobbying organizations, legal defense funds — that gave conservative Christianity a permanent infrastructure of political power.

And yet. By the third decade of the twenty-first century, the culture war strategy had produced the opposite of what its architects intended. Public support for same-sex marriage went from 27 percent in 1996 to 71 percent in 2023. Church membership fell below 50 percent for the first time in recorded history. The religiously unaffiliated — the "nones" — became the fastest-growing religious demographic in America. Among adults under thirty, nearly four in ten claimed no religious affiliation at all. The word "evangelical" became, for a majority of Americans, a political identity rather than a spiritual one. And the generation most alienated from the church was precisely the generation the culture war was supposed to protect.

The church did not merely lose the culture war. It lost something far more consequential. It lost the capacity to be heard.

The Strategy and Its Logic

The culture war strategy rested on a specific theory of social change: that culture is shaped primarily from the top down, through law, policy, and institutional control. If Christians could elect the right leaders, appoint the right judges, and pass the right legislation, the moral character of the nation could be preserved — or restored — by political means. The family would be protected by law. Abortion would be restricted or prohibited. Prayer would return to schools. The Christian moral framework would remain the default operating system of American public life.

This theory was not without historical precedent. Christendom — the arrangement in which church and state mutually reinforced each other's authority — had operated on this logic for over a millennium. The culture war was, in a sense, an attempt to preserve the last vestiges of Christendom in an increasingly post-Christian society. It sought to maintain by political force what could no longer be sustained by cultural consensus.

The theory was wrong. Not wrong in its assessment that the culture was changing — the culture was changing, rapidly and irreversibly. Wrong in its assumption that political power was the appropriate tool for shaping moral formation. James Davison Hunter, in his landmark work To Change the World, dismantled this assumption with surgical precision. Culture, Hunter argued, is not changed primarily through grassroots mobilization, electoral politics, or legislative victory. It is changed through the formation of overlapping networks of cultural elites who create the ideas, narratives, institutions, and practices that shape how people understand the world. You cannot legislate formation. You cannot mandate conviction. You cannot coerce the kind of deep cultural change that actually transforms how people live.

The culture war strategy attempted to do all three. It tried to legislate what can only be formed. It tried to mandate what can only be modeled. It tried to coerce what can only be invited. And in the process, it transformed the church from a community of formation into an interest group — one political faction among many, competing for power in the same terms and by the same means as every other faction.

What Was Sacrificed

The cost of the culture war was not primarily political. It was spiritual. And it was paid by people who never signed up for the fight.

The first casualty was credibility. When the church aligned itself with a political party, it became subject to the same skepticism that attaches to all political actors. Every moral pronouncement was filtered through partisan suspicion. When evangelical leaders condemned sexual immorality while supporting political candidates credibly accused of it, the public did not conclude that the leaders were applying a complex moral calculus. The public concluded that the moral pronouncements were instrumental — tools for mobilizing a base, not convictions held with integrity. The church's moral authority, which depends entirely on the perception that its convictions transcend political convenience, was spent as political currency. It cannot be easily recovered.

The second casualty was witness. The New Testament presents the church as a community whose distinctive way of life serves as a sign — a visible demonstration that another way of being human is possible. The early church attracted converts not primarily through arguments but through the observable quality of its common life: its care for the poor, its inclusion of the excluded, its willingness to suffer rather than dominate. The culture war inverted this logic. It substituted political advocacy for embodied witness. It said to the watching world: we will change your behavior through legislation rather than attract your allegiance through demonstration. The result was a church perceived not as a community of sacrificial love but as a lobbying organization with a cross on its letterhead.

The third casualty was the next generation. Millennials and Generation Z were raised in the culture war. They watched it from the inside. And what they saw — the selective outrage, the political captivity, the gap between proclaimed values and institutional behavior — drove them away in historically unprecedented numbers. The Barna Group's research has consistently shown that young adults associate Christianity with being anti-gay, judgmental, hypocritical, and overly political. These are not misperceptions imposed from outside. They are observations drawn from direct experience of the culture war church.

The church set out to save the culture and lost a generation instead. It is difficult to imagine a more comprehensive strategic failure.

The Idol of Influence

Beneath the culture war strategy lay a deeper theological error: the belief that the church's faithfulness is measured by its cultural influence. This belief is nowhere supported in the New Testament. Jesus explicitly rejected the model of a kingdom that operates through political power. "My kingdom is not of this world," he told Pilate — not because his kingdom is irrelevant to the world but because it does not operate by the world's mechanisms of coercion and control. The early church existed as a tiny, powerless, persecuted minority within the Roman Empire. It did not lobby Caesar. It did not form political action committees. It did not seek to impose its moral framework through legislation. It formed communities of radical mutual care, practiced an ethic that astonished its neighbors, and trusted that the quality of its common life would bear witness to the truth of its confession.

The culture war represented a loss of nerve — a failure to trust that the church's witness could be sustained without the backing of political power. It was, at its root, an act of faithlessness disguised as an act of faithfulness. And the theological tradition has a word for the elevation of a good thing — cultural influence — to the status of an ultimate thing. The word is idolatry.

Why Losing Might Be the Best Thing

There is an older Christian vision of the church's role in culture that the culture war displaced but did not destroy. It is the vision of the church as a prophetic minority — not a moral majority seeking to impose its values from the top but a prophetic community embodying an alternative way of life from the margins.

This is, in fact, the church's native posture. The Hebrew prophets spoke from outside the structures of power, not from within them. Jesus was executed by the state, not enthroned by it. The early church's most powerful witness was offered not from positions of cultural dominance but from positions of cultural vulnerability. The church has always been most faithful — and, paradoxically, most influential — when it has not been in charge.

The end of the culture war opens the possibility of recovering this posture. Freed from the obligation to defend political allies and maintain political coalitions, the church can recover the prophetic freedom to speak truth to power regardless of which party holds it. Freed from the expectation that legislation will accomplish the work of formation, the church can rediscover its own formative practices — worship, prayer, community, service, the slow and patient work of discipleship that cannot be outsourced to a political movement. Freed from the illusion that cultural dominance is the measure of faithfulness, the church can rediscover what faithfulness actually looks like: not winning, but witnessing.

The theologian Stanley Hauerwas has argued for decades that the church's primary political task is not to make the world more just — though justice matters — but to be the church: a community whose practices, convictions, and common life offer a visible alternative to the world's ways of organizing power. The church does not need to run the culture. It needs to be the church within the culture — a community so distinctive in its love, its justice, its care for the vulnerable, and its refusal to worship the idols of power that it provokes the question: What makes these people different?

The culture war made the church indistinguishable from every other political faction. Its end — painful, humiliating, and long overdue — creates the possibility of becoming distinguishable again. Not by retreating from the world but by engaging it on different terms. Not by seeking power but by practicing faithfulness. Not by winning but by witnessing.

The church lost the culture war. The question now is whether it will learn anything from the defeat — or whether it will simply find a new war to fight, and lose that one too.
excerpt: The church spent forty years trying to win a culture war it was never meant to fight. The cost was not just political defeat. It was the loss of the one thing the church cannot function without: moral credibility.

title: White Evangelicalism and Race
body:
On May 10, 1845, in Augusta, Georgia, 293 delegates from Southern Baptist churches gathered to form a new denomination. The immediate cause was a dispute with their Northern counterparts over whether slaveholders could serve as missionaries. The Northern board had refused to appoint a slaveholder. The Southern delegates, unwilling to accept this restriction, withdrew and constituted themselves as the Southern Baptist Convention.

The SBC was not founded despite slavery. It was founded because of it. Its founding documents make this explicit. Its early leaders made it explicit. The theological case for slavery was not an embarrassing footnote to an otherwise noble enterprise. It was the enterprise. The denomination that would become the largest Protestant body in America — claiming over thirteen million members at its peak — came into existence for the express purpose of defending the right of Christians to own other human beings.

This is not ancient history. The SBC did not formally apologize for its slaveholding origins until 1995 — one hundred and fifty years after its founding. And the apology, while significant as a symbolic gesture, did not include any concrete measures of restitution, structural reform, or sustained institutional reckoning with the theological traditions that had made the defense of slavery possible.

The Slaveholder's Theology

The Christian defense of slavery was not a crude rationalization imposed on Scripture by cynical men who knew better. It was a sophisticated, internally consistent theological system, constructed by some of the most respected biblical scholars of the antebellum South. This is what makes it so dangerous — and so relevant to the present.

The slaveholder's theology rested on several pillars. First, the curse of Ham in Genesis 9, which was interpreted as a divine decree of perpetual servitude for the descendants of Canaan — identified, through a chain of exegetical reasoning that would not survive scrutiny, with the peoples of Africa. Second, the Pauline household codes, particularly Ephesians 6:5 ("Slaves, obey your earthly masters") and Colossians 3:22, which were read as divine endorsements of the institution of slavery rather than pastoral instructions addressed to people trapped within an existing social system. Third, a providentialist argument: God, in his sovereignty, had allowed slavery to exist; therefore slavery was part of the divine plan. To oppose it was to oppose God.

What made this theology so durable was not its quality — by any serious hermeneutical standard, it was terrible exegesis — but its function. It provided religious legitimation for an economic system on which the entire Southern economy depended. It sacralized the social order. It transformed a brutal institution of human exploitation into a divinely ordained arrangement that was good not only for the slaveholder but, in the tortured logic of paternalism, for the enslaved. Ministers preached from their pulpits that slavery was a benevolent institution through which African people were introduced to Christianity — a spiritual benefit that, they argued, far outweighed the temporal suffering of bondage.

The theological habits that produced this system — selective literalism, providentialist rationalization, the sacralization of existing power arrangements, the reading of Scripture through the lens of the interpreter's material interests — did not end with emancipation. They persisted. They adapted. They found new applications.
