The Silent Church During Civil Rights

On April 16, 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. sat in a jail cell in Birmingham, Alabama, and wrote a letter. It was addressed not to the segregationists who had arrested him, not to the politicians who enforced Jim Crow, not to the Klan members who bombed churches and murdered children. It was addressed to eight white clergymen — Christian ministers and a Jewish rabbi — who had published a statement calling King's nonviolent protests "unwise and untimely."

King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail" remains the most devastating indictment of white moderate Christianity ever written, and its central argument has lost none of its force. "I have almost reached the regrettable conclusion," King wrote, "that the Negro's great stumbling block in the stride toward freedom is not the White Citizen's Counciler or the Ku Klux Klanner but the white moderate who is more devoted to order than to justice; who prefers a negative peace which is the absence of tension to a positive peace which is the presence of justice."

The white church during the civil rights era was not, for the most part, actively engaged in the violent defense of segregation. It did something arguably worse. It was silent. It counseled patience. It urged moderation. It spiritualized the question — framing racial justice as a matter of individual hearts rather than structural change, assuring Black Americans that heaven would make up for the injustices of earth, treating calls for concrete political action as a distraction from the church's spiritual mission.

This silence was not passive. It was a choice — a choice that had the practical effect of supporting the status quo. When white ministers told Black Christians to wait, to be patient, to trust that change would come in God's time, they were providing theological cover for a system of racial domination. They were using the language of faith to counsel submission to injustice. They were doing, in a softer register, what the slaveholder theologians had done a century earlier: deploying Scripture to protect the interests of the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable.

There were exceptions. There were white Christians who marched, who risked their safety, who stood with the movement at personal cost. Their existence is important and should be honored. But they were exceptions. The institutional white church — its denominations, its seminaries, its leadership structures — was overwhelmingly on the wrong side of the most significant moral struggle of the twentieth century. And it arrived there not despite its theology but because of it.

The Southern Strategy and Its Heirs

In 1968, Richard Nixon's presidential campaign developed what came to be known as the Southern Strategy: a deliberate effort to win the votes of white Southerners who had been alienated from the Democratic Party by its support for civil rights legislation. The strategy relied on coded racial appeals — "law and order," "states' rights," "welfare reform" — that communicated racial resentment without the vulgarity of explicit racism. Lee Atwater, a Republican strategist, later described the mechanism with brutal candor: "You start out in 1954 by saying, 'N-----, n-----, n-----.' By 1968, you can't say 'n-----' — that hurts you, backfires. So you say stuff like 'forced busing,' 'states' rights,' and all that stuff."

The Southern Strategy succeeded in realigning American politics. It also succeeded in realigning American Christianity. White evangelicals, who had been politically diverse through the mid-twentieth century, became overwhelmingly Republican. The alignment was not primarily theological. It was racial. The issues that initially mobilized white evangelical political engagement — opposition to the IRS revoking the tax-exempt status of segregated Christian schools, as documented by Randall Balmer — were racial issues. The "family values" agenda that later became the public face of the religious right was, in significant part, a laundered version of racial politics.

This does not mean that every white evangelical who voted Republican was motivated by racial animus. Individual motivations are complex and varied. But the structural alignment between white evangelicalism and a political movement built on racial resentment is not a matter of interpretation. It is a matter of documented historical fact. And its consequences — for the church's witness, for its credibility among people of color, for its capacity to speak with moral authority on questions of justice — have been devastating.

The Current Moment

In 2020, the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer prompted a national reckoning with racial injustice. The response within white evangelicalism was revealing. Some churches and leaders spoke clearly about systemic racism and committed to concrete action. Many more retreated into the same patterns that have characterized white Christian responses to racial crisis for two centuries: spiritualization ("the real problem is sin, not systems"), individualization ("I am not personally racist, therefore there is no problem"), and deflection ("this is a political issue, not a church issue").

The panic over Critical Race Theory provided the deflection a name and a mechanism. CRT — an academic legal framework developed by scholars like Derrick Bell and Kimberle Crenshaw to analyze how racial inequality is embedded in legal and institutional structures — became, in the hands of political operatives and church leaders, a catch-all term for any analysis of systemic racism. Southern Baptist seminaries issued statements condemning CRT. Churches split over whether acknowledging systemic racism was compatible with Christian orthodoxy. Pastors who preached on racial justice faced congregational resistance, and some were forced out of their positions.

The irony was lost on few observers outside the white evangelical bubble. A tradition that had spent a century and a half avoiding, minimizing, and theologizing away its own racial history was now deploying a new set of theological and political tools to avoid, minimize, and theologize away the present consequences of that history. The content changed. The pattern did not.

Jemar Tisby, in The Color of Compromise, documents this pattern with devastating thoroughness: complicity through silence, complicity through theology, complicity through institutional inaction, repeating across every era of American history. The white church has never been at the forefront of racial justice in America. It has consistently been behind the culture, not ahead of it — adopting positions on race only after those positions have become culturally safe, and treating each belated acknowledgment as evidence of moral progress rather than as an indictment of moral delay.

The question is not whether the white church has been complicit in racial injustice. The historical record is unambiguous. The question is whether the white church is willing to do what complicity demands: not an apology, which costs nothing, but repentance, which costs everything.

What Repentance Actually Requires

The distinction between apology and repentance is not semantic. It is structural. An apology is a statement about the past. Repentance is a reorientation of the present. An apology says, "We are sorry for what was done." Repentance says, "We are changing what we are doing." The white church has become adept at apology. It has shown almost no capacity for repentance.

Repentance for racial injustice would require, at minimum, the following. First, honest historical reckoning. Not sanitized narratives that treat slavery and segregation as regrettable episodes in an otherwise noble story, but unflinching confrontation with the theological systems that justified racial domination and the institutional structures that enforced it. This reckoning must be embedded in seminary curricula, preaching, and congregational education — not as a one-time event but as a permanent feature of the church's self-understanding.

Second, structural change. Repentance that does not alter structures is performance. White-led denominations and churches must examine their governance, hiring, leadership development, and resource allocation through the lens of racial equity — not as a concession to secular pressure but as a requirement of biblical justice. The prophetic tradition is unambiguous: God judges communities not by their stated intentions but by their measurable practices.

Third, material restitution. The wealth of white America — including the wealth of white churches and white Christian institutions — was built, in significant part, on the exploitation of Black labor. This is not a controversial claim. It is an economic fact. Restitution is not charity. It is justice. It is the return of what was taken. And the church, which claims to worship a God of justice, cannot credibly refuse it.

Fourth, redistribution of power. The most consequential form of repentance is not what white Christians say about race but who they are willing to follow. Are white congregations willing to be led by pastors of color — not as tokens but as leaders with genuine authority? Are white denominations willing to submit their institutional priorities to the perspectives of their members of color? Are white Christians willing to listen without defensiveness, to learn without centering their own discomfort, to follow without insisting on control?

Fifth, sustained commitment. Racial reconciliation is not a project with a timeline and a completion date. It is a permanent posture of repentance, learning, and relationship-building that will extend across generations. The damage was done over centuries. It will not be undone in a single denominational resolution or a single season of sermons.

The white church will resist every item on this list. It will call the historical reckoning divisive. It will call the structural changes political. It will call the restitution unreasonable. It will call the redistribution of power impractical. It will call the sustained commitment exhausting. And in each case, the resistance will be framed in theological language — the language of unity, of gospel priority, of spiritual over political, of patience over urgency.

That language is familiar. It is the same language the white church has always used to avoid the cost of justice. King heard it in Birmingham. The enslaved heard it on the plantation. And people of color in white evangelical churches hear it today, every time they raise the subject and watch the room go cold.

The work is not optional. It is not a concession to culture. It is a requirement of the gospel the white church claims to preach. A church that cannot do justice cannot preach grace. A church that will not name its own sin cannot call others to repentance. A church that protects its comfort at the expense of its neighbor's dignity has not yet understood the cross it claims to carry.
excerpt: The American church did not merely tolerate slavery. It theologized it. And the theological habits that justified the slaveholder's religion are not historical curiosities. They are still operative.

title: The Megachurch Model: What Worked, What Didn't, What's Next
body:
In 1975, Bill Hybels rented a movie theater in Palatine, Illinois, and launched a church service designed for people who did not go to church. He had conducted door-to-door surveys in the surrounding suburbs, asking unchurched residents what they disliked about church. Their answers were consistent: it was boring, irrelevant, always asking for money, and made them feel guilty. Hybels built Willow Creek Community Church as the answer to those objections. The music was contemporary. The messages were practical. The atmosphere was welcoming, nonthreatening, and intentionally modeled on the spaces where suburban Americans already felt comfortable — corporate auditoriums, shopping malls, entertainment venues.

It worked. Willow Creek grew to over twenty-five thousand weekly attendees. It became the prototype for a movement. Rick Warren applied similar principles at Saddleback Church in Lake Forest, California, which grew to comparable size and produced The Purpose Driven Life, one of the best-selling nonfiction books in American history. By the early 2000s, the megachurch model — defined as a church with weekly attendance of two thousand or more — had spread across the country. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research counted over seventeen hundred megachurches in the United States by 2020, a number that had more than doubled since 2000.

The megachurch movement was the most significant development in American Protestant Christianity in the second half of the twentieth century. It reshaped the terrain of American religion, the expectations of churchgoers, the economics of ministry, and the culture of pastoral leadership. It did some things remarkably well. It did other things catastrophically badly. And the reckoning that followed has forced a conversation about what the church is actually for — a conversation that is still far from resolved.

What Worked

The megachurch movement's most significant achievement was accessibility. For millions of Americans who had been alienated by traditional church culture — its unfamiliar rituals, its insider language, its assumption that newcomers already knew the rules — the megachurch offered a genuine on-ramp. You could walk in without knowing anything about Christianity and not feel stupid, excluded, or judged. The music was in a key you recognized. The sermon addressed problems you actually had. The building looked like a place where normal people gathered, not a medieval artifact that required a guide.

This accessibility was not superficial. It represented a serious theological commitment: the belief that the gospel is for everyone, and that the church bears responsibility for removing unnecessary barriers to encounter. The seeker-sensitive movement, at its best, was an exercise in contextual theology — translating the message of Christianity into the vernacular of contemporary American culture without compromising its substance. Paul did this in Athens. The Jesuits did it in China. Hybels and Warren did it in the suburbs.

The megachurch also excelled at organizational excellence. Whatever criticisms can be leveled at the movement, it is difficult to argue that the average megachurch was not better organized, better managed, and more intentional about its operations than the average small church. Volunteer coordination, children's ministry, facility management, communication — the megachurch brought a level of institutional competence to these functions that smaller churches often lacked. For families with young children, in particular, the difference was palpable. A well-run children's ministry, a clean and safe facility, a service that started on time — these things matter, and the megachurch delivered them consistently.

The movement also demonstrated the power of strategic thinking about mission. The megachurch leaders were, for all their flaws, deeply serious about reaching people outside the church. They thought carefully about demographics, communication, cultural barriers, and the psychology of spiritual seeking. They approached evangelism not as a duty performed through guilt but as a strategic enterprise that deserved the same level of planning and investment as any other serious undertaking.

What Didn't Work

The megachurch model contained structural flaws that became visible only over time — flaws that were not incidental to the model but embedded in its foundational assumptions.

The first flaw was the celebrity pastor. The megachurch, by its nature, concentrates enormous attention, authority, and resources in a single leader. The senior pastor becomes the brand. The church's identity, its growth, its financial viability, and its public reputation are all tethered to one person. This structure creates conditions that are almost perfectly designed to produce the pathologies of celebrity: isolation, entitlement, unaccountability, the gradual erosion of the boundary between the leader's identity and the institution's mission.

The Willow Creek Association, which Hybels founded to export the megachurch model to churches worldwide, marketed not just a methodology but a personality. When Hybels was accused of sexual harassment and misconduct — allegations that were eventually substantiated by an independent investigation — the entire enterprise was compromised. The model had no mechanism for holding its central figure accountable because the central figure was the model.

The second flaw was consumer Christianity. The seeker-sensitive approach, which began as a missiological strategy, gradually became a market strategy. The church adopted the logic of the marketplace: the congregation as customer base, the sermon as product, the worship service as experience to be consumed. Satisfaction surveys replaced confession. Preference became the organizing principle of ministry. Churches competed for market share — not consciously, perhaps, but functionally — by offering better programming, more convenient services, superior production values.

The result was a form of Christianity shaped more by consumer preference than by the costly demands of discipleship. The megachurch excelled at attracting people. It struggled to form them. Willow Creek's own internal research, published in the 2007 study Reveal, acknowledged this problem with surprising candor: the church had been more effective at creating consumers of religious programming than disciples of Jesus Christ. The most spiritually mature members, the study found, were the least satisfied — because the church had been designed for seekers, not for saints.

The third flaw was shallow discipleship. The megachurch service, optimized for accessibility, often achieved accessibility at the expense of depth. Sermons were practical, relevant, and application-oriented — but they frequently lacked theological substance. Complex doctrines were simplified to the point of distortion. The Bible was mined for principles rather than encountered as a text. The liturgical traditions of the church — the creeds, the sacraments, the rhythms of the church year — were jettisoned as barriers to accessibility, and with them went centuries of accumulated wisdom about how to form the human soul.

The megachurch asked the right question: How do we reach people who are not here? But it failed to ask the harder question: What do we do with them once they arrive?

The Reckoning

The scandals that engulfed megachurch leaders in the 2010s and 2020s were not isolated incidents. They were structural consequences of the model itself. Bill Hybels at Willow Creek. Mark Driscoll at Mars Hill. Carl Lentz at Hillsong New York. James MacDonald at Harvest Bible Chapel. Each case followed the same arc: a charismatic leader builds a massive institution around his personality, concentrates authority in himself, marginalizes or eliminates internal accountability, and eventually falls — taking the institution, or large parts of it, down with him.

Driscoll's case is particularly instructive. Mars Hill Church in Seattle grew from a handful of people to over fourteen thousand weekly attendees in fifteen years. Driscoll's aggressive, confrontational style — described by Christianity Today as "the cussing pastor" — attracted young men in numbers that few other churches could match. But the same authoritarianism that drove the church's growth eventually destroyed it. Former elders described a culture of fear, bullying, and spiritual abuse. When the church's board attempted to hold Driscoll accountable, he resigned and the church collapsed, closing all of its campuses within months.

Lentz at Hillsong was fired for "moral failures" — a euphemism that later expanded into a broader picture of a church culture built on celebrity, image management, and the systematic prioritization of the brand over the well-being of staff and congregants. MacDonald at Harvest was removed after recordings surfaced of him making vulgar, racially insensitive, and threatening remarks — but only after years of financial misconduct, bullying of staff, and suppression of dissent that the church's governance structures had failed to address.

The pattern is not coincidental. It is architectural. Build a church around a personality. Give that personality unchecked authority. Remove the structural safeguards — elder boards with real power, financial transparency, congregational governance — that might constrain that authority. And wait. The fall is not guaranteed, but the conditions for it are. The megachurch model, as commonly practiced, is a machine for producing exactly the kind of leadership failures it has produced.

What Comes Next

The post-megachurch reality is still emerging, but its contours are becoming visible. The movement is not dying — megachurches continue to exist and, in some cases, to thrive. But the assumptions that drove the movement are being questioned in ways they have not been before, and the alternatives being explored suggest a significant shift in what American Protestantism considers a healthy church.

Smaller is being reconsidered. The assumption that bigger is better — that numerical growth is the primary indicator of ministerial health — is being challenged by a growing number of pastors, theologians, and church planters who argue that the most significant work of the church happens at a scale that megachurches cannot reach. Relationships of genuine depth. Mutual accountability. The slow, patient work of formation that requires a pastor who knows your name, your story, your struggles — not a communicator on a stage who delivers content to an audience.

Deeper is being prioritized. The reaction against seeker-sensitive shallowness has produced a renewed interest in theological depth, liturgical richness, and the formative practices of the historic church. Young evangelicals are discovering the church fathers, the Book of Common Prayer, the contemplative tradition, the rhythms of the church year. They are hungry not for relevance but for rootedness — not for a Christianity that accommodates the culture but for one that offers a genuine alternative to it.

More accountable structures are being designed. The celebrity pastor model is being replaced, in some quarters, by team leadership, plural eldership, and governance structures that distribute authority rather than concentrating it. Churches are implementing financial transparency, independent audits, and formal accountability mechanisms that do not depend on the goodwill of the leader being held accountable.

None of this guarantees a better outcome. Small churches can be abusive. Liturgical churches can be shallow. Accountability structures can be performative. The problem is not merely structural but spiritual — rooted in the human capacity for self-deception and the institutional tendency toward self-preservation. But the megachurch era has taught the American church something it needed to learn: that growth is not the same as health, that efficiency is not the same as faithfulness, and that the size of the crowd tells you nothing about the depth of the formation happening within it.

The church Jesus described — a community of mutual service, sacrificial love, genuine accountability, and radical commitment to the way of the cross — has never been efficiently scalable. That may be the point.
excerpt: The megachurch movement reached millions and revealed something important about American Christianity's hunger for accessibility. It also revealed something about what happens when the church mistakes growth for faithfulness.

title: Women in Ministry: The Biblical Case the Church Keeps Ignoring
body:
In Romans 16, Paul greets twenty-nine people by name. Ten of them are women. He calls Phoebe a deacon — using the same Greek word, diakonos, that he uses to describe his own ministry elsewhere. He calls Junia "outstanding among the apostles" — a title that early church fathers uniformly understood as designating her an apostle, not merely someone admired by apostles. He identifies Priscilla as a co-worker in Christ Jesus who, along with her husband Aquila, "risked their lives" for him. In Acts 18, Luke records that Priscilla (named first, which in the conventions of the time indicated prominence) instructed Apollos — a learned man, "mighty in the Scriptures" — in the way of God more accurately.

These are not marginal figures mentioned in passing. They are leaders, teachers, and ministers whom Paul explicitly recognizes, commends, and depends upon. They exercise authority, provide instruction, bear the title of apostle and deacon, and are woven into the fabric of the early church's leadership. Their presence in the text is undeniable. And yet, for most of church history, their presence has been systematically minimized, explained away, or rendered invisible by interpreters who approached the text with a conclusion already in hand.

The Women the Bible Names

The biblical record of women in leadership begins long before Paul. Deborah, in Judges 4-5, serves as a judge over Israel — the highest political, military, and spiritual authority in the pre-monarchic period. She is not presented as an exception forced by the absence of qualified men. She is presented as a leader whom God raised up, whom Israel followed, and whose authority was unquestioned. Barak, the military commander, refuses to go into battle without her. The text offers no apology for her leadership and no suggestion that it was irregular.

Huldah, in 2 Kings 22, is a prophet to whom King Josiah sends the high priest for a word from God. When the book of the law is discovered in the temple, the most powerful men in Israel bring it to a woman for authoritative interpretation. Miriam is identified as a prophet alongside Moses and Aaron. Esther exercises political authority that saves her people. Ruth's story is one of the four Old Testament books named for a woman.

In the New Testament, the record is even more striking. Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the resurrection — commissioned by Jesus himself to announce the news to the other disciples. In a culture where women's testimony was not accepted in court, Jesus chose a woman as the first evangelist of the most important event in Christian history. This was not incidental. It was deliberate, and it was subversive.

Lydia, in Acts 16, is the first convert in Europe and the host of the church that meets in her house. The Philippian church — the church Paul loved most, the one that supported him financially, the one to which he wrote with the most warmth — was founded in a woman's home, under a woman's patronage. Nympha, in Colossians 4:15, hosts a house church. Chloe, in 1 Corinthians 1:11, is a church leader whose people report to Paul about the Corinthian situation. Euodia and Syntyche, in Philippians 4:2-3, are described as women who "contended at my side in the cause of the gospel" — language Paul uses elsewhere for his closest ministry partners.

The Samaritan woman at the well in John 4 becomes the first cross-cultural evangelist in the Gospel narrative. Philip's four daughters are prophets. The elder women in Titus 2 are instructed to teach — the same word, kalodidaskalous, that denotes authoritative instruction elsewhere in the pastoral epistles.

The cumulative weight of this evidence is overwhelming. The biblical record presents women as prophets, judges, apostles, deacons, teachers, evangelists, church hosts, and ministry partners. The question is not whether the Bible records women in leadership. The question is how the church has managed, for so long, to read a text so full of women leaders and conclude that women cannot lead.

The Restrictive Texts

The case for restricting women from ministry rests primarily on two passages: 1 Timothy 2:11-12 and 1 Corinthians 14:34-35. Both deserve careful examination — more careful than they typically receive from either side of the debate.

In 1 Timothy 2:12, Paul writes: "I do not permit a woman to teach or to assume authority over a man; she must be quiet." The passage has been treated, in many traditions, as a universal, timeless prohibition — a divine decree applicable to all churches in all times and all places. But this reading requires ignoring several features of the text that complicate the universal interpretation.

The verb Paul uses — authentein, translated "assume authority" — appears only here in the entire New Testament. It is not the ordinary Greek word for authority (exousia), which Paul uses freely elsewhere. Authentein carries connotations of domination, usurpation, or inappropriate exercise of power. If Paul had intended to prohibit the ordinary exercise of teaching authority, he had a perfectly good word for that. He chose a different word — a word that suggests not authority per se but a particular kind of authority wielded in a particular kind of way.

The context matters. First Timothy is addressed to Timothy in Ephesus — a city dominated by the cult of Artemis, in which women held prominent religious roles and certain heretical teachings were being propagated, apparently by women, within the Christian community. Paul's restriction may be a response to a specific, local problem — not a universal legislative act. The phrase "I do not permit" (ouk epitrepo) is the language of personal apostolic instruction addressed to a specific situation, not the language of eternal decree.

In 1 Corinthians 14:34-35, Paul writes: "Women should remain silent in the churches." But three chapters earlier, in 1 Corinthians 11:5, Paul gives instructions for how women should pray and prophesy in the assembly — tacitly acknowledging that they do, in fact, speak. If Paul intended an absolute prohibition on women speaking in church, he contradicted himself within the same letter. The more plausible reading — and the one adopted by most New Testament scholars across the theological spectrum — is that Paul is addressing a specific form of disruptive speech in a specific context, not issuing a blanket prohibition.

Some scholars have argued that 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 is an interpolation — a later addition to the text by a scribe. The textual evidence for this view is significant: in some early manuscripts, these verses appear after verse 40 rather than after verse 33, suggesting they may have been a marginal note that was incorporated into the text at different points by different copyists. This is a text-critical argument, not a theological dodge, and it deserves serious consideration.

The Complementarian Position

The complementarian position — the view that men and women are equal in dignity but assigned different, complementary roles, with leadership and teaching authority reserved for men — is held by a significant number of thoughtful, biblically serious Christians. It deserves to be stated fairly.

Complementarians argue that the created order established in Genesis 1-2 assigns distinct roles to men and women, with male headship as a feature of creation, not a consequence of the fall. They point to the consistent pattern of male leadership in the biblical narrative — patriarchs, priests, kings, apostles — as evidence of a divinely intended pattern. They read the restrictive texts in 1 Timothy and 1 Corinthians as universal prescriptions, consistent with the broader biblical witness. They argue that role distinctions do not imply inequality of worth, just as the distinct roles of the persons of the Trinity do not imply inequality of being.

The most sophisticated complementarian scholarship — represented by scholars like Thomas Schreiner, Andreas Kostenberger, and Wayne Grudem — is serious, textually engaged, and theologically coherent within its own framework. Dismissing it as mere patriarchy dressed in theological clothing is neither accurate nor helpful. The position has genuine biblical and theological warrant, even if that warrant is, in my judgment, ultimately outweighed by the counter-evidence.

The Egalitarian Position

The egalitarian position — the view that the Bible, rightly interpreted, places no gender-based restrictions on ministry roles — rests on several converging lines of argument.

First, the trajectory of Scripture. The Bible was written within patriarchal cultures, and it bears the marks of those cultures. But the overall trajectory of Scripture — from the subjugation of women in the ancient Near East, through the countercultural practices of Jesus, to the radical inclusivity of Paul's baptismal declaration in Galatians 3:28 ("There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus") — is toward the full inclusion of women in every dimension of the community's life. Reading the restrictive texts as permanent legislation rather than contextual instructions arrests this trajectory at its most restrictive point rather than following it to its destination.

Second, the practice of Jesus. Jesus' treatment of women was, by the standards of his culture, revolutionary. He taught women (Mary of Bethany, the Samaritan woman). He included women in his traveling company. He appeared first to women after his resurrection and commissioned them as the first witnesses. He never restricted women from learning, teaching, or bearing witness. If Jesus intended to establish a permanent restriction on women's leadership, his own behavior was a remarkably poor way of communicating it.

Third, the practice of the early church. As documented above, the early church included women in roles of leadership, teaching, and authority. Paul's own letters — including the letter in which the restrictive passage in 1 Timothy appears — identify women as apostles, deacons, teachers, and co-workers. The early church's practice was more egalitarian than the later tradition that claimed to follow it.

Fourth, the hermeneutical principle. The church does not treat every instruction in the pastoral epistles as a permanent universal law. Paul instructs Timothy to bring his cloak from Troas. He instructs slaves to obey their masters. He instructs women to cover their heads in worship. The church has recognized that some of these instructions are contextual — addressed to specific situations in specific communities — while others are universal. The question is not whether contextual discernment is appropriate but which texts it applies to. The case for applying it to the restrictive passages on women is at least as strong as the case for applying it to head coverings — which virtually all churches have done.

The church that silences half its members has not protected the biblical order. It has impoverished its own witness, squandered its own resources, and grieved the Spirit who distributes gifts without regard to gender.

The Cost of Silencing

The theological debate matters, but it is not abstract. Behind the exegetical arguments are real women whose callings have been denied, whose gifts have been suppressed, and whose contributions have been erased from the church's memory and its present life.

Women who sense a call to pastoral ministry in traditions that prohibit it face an impossible choice: deny the call and remain in a community that does not recognize them, or follow the call and leave the community that formed them. Neither option is without cost. Women who stay often find themselves confined to roles that are carefully circumscribed to avoid the appearance of authority — teaching children but not adults, leading worship but not preaching, counseling women but not men. The theological justification for these distinctions is often tortured, drawing lines that the text itself does not draw.

The church's loss is not only individual but corporate. When women are excluded from preaching, the church hears only half the human experience reflected in its pulpit. When women are excluded from leadership, the church's decision-making is shaped by only one gender's perspective. When women's scholarship is marginalized, the church's theological tradition is impoverished. The gifts of the Spirit, Paul tells us, are given for the common good. To suppress them on the basis of gender is to tell the Spirit that his distribution was a mistake.

The history of the church's treatment of women in ministry is not a story of faithful preservation of a biblical principle. It is a story of selective reading, cultural accommodation, and institutional self-interest that has used Scripture to justify what culture had already decided. The same hermeneutical methods that were used to justify slavery — selective literalism, appeals to created order, arguments from silence — have been used to justify the exclusion of women. The church eventually recognized that its reading of Scripture on slavery was wrong. The same recognition on women is overdue.

This is not a call to abandon Scripture but to read it more carefully — to let the full witness of the text speak, rather than silencing the parts that complicate the conclusion we have already reached. The Bible is full of women who led, taught, prophesied, and served. The church's tradition of ignoring them does not change what the text says. It only reveals what the tradition was unwilling to hear.
excerpt: The Bible contains a robust record of women exercising leadership, teaching, and authority in the life of God's people. The church's refusal to see it says more about the church than about the Bible.

title: How the Church Handles Mental Health (Badly)
body:
In 2013, Matthew Warren — the twenty-seven-year-old son of Rick Warren, pastor of Saddleback Church and author of The Purpose Driven Life — died by suicide after a lifelong struggle with mental illness. Rick Warren, one of the most influential pastors in America, a man whose book had sold over fifty million copies and whose church had helped shape the theology and practice of a generation of evangelical Christianity, could not save his own son. Not because he lacked faith. Not because he lacked resources. Not because he failed to pray. Because mental illness is an illness, and prayer, however essential to the life of faith, is not a substitute for clinical treatment.

Warren's tragedy forced an unwelcome confrontation with a reality that the American church has spent decades avoiding: the church's dominant framework for understanding mental health is not merely inadequate. It is harmful. It has caused measurable damage to real people. It has driven the suffering away from the one community that claims, as its founding mission, to welcome the broken and bind their wounds.

The church has a mental health problem. Not merely in the sense that its members struggle with mental illness — though they do, at rates comparable to the general population. The church has a mental health problem in the sense that its theology, its culture, and its institutional practices have made it one of the worst places in American life for a person struggling with mental illness to seek help.

The Damage of Spiritual Bypassing

Spiritual bypassing is the use of spiritual beliefs and practices to avoid confronting painful emotions, unresolved psychological wounds, or legitimate mental health conditions. In the church, it takes predictable forms. A person struggling with clinical depression is told to "pray harder," "trust God more," or "find their joy in the Lord." A person experiencing anxiety is told that anxiety is a sin — a failure of faith — and that the solution is repentance rather than treatment. A person with PTSD is told to "give it to God" and "let go of the past." A person considering medication is warned that pills are a crutch, that true Christians rely on God alone, that seeking help from a therapist is a sign of spiritual weakness.

These responses are not well-intentioned but misguided. They are destructive. They compound the suffering of the person seeking help by adding a layer of spiritual shame to their psychological pain. The depressed person is now depressed and convinced that their depression is evidence of spiritual failure. The anxious person is now anxious and guilty about being anxious. The person in crisis is now in crisis and afraid to seek professional help because their faith community has told them that doing so would be a betrayal of God.

The theology behind spiritual bypassing is simple and wrong. It assumes that all human suffering is spiritual in origin and therefore amenable to spiritual solutions. If you are depressed, the reasoning goes, the root cause must be a spiritual deficiency — insufficient faith, unconfessed sin, distance from God. The solution, therefore, is spiritual: more prayer, more Scripture, more church involvement, more faith. If the depression persists, the implication is clear: you have not prayed enough, believed enough, or surrendered enough. The failure is yours.

This framework is not merely bad psychology. It is bad theology. It attributes to sin what is often attributable to neurochemistry, trauma, genetics, or the ordinary brokenness of the human condition. It treats the brain as the one organ exempt from the fall — the one part of human experience where physical malfunction is impossible and spiritual failure is the only explanation. A church that would never tell a diabetic to pray instead of taking insulin routinely tells the depressed to pray instead of seeking treatment. The inconsistency is glaring. The cost is measured in suffering, isolation, and, in the most devastating cases, lives lost.

The False Dichotomy

The church's resistance to mental health treatment is rooted in a false dichotomy: the belief that faith and therapy, prayer and medication, spiritual care and clinical care are competing rather than complementary. This dichotomy has no basis in Scripture, no basis in the Christian theological tradition, and no basis in the observable reality of how human beings are constituted.

Human beings are integrated wholes — body, mind, and spirit inextricably woven together. This is not a concession to secular anthropology. It is a biblical claim. The Hebrew word nephesh, often translated "soul," denotes the whole person — the embodied, thinking, feeling, relational creature that God formed from dust and breath. There is no biblical warrant for treating the spiritual dimension of human experience as separable from the physical and psychological dimensions. A person struggling with depression is not experiencing a purely spiritual crisis. They are experiencing a crisis of the whole person — a crisis that may involve neurochemistry, life circumstances, relational wounds, existential questions, and spiritual dimensions all at once.

Effective care for the whole person requires multiple forms of intervention. A depressed person may need medication to address the neurochemical dimensions of their illness. They may need therapy to process the relational and experiential dimensions. They may need spiritual direction, prayer, and community to address the existential and spiritual dimensions. These are not competing treatments. They are complementary dimensions of care for an integrated human being. The church that insists on spiritual solutions alone is not treating the whole person. It is treating a fraction of the person while ignoring the rest — and calling this truncated care "faith."

What the Bible Actually Says

The church's approach to mental health is ironic in the extreme, because the Bible it claims to follow contains some of the most honest, unvarnished depictions of mental anguish in all of literature.

David, the man after God's own heart, wrote psalms of such raw psychological distress that any contemporary therapist would recognize the symptoms of clinical depression. "My bones wasted away through my groaning all day long," he writes in Psalm 32. "I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears," he writes in Psalm 6. "Why are you cast down, O my soul? Why are you in turmoil within me?" he asks in Psalm 42 — a question that names, with remarkable psychological precision, the experience of depression as a state that the sufferer can observe but not control.

Elijah, after his greatest prophetic victory on Mount Carmel, collapsed into a depression so severe that he asked God to take his life. "It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life," he said in 1 Kings 19. God's response is instructive. God did not rebuke Elijah for lack of faith. God did not deliver a sermon on the sin of despair. God sent an angel with food and water and told Elijah to sleep. God addressed the physical needs of the prophet's body before addressing the spiritual needs of his soul. The first act of divine care for a depressed man was not a Bible study. It was a meal and a nap.

Jeremiah, the weeping prophet, expressed such sustained anguish that his writings have given the English language the word "jeremiad." "Cursed be the day on which I was born," he wrote in Jeremiah 20:14 — a statement that, in a contemporary church context, would likely prompt a referral to the pastor rather than inclusion in the canon of Scripture. Job sat in ashes and cursed the day of his birth. Jonah asked God to kill him. The psalmist in Psalm 88 — the darkest psalm in the Psalter — ends without resolution, without comfort, without the expected turn to hope. "Darkness is my closest friend," it concludes. The Bible includes that psalm. The church should learn from its inclusion.

The biblical witness does not treat mental anguish as a moral failing. It treats it as a human reality — one that can coexist with deep faith, prophetic calling, and intimate relationship with God. The church's insistence on treating mental illness as a spiritual deficiency is not a biblical position. It is a betrayal of the Bible's own testimony.

The God who sent an angel with bread for a suicidal prophet did not ask Elijah to pray harder. The church should take the hint.

Trauma-Informed Ministry

Trauma-informed ministry begins with a simple recognition: a significant number of the people sitting in church pews on any given Sunday are carrying the effects of traumatic experiences — abuse, neglect, violence, loss, abandonment, betrayal — that shape how they hear the gospel, how they experience community, and how they relate to God. A church that is not aware of this reality will inadvertently retraumatize the people it is trying to help.

Consider the standard evangelical altar call. A preacher asks people to come forward, publicly, in front of the entire congregation, to confess their brokenness and surrender to God. For many people, this is a meaningful and genuine spiritual experience. For a survivor of sexual abuse — for whom public vulnerability was precisely the mechanism of their violation — this invitation may trigger a trauma response. The church, without knowing it, has reenacted the dynamics of the survivor's abuse in a spiritual register.

Trauma-informed ministry does not abandon the gospel. It delivers the gospel with awareness of how it will be received by wounded people. It trains pastors and lay leaders to recognize the signs of trauma. It creates multiple pathways for response that do not require public vulnerability. It ensures that counseling ministries are staffed by people with actual training, not merely good intentions. It maintains clear boundaries around confidentiality, physical contact, and the use of authority. It recognizes that spiritual care and clinical care are partners, not competitors, and it builds relationships with licensed mental health professionals to whom it can refer people whose needs exceed its competence.

This is not a capitulation to secular psychology. It is an application of the biblical mandate to love one's neighbor — a mandate that requires caring enough about the neighbor's actual experience to learn how to help without doing harm.

Becoming Places of Healing

The church has the potential to be one of the most powerful resources for mental health in American life. It has what no clinical practice can offer: a sustained community of care that extends beyond the fifty-minute therapeutic hour, a framework of meaning that addresses the existential dimensions of suffering, rituals and practices that orient the sufferer toward hope without demanding premature resolution, and a theological tradition that insists — against every culture of toxic positivity — that suffering is real, that lament is faithful, and that God is present in the darkness.

To realize this potential, the church must first do no harm. It must stop treating mental illness as a spiritual failing. It must stop offering spiritual solutions to clinical problems. It must stop stigmatizing therapy, medication, and professional mental health care. It must stop pretending that prayer and Bible study are sufficient responses to clinical depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, PTSD, and the full spectrum of mental health conditions that affect its members.

Then it must take positive steps. Train pastoral staff in mental health first aid. Build relationships with licensed therapists and counselors in the community. Create support groups for people living with mental illness and their families. Preach honestly about mental health — not as a special topic for a designated Sunday but as an integrated dimension of the church's ongoing pastoral care. Normalize the language of mental health in the same way the church has normalized the language of physical health. When someone says, "I am seeing a therapist," the response should be the same as when someone says, "I am seeing a doctor": support, not suspicion.

The church that tells a depressed person to pray harder is not exercising spiritual authority. It is exercising spiritual malpractice. And the most faithful thing it can do — the thing most consistent with the example of a God who sent bread to a suicidal prophet and let the darkest psalm stand in the canon without resolution — is to sit with the suffering, take it seriously, and offer every resource available to address it. Spiritual and clinical. Prayer and treatment. Community and competence. The whole response for the whole person.

That is not a compromise of faith. It is faith doing what faith is for.
excerpt: The church that tells a depressed person to pray harder is not offering spiritual counsel. It is practicing spiritual malpractice. And the Bible it claims to follow knows better.

title: Toxic Masculinity in the Pulpit
body:
In 2006, Mark Driscoll stood before a conference of pastors and declared that the problem with the American church was that it had become too feminine. The church needed men, he argued — real men, tough men, men who would fight and lead and dominate. He mocked pastors who were gentle, who wept, who preferred diplomacy to confrontation. He described Jesus as a cage fighter, an alpha male, a warrior who would return at the end of days to deliver divine violence. The message was clear: godly manhood was aggressive, confrontational, and unapologetically dominant. Anything else was weakness. Anything else was feminization. Anything else was failure.

Driscoll was not an outlier. He was the loudest voice in a movement that had been building for decades — a movement that defined masculinity in terms of power, authority, and control, and that located these qualities at the center of God's design for men. John Eldredge's Wild at Heart, published in 2001 and eventually selling over four million copies, told men that they were designed to be warriors, adventurers, and rescuers — and that the modern church, with its emphasis on gentleness, servanthood, and emotional vulnerability, had stolen their masculine identity. The Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood, founded in 1987, codified a vision of gender in which male leadership and female submission were presented as the eternal, unchangeable order of creation.

The result was a theology of masculinity that bore almost no resemblance to the man at the center of the Christian story. It looked, instead, remarkably like the cultural ideal of the American alpha male — competitive, dominant, emotionally controlled, sexually aggressive — dressed in theological clothing and marketed as God's original design.

The Driscoll Playbook

Mark Driscoll built Mars Hill Church in Seattle from a handful of people meeting in a living room to over fourteen thousand weekly attendees in fifteen years. His appeal was concentrated among young men — a demographic that most churches struggled to reach. He succeeded by offering them a Christianity that affirmed the version of masculinity they already held: aggressive, competitive, uncompromising, and contemptuous of softness in any form.

Driscoll's preaching was laced with the language of domination. He publicly humiliated men he considered insufficiently masculine. He described stay-at-home fathers as failures. He joked about men who displayed emotion. He wielded theological authority as a weapon, framing disagreement with his leadership as rebellion against God. Former elders and staff members have described a culture of intimidation, bullying, and spiritual coercion in which Driscoll's word was effectively law and dissent was treated as disloyalty.

The Mars Hill experiment ended in 2014, when the accumulated weight of Driscoll's behavior — plagiarism, financial impropriety, bullying, abuse of authority — finally exceeded what the institution could sustain. The church dissolved. Its campuses closed. Thousands of members were scattered, many of them deeply wounded by an experience they had been told was biblical Christianity.

But Driscoll did not disappear. He moved to Arizona and planted a new church, which grew rapidly. The market for his version of masculinity had not diminished. It had, if anything, expanded — fueled by a broader cultural anxiety about masculinity that Driscoll was positioned to exploit. The pattern repeated itself, with new allegations of authoritarian leadership, staff abuse, and institutional control emerging from the new church. The product had not changed. It did not need to. The demand was still there.

The Warrior-Poet Myth

Eldredge's Wild at Heart offered a softer version of the same essential message. Men, Eldredge argued, are hardwired for three things: a battle to fight, an adventure to live, and a beauty to rescue. These desires are not cultural constructions but divine implants — the fingerprints of God on the male soul. The modern church, Eldredge argued, had domesticated men, turning them into "really nice guys" who had lost touch with their primal masculine energy.

The appeal is understandable. Many men in the church do feel that their experience is not reflected in the prevailing culture of evangelical Christianity — a culture that often emphasizes emotional expression, relational intimacy, and gentle compliance in ways that feel foreign to their lived experience of masculinity. Eldredge gave these men permission to be something other than domesticated — to embrace risk, physicality, and strength as features, not bugs, of their masculine design.

The problem is not the affirmation of masculine energy per se. The problem is the definition of masculine energy that Eldredge assumes. The warrior-poet framework draws its vision of manhood not from the life of Christ but from romantic mythology, Hollywood action narratives, and Jungian archetypes. The "battle" is framed in terms of conquest and competition. The "adventure" is framed in terms of individual heroism. The "beauty" is framed in terms of rescue — positioning women as objects to be saved rather than agents in their own right. The entire framework is self-referential: it centers male experience, male desire, and male self-actualization. The other — whether woman, neighbor, or God — exists primarily as a mirror for the man's heroic arc.

Jesus does not appear in this framework except as an afterthought — a divine endorsement of the masculine ideal the author has already constructed. And the Jesus who does appear is selectively edited: the Jesus who overturned tables makes the cut, but the Jesus who washed feet does not. The Jesus who confronted the Pharisees makes the cut, but the Jesus who wept at Lazarus's tomb is treated as an anomaly rather than a revelation.

What Biblical Manhood Actually Looks Like

The New Testament presents a vision of manhood that is, by the standards of both first-century Mediterranean culture and twenty-first-century American culture, profoundly countercultural. It does not affirm the alpha-male ideal. It crucifies it.

Jesus wept. Publicly. At the tomb of a friend. In a culture where male tears were a sign of weakness, Jesus wept without apology, without explanation, without the macho caveat that he was only crying because he was about to do something powerful. He wept because his friend was dead and grief was the appropriate response to death. The Son of God modeled emotional vulnerability as an expression of strength, not a lapse from it.

Jesus washed feet. The act of a slave — the lowest act of service in the ancient household — performed by the one who held all authority. He knelt before his disciples, took off his outer garment, and did the work that no self-respecting man would do. And when Peter objected — when Peter displayed the masculine instinct to refuse the humiliation of being served — Jesus told him that unless he accepted it, he had no part in the kingdom. The kingdom's definition of greatness was not power exercised over others but service rendered to others. "The greatest among you shall be your servant," Jesus said. He was not speaking metaphorically.

Jesus refused violence. In the Garden of Gethsemane, when Peter drew a sword to defend him, Jesus told him to put it away. "Those who live by the sword will die by the sword." He submitted to arrest, trial, torture, and execution without resistance — not because he lacked power but because the kingdom he embodied operated on fundamentally different terms than the kingdoms of the world. The cross is not a warrior's victory. It is a servant's sacrifice. And it is the central symbol of the faith that the toxic masculinity movement claims to represent.

Paul's vision of manhood is consistent with Jesus' example. The fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — reads like a deliberate inversion of the warrior-male ideal. Gentleness is listed as a spiritual virtue, not a feminine weakness. Self-control is valued over aggression. Patience is prized over decisive action. The man shaped by the Spirit looks nothing like the man shaped by the Driscoll playbook. He looks, instead, like someone whose strength is expressed in service, whose authority is exercised in humility, and whose courage is demonstrated not in domination but in vulnerability.

The church does not need more alpha males. It needs more men willing to do what Jesus did: kneel, serve, weep, and absorb the world's violence rather than return it.

The Damage Done

The toxic masculinity movement in the church has caused damage in every direction. It has damaged women, who have been told that their role is to submit, support, and admire — and that resistance to male authority is resistance to God. Women in churches shaped by this theology report feeling invisible, silenced, and instrumentalized — valued for their compliance rather than their gifts, their beauty rather than their wisdom, their willingness to serve male vision rather than their capacity to lead in their own right.

It has damaged men, who have been given a vision of manhood that is impossible to sustain without constant performance and self-suppression. Men who do not fit the alpha-male template — men who are gentle, artistic, emotionally expressive, contemplative — are made to feel that their masculinity is deficient, that they are not the men God designed them to be. The suicide rate among men, the epidemic of male loneliness, the crisis of male emotional illiteracy — these are not unrelated to a cultural and religious framework that tells men their value lies in dominance and their vulnerability is weakness.

It has damaged families, where the theology of male headship has been used to justify patterns of control, emotional abuse, and domestic violence. Not every complementarian household is abusive. But a theology that locates final authority in the husband and frames wifely submission as a divine mandate provides structural cover for abuse when it occurs. The wife who questions her husband's authority can be told she is disobeying God. The husband who controls his wife can frame his control as spiritual leadership. The children who grow up in these households learn that power is gendered, that authority flows in one direction, and that the strongest person in the room is, by definition, the one God has placed in charge.

It has damaged the church's witness. A church that preaches a gospel of sacrificial love while modeling a culture of masculine domination is not merely inconsistent. It is unintelligible. The watching world sees the contradiction even when the church does not. And the watching world draws the obvious conclusion: the church's gospel is not powerful enough to transform its own culture.

Healthy Masculinity in Pastoral Leadership

Healthy masculinity in the pulpit does not require the abandonment of strength, courage, or conviction. It requires the redefinition of these qualities in light of the gospel rather than in light of cultural mythology.

Strength, in the gospel, is the capacity to bear the weight of another's suffering without flinching — not the capacity to impose one's will. Courage is the willingness to be vulnerable, to admit error, to name one's own sin before naming others' — not the willingness to dominate a room. Conviction is fidelity to the truth even when the truth is costly — not the rhetorical force to shout down disagreement.

A pastor who leads with healthy masculinity creates space for others rather than filling it himself. He listens more than he speaks. He asks questions rather than issuing pronouncements. He shares power rather than hoarding it. He admits what he does not know. He models emotional honesty — not the performed vulnerability of the confessional sermon illustration but the genuine, unscripted honesty of a man who has learned that his authority does not depend on his perfection.

He holds his authority lightly, knowing that it belongs to God, not to him. He exercises discipline when necessary — but with grief, not satisfaction. He confronts sin — but his own first. He leads — but toward the cross, not toward the throne.

This is not weakness. It is the hardest kind of strength. The strength to serve rather than dominate. The strength to absorb rather than inflict. The strength to follow a Savior who demonstrated, in the most definitive way possible, that the way up is down, the way to power is through service, and the way to life is through death.

The church that grasps this will not need to manufacture masculine energy or market warrior theology. It will have something far more compelling: men who look like Jesus. And that — not aggression, not domination, not the swagger of the celebrity pastor — is what the world has never seen enough of and has always, whether it knows it or not, been waiting for.
excerpt: The church that confuses aggression with authority and domination with leadership has not recovered biblical manhood. It has baptized the very thing the gospel came to crucify.

title: Colonialism and Missions
body:
On mission Sundays in American churches, the story is always the same. Brave missionaries cross oceans and jungles to bring the gospel to people who have never heard it. The emphasis is on sacrifice, heroism, and the life-altering power of the Christian message. Slides show smiling children. Testimonies recount dramatic conversions. The offering plate circulates with a special appeal for the unreached. It is a stirring narrative. It is also, in its selective telling, a profoundly dishonest one.

The parts we do not tell on mission Sundays are the parts that matter most for understanding why the word "missionary" carries, in much of the non-Western world, connotations not of love but of destruction. The history of Christian missions is inseparable from the history of European colonialism. The gospel traveled in the holds of slave ships, in the baggage trains of conquering armies, in the administrative apparatus of colonial governments that used Christianity as a tool of cultural subjugation. This does not mean that every missionary was a colonialist, or that every conversion was coerced, or that the gospel itself is reducible to its colonial carriers. But it means that any honest reckoning with the history of Christian missions must contend with the entanglement of the gospel with empire — an entanglement that was not incidental but structural, not accidental but theological.

The Doctrine of Discovery

In 1452, Pope Nicholas V issued the papal bull Dum Diversas, authorizing King Alfonso V of Portugal to "invade, search out, capture, vanquish, and subdue" all non-Christians, to reduce them to perpetual slavery, and to take their possessions and lands. In 1493, Pope Alexander VI issued Inter Caetera, granting Spain sovereignty over the lands Columbus had "discovered" in the Western Hemisphere. These documents — collectively known as the Doctrine of Discovery — provided the theological foundation for European colonialism. They established the principle that Christian nations had a divinely sanctioned right to claim sovereignty over non-Christian lands and peoples.

The Doctrine of Discovery was not a marginal theological opinion. It was official church teaching, ratified by papal authority and implemented by Christian governments across Europe. It provided the legal and theological basis for the conquest of the Americas, the colonization of Africa and Asia, the displacement and destruction of indigenous peoples on every continent. It was cited in U.S. Supreme Court decisions — notably Johnson v. McIntosh (1823) — as the foundation of American property law. Its effects are not historical curiosities. They are structural features of the world we inhabit.

The theological logic of the Doctrine of Discovery rested on a simple premise: non-Christian peoples were, by virtue of their unbelief, less than fully human and therefore incapable of legitimate sovereignty over their own lands and lives. The gospel was not offered as an invitation but wielded as a justification — a theological mechanism for transferring the wealth, land, and autonomy of non-Christian peoples to Christian ones. The cross was not separate from the conquest. It was the conquest's authorization.

Residential Schools and Forced Conversion

The residential school system — implemented in the United States, Canada, Australia, and other settler-colonial states — represents one of the most devastating intersections of Christianity and colonialism. In Canada alone, over 150,000 indigenous children were removed from their families and placed in church-run residential schools between the 1880s and the 1990s. The schools were operated by Catholic, Anglican, United, and Presbyterian churches with government funding and government sanction. Their explicit purpose, in the words of one Canadian official, was to "kill the Indian in the child."

Children were forbidden to speak their languages, practice their spiritual traditions, or maintain contact with their families. They were given Christian names, forced to attend Christian worship, and punished — often severely — for any expression of their indigenous identity. Physical abuse, sexual abuse, malnutrition, and medical neglect were widespread. Thousands of children died in the schools. Many were buried in unmarked graves. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, which spent six years documenting the system's history, called it "cultural genocide."

The churches that operated these schools did so in the sincere belief that they were saving souls. This sincerity does not mitigate the harm. It deepens it. The damage was done not by people who cynically exploited Christianity for colonial purposes but by people who genuinely believed that the destruction of indigenous culture was a necessary condition for indigenous salvation. The theology was the problem. A theology that cannot distinguish between conversion and cultural destruction, between the gospel and the erasure of identity, between salvation and assimilation is a theology that has lost its way so completely that its sincerity makes it more dangerous, not less.

The pattern extends far beyond North America. In Australia, the Stolen Generations — Aboriginal children forcibly removed from their families and placed in church-run institutions — suffered similar abuses. In Africa, missionaries frequently served as advance agents for colonial governments, establishing schools and hospitals that, however beneficial in their immediate effects, functioned within a colonial framework that undermined indigenous social structures, political systems, and spiritual traditions. In Latin America, the Spanish encomienda system granted colonizers the right to indigenous labor in exchange for Christian instruction — a system that amounted, in practice, to enslavement under a theological veneer.

The Indigenous Christian Response

The relationship between indigenous peoples and Christianity is not, however, a simple story of victimization. Indigenous Christians have, from the beginning, engaged the gospel on their own terms — accepting what resonated with their traditions, rejecting what was merely colonial, and creating forms of Christian faith that are rooted in indigenous soil rather than transplanted from European greenhouses.

Liberation theology — born in Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s — emerged from the experience of colonized peoples who read the Bible and found in it not the justification for their oppression but the resources for their liberation. Gustavo Gutierrez, the Peruvian theologian who gave the movement its name, argued that the God of the Bible is a God who takes the side of the poor, the oppressed, and the marginalized — not the side of their oppressors, however Christian those oppressors may claim to be. The Exodus narrative, the prophetic tradition, the Magnificat of Mary, the Sermon on the Mount — all of these point toward a God whose justice flows downward, toward the bottom, toward the people the powerful have forgotten.

Richard Twiss, a Lakota/Sicangu member of the Rosebud Sioux tribe and a Christian theologian, spent his life articulating an indigenous Christian theology that refused the colonial binary — the assumption that becoming Christian required ceasing to be indigenous. Twiss argued that indigenous cultural forms — drumming, dance, ceremony, artistic expression — could be legitimate vehicles for Christian worship, just as European cultural forms — organ music, Gothic architecture, clerical vestments — had always been. The gospel, he insisted, is translatable into every culture precisely because it belongs to none of them. The colonial error was not the introduction of the gospel to indigenous peoples but the insistence that the gospel could only be received in European packaging.

In Africa, the independent church movement — churches founded and led by Africans, free from European missionary control — has produced some of the most vibrant and creative expressions of Christianity in the world. These churches draw on African cultural resources — communal worship, ancestor awareness, healing practices, oral tradition — in ways that European missionaries would not have sanctioned. They represent not a departure from Christianity but a decolonization of it — a refusal to accept the colonial premise that African culture is incompatible with Christian faith.

The gospel does not require the destruction of culture. It requires the transformation of culture. And the people best equipped to lead that transformation are the people whose culture it is — not the foreigners who arrive with the answers already written.

How to Do Missions Without Colonialism

The colonial model of missions was built on a set of assumptions that the church must name and reject. The assumption that the missionary brings God to a place where God is absent — as if the Creator of all things had no presence among the peoples he created before the missionary arrived. The assumption that Western culture is the natural container for the gospel — as if the faith born in Palestine, shaped by Greek philosophy, preserved by Middle Eastern monks, and carried to Europe by North African theologians was inherently European. The assumption that the missionary's role is to teach and the indigenous person's role is to learn — as if the encounter between the gospel and a new culture were a one-way transmission rather than a mutual discovery.

Partnership models of mission begin with a different set of assumptions. They assume that God is already at work in every culture and that the missionary's first task is not to speak but to listen — to discern what God has been doing before the missionary arrived. They assume that the indigenous community is not a passive recipient of the gospel but an active participant in its interpretation and embodiment. They assume that the gospel will take forms in the new culture that the missionary could not have predicted and may not recognize — and that this is not a failure of the mission but its success.

Concrete practices follow from these assumptions. Short-term mission trips, as commonly practiced, should be radically reconceived. The typical short-term trip — in which a group of American teenagers spends a week painting an orphanage, taking selfies with local children, and returning home with a story about how the experience "changed their perspective" — is, at best, a form of spiritual tourism. At worst, it reinforces the colonial dynamic: wealthy outsiders arrive, perform charity, extract emotional benefit, and leave. The local community is not transformed. The visitors are not formed. And a great deal of money that could have funded local workers has been spent on airfare.

Long-term mission work, when it is done well, looks like partnership. It means working under indigenous leadership rather than over it. It means funding local organizations rather than building parallel structures. It means learning the language, the culture, the history, and the theological categories of the community being served — not as a prerequisite for preaching but as a form of respect for the people being encountered. It means being willing to receive as well as give, to learn as well as teach, to be changed as well as to change.

It means, ultimately, doing what the incarnation itself demonstrates: entering another's world on their terms, not your own. God did not send the gospel from a distance. God entered human culture, took on human flesh, spoke a human language, ate human food, lived within the constraints of a particular time and place. The incarnation is the model for all Christian mission: not the imposition of one culture on another but the translation of the gospel into the idiom of the community it encounters.

The church cannot undo the damage of colonial missions. The children who died in residential schools cannot be brought back. The cultures that were destroyed cannot be fully recovered. The trust that was violated cannot be easily rebuilt. But the church can tell the truth about what happened. It can repent of the theological errors that made it possible. It can commit to forms of mission that honor the dignity, agency, and cultural integrity of the communities it serves. And it can listen — genuinely, humbly, without defensiveness — to the voices of those who bear the scars of its history.

That listening is not optional. It is the beginning of the repentance the church owes to the peoples it harmed in Christ's name. And it is the only foundation on which a genuinely Christian practice of mission can be rebuilt — a practice that carries the cross without the sword, that offers the gospel without demanding the surrender of identity, and that trusts the Spirit to do what missionaries, in their colonial confidence, always believed only they could do: bring the good news to life in soil that is not their own.
excerpt: The cross arrived in the colonies alongside the sword. The church has spent centuries celebrating the gospel's spread while refusing to examine the wreckage it left behind. That refusal is itself a theological failure.

title: What Christians Can Learn From Judaism
body:
Jesus was Jewish. This statement is so obvious that it should not need saying, and so consistently ignored in its implications that it cannot be said often enough. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day. He was presented at the temple according to the law of Moses. He attended synagogue. He observed the feasts. He wore tzitzit. He debated Torah with rabbis. He quoted the Psalms from the cross. The prayer he taught his disciples — the Lord's Prayer — is structured on Jewish liturgical patterns. The meal he shared on his last night — the Last Supper — was a Passover seder. The faith that Christians call their own was born inside Judaism, shaped by Jewish categories, expressed in Jewish idiom, and proclaimed by Jewish apostles to a world that had no framework for understanding it apart from the Jewish story of God, creation, covenant, and redemption.

And yet, within a few centuries, Christianity had not merely distinguished itself from Judaism but defined itself against it. The synagogue became the enemy. The Torah became the old dispensation, superseded and surpassed. The people of Israel became the people who had rejected their own Messiah — a rejection that, in the hands of Christian theologians from John Chrysostom to Martin Luther, justified centuries of persecution, forced conversion, ghettoization, and, in its most catastrophic expression, the theological soil in which the Holocaust took root.

The recovery of Christianity's Jewish roots is not a matter of interfaith politeness. It is a matter of theological survival. A Christianity severed from Judaism is a Christianity that has lost access to the intellectual, spiritual, and moral resources of its own foundation. And the things that Judaism preserves — things that Christianity has largely forgotten — are precisely the things that the contemporary church most desperately needs.

Torah Study as a Way of Life

In Judaism, the study of Torah is not preparation for something else. It is the thing itself. The Talmud Torah — the study of Torah — is considered one of the highest forms of worship, an act of devotion that is its own reward. The Talmud teaches that the study of Torah is equal to all the other commandments combined. This is not because Judaism is a religion of the intellect rather than the heart. It is because Judaism understands that the intellect and the heart are not separable — that the rigorous, disciplined engagement with a sacred text is itself a form of encounter with the God who gave it.

The contrast with contemporary evangelical Christianity is stark. In much of American Christianity, the Bible is a resource to be mined for principles, a sourcebook for sermon illustrations, a collection of promises to be claimed. It is rarely studied with the kind of sustained, rigorous, communal attention that characterizes Jewish Torah study.
